folkways.japan: Reflects 1960s Japan: the San'ya day-labor district, juvenile reformatories, the postwar economic boom and its losers, the boxing world of Korakuen Hall, and ideals of endurance (gaman) and sincerity; Chiba tied it to the national effort to recover after the war (Peter Tasker). Kim Yong-bi's arc brings in the Korean War.

delivery.evidence: Noriko states the case against boxing and is treated sympathetically; Rikiishi, Carlos and Mendoza are given dignity and motives; the creators left the ending open (Wikipedia; Tokyo Dome interview).
delivery.note: The message is carried by Joe's fights and their cost rather than stated as a moral; Joe's own wish to burn to white ash is the nearest thing to a thesis.

personified.ideology: Burn out completely for a passion
Faith in a protege; redemption through purpose

31303.dominant: Existentialism (total commitment as meaning), Bushido / honor code (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Marxism (class struggle, explored).

87442.heading: Astra Lost in Space
87442.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: A Japanese school-trip framing, high-pressure parents who see children as extensions of family image (Yun-Hua's famous mother, Kanata's athlete father), and the Jump ideal of friendship and effort; the setting itself is multinational and the plot model is French (Verne).

delivery.evidence: The message arrives through mystery reveals and character backstories; Kanata states it once plainly when he tells the crew they are a family (ch. 34). folkways.japan: Loyalty to a superior who becomes a lifelong commander, Levi's obsession with cleaning (ch. 3) and the barracks discipline reflect Japanese school and workplace norms; the title's "kui naki sentaku" (a choice without regret) is a common Japanese phrase of resolve. delivery.evidence: The title states the theme, and Erwin speaks it at the end (ch. 8; Wikipedia OVA summary). Lovof is a flat villain; Levi's objections are given real weight before he yields.

53390.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
53390.label: From summaries
53390.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown to bring understanding, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-sacrifice for friends; the dignity of the enemy shown from inside Marley; forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi).
frames.concerns: A "devil" origin myth; no hope beyond death; a suicide attempt (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Repentance as a long road (Reiner, Gabi); the burden of killing even in war.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact imagery may be a concern where evil spirits are taken as real; no transcendent hope. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Clear picture of sin passed down and of human evil; sacrifice for others; revenge shown to destroy. Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact as myth; no gospel answer.

frames.aligns: Christian writers draw out sin, sacrifice and overcoming evil with good (Thirst.sg and Christ and Pop Culture titles; not opened). Depicts a mass killer without endorsing him.
frames.concerns: Nihilistic voices (Kenny, Zeke); a hero who becomes a mass killer needs careful reading.

frames.aligns: Longing for freedom and deliverance; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": power from a pact with a "devil" (ch. 122); Paths and a spirit world binding a people.

frames.aligns: Realism about total depravity: no one is innocent, including the heroes. Common grace lets readers value the art and its questions.
frames.concerns: Little answer beyond human effort; a suicide attempt (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms questions: governments lie and wage war, yet order matters. Law exposes guilt (Reiner, Gabi).
frames.concerns: Little gospel (forgiveness is human, not divine). LCMS and ELCA families may weigh the content differently.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace glimpsed in former enemies changing (Gabi, Reiner); social holiness against ethnic hatred.
frames.concerns: Profanity; no transcendent hope. Holiness churches more cautious about the content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just-war tradition (Article 37) fits the story's questions; forgiveness of enemies; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Suicide attempt; no transcendent hope. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on the gender questions.

frames.aligns: Violence is not shown as heroic in the end: it is a cycle that corrupts everyone, and the ending sides with Armin's choice to talk rather than kill.
frames.concerns: Most conflicts are still settled by force; children trained as soldiers. Old Order and conservative groups avoid most popular media regardless; MC USA families may read it as an anti-war text.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice and family love; repentance of former enemies.
frames.concerns: Eren's preemptive war; no afterlife hope; a suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Death shown as final rather than as roaming spirits; the cost of hatred; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: The Paths and a "devil" origin myth. Glorified violence is a concern, though the story does not glorify it in the end.

frames.aligns: Christian neutrality echoed: war and nationalism are shown to destroy everyone; honesty about guilt.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact myth; the military as the main path for the heroes.

frames.aligns: Understanding ends hatred; fear shown as the root of violence.
frames.concerns: Evil, fear and death shown as overwhelming realities; despair.

frames.aligns: Peace-and-justice reading: a critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics' concern that Holocaust imagery is used carelessly (New Republic, JTA); a female lead centered on a man.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution and the cost of dehumanization; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Armbands, internment zones and a "euthanasia" plan echo the Holocaust (ch. 86-88, 114); some see antisemitic tropes (Eldians as a "devil" people whose blood carries power). Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution; self-defense debated; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Split on whether the Eldian story honors or distorts Holocaust memory (JTA); Jewish dignity is a stated family concern.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: critique of ethnonationalism and dehumanization.
frames.concerns: Attention to antisemitism and stereotypes: some Jewish fans quoted by JTA felt the Holocaust was reduced to a trope, while Israeli scholars in the same piece read it as about Japanese militarism.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; courage; the horror of killing innocents is not hidden; collective guilt rejected.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact as source of power; spiked wine; a suicide attempt (forbidden). Titan nudity is non-sexual.

frames.aligns: Dharma and righteous war are central questions; karma-like cycles of action and consequence across generations.
frames.concerns: Children as soldiers; Eren's certainty without dharma.

frames.aligns: The cycle of hatred and revenge is the core theme; attachment and fear drive suffering; the ending sides with non-hatred.
frames.concerns: Despair; a suicide attempt; spiked wine (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Harmony with others restored only through sincerity; ancestors' burdens.
frames.concerns: No sacred framing; impurity of death everywhere.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; anger and ego shown to destroy (Eren); equality of all people against ethnic hatred.

frames.aligns: Each side gets a fair hearing; Ymir's origin and the Paths stay a mystery; the ending leaves readers to weigh Eren rather than handing down a verdict.
frames.concerns: Readers disagree sharply on what it endorses, so younger readers may need help with the nationalism and genocide themes.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fairness to the enemy once you know them, and the dead honored by those who carry on (Erwin, ch. 80; Hange, ch. 132).
frames.concerns: Graphic violence, the death of most of humanity in the Rumbling and an epilogue where war returns can feel hopeless.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Eren's vow of revenge (ch. 1-2) drives the plot, but the story shows revenge spreading hatred (Gabi kills Sasha, ch. 105) and honors forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi). The ending sides with Armin's dialogue over vengeance (ch. 138-139).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Freedom is the core value: birds and the world beyond the walls; choosing so as not to regret it (vols. 5-8). Governments that lie are overthrown (Uprising arc, vols. 13-17). Eren's absolute freedom is shown as a trap (ch. 139), which keeps the position below the top.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to comrades is honored (Erwin, ch. 80; Hange, ch. 132), but blood loyalty is critiqued: Grisha uses Zeke, Historia defies her father, and ethnic "our people" thinking becomes the Rumbling. Closing hope rests on a cross-national alliance.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The Survey Corps chain of command (Erwin, Levi) is honored; the walled monarchy and the Church are overthrown (vols. 13-17); Marley's ethnic ranks and armbands are condemned (ch. 86-88).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The wall cult hides the truth (vol. 9, Uprising arc); the royal pacifism vow is shown as harmful; truth-seeking by Armin and Hange is honored. Faith appears as cult and myth (ch. 122), not as a guide the story endorses.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security and survival dominate a cruel world; courage, duty and sacrifice are honored (ch. 80, 132). Curiosity (the ocean, vol. 22) and Armin's answer to Zeke that small moments make life worth living (ch. 137, fan wiki) give self-expression a place.

folkways.japan: The military chain of command, duty and self-sacrifice for the group echo Japanese norms of group loyalty; producer George Wada linked the walls to the closed nature of Japanese society (Creator context). Critics also read the island-against-the-world story against Japan's wartime history, a reading Isayama has rejected.

delivery.evidence: New Republic (Amin) and Berkeley Political Review read a clear warning about fascism; no review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Characters state their positions on freedom, revenge and peace openly, and the story gives each side a hearing before its ending.

30142.heading: Battle Royale
30142.label: From summaries
30142.life_message: Even when a cruel state forces people to turn on each other, trust, loyalty and love are what keep you human, and the real enemy is the system that hands out the guns.

101625.heading: Berserk of Gluttony

folkways.japan: The European setting is a Japanese seinen artist's version of medieval Europe; the Hawks' loyalty to their leader and the bond of comrades echo Japanese school and work friendships Miura drew on (Wikipedia), while the critique of the church draws on European history.

delivery.evidence: Themes of fate, free will and religion are argued through characters (Guts, Griffith, Mozgus, Farnese; Wikipedia themes); Mozgus is deliberately one-sided (Miura via Wikipedia), while Griffith is given a strong case.

126135.heading: Bibliomania
126135.label: From summaries
126135.life_message: Perfect wish-worlds, whether fantasies, games or endless reading, can quietly devour a person, and a hunger to consume everything, even knowledge, becomes a monster; the imperfect real world, with its small joys and real people, is worth more than any dream that eats you.

folkways.japan: The guests embody Japanese social problems the creators name or show: ijime (bullying), hikikomori withdrawal, a father's demand to work, study and marry, and isolation of the sick; the work borrows a Western frame (Alice, biblical imagery) to examine them.

delivery.evidence: The serpent's defense of staying (the real world is pain) is given strongly by the guests themselves (ch. 5), and Alice answers it; the twist then turns her answer against her.
delivery.note: The message is carried by allegory and a final reveal rather than by narration; readers are invited to re-read.

31409.heading: Biomega
31409.label: From summaries
31409.life_message: One loyal protector and a few companions can carry hope for human beings through the end of the world, and no power has the right to force a "new humanity" on everyone else.

folkways.japan: Nihei's cyberpunk megastructures, corporate synthetic agents and silent, art-driven storytelling belong to the Japanese seinen science-fiction tradition of Akira and Ghost in the Shell (Wikipedia, Nihei); described here as context.

folkways.japan: A lone gunman who leaves his organization echoes the masterless samurai (ronin); friendship, rivals who become allies and mercy to a defeated foe are Weekly Shonen Jump staples. The Western-styled setting and gunfighter look borrow from American and Hong Kong action films; Manga Life found its restrained pacing closer to Western comics than to Japanese ones (via Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: The no-kill and anti-revenge lessons are taught through events (the paralysis bullet lesson, v7; taking Creed alive, VIZ v20); Creed is given a backstory of abuse but no persuasive case (fan wiki).
delivery.note: Both the ruling organization and the revolutionaries are shown as dangerous, with the hero standing apart from each; the message is carried by action and comedy rather than speeches.

86123.heading: Black Clover

frames.aligns: Social holiness: lifting up the poor and the excluded; works of mercy; former enemies who turn.
frames.concerns: The devil alliance; drinking played for laughs. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by how it frames good and evil, in a fantasy tradition (Tolkien's Lord of the Rings is among Tabata's influences, per Wikipedia); justice for the excluded.
frames.concerns: The devil alliance and inverted angel imagery; the nun gag. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on other questions.

frames.aligns: Care for outsiders, a community of misfits, forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Heroic violence is the main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Agency and effort; family, including adoptive family; service in a squad.
frames.concerns: Devil power and magic; fan service and drinking. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: A strong critique of class, birth and ethnic prejudice; the excluded become heroes; a church that shelters children.
frames.concerns: The nun gag and an early thin female cast (Anime Feminist); violence as the means.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, care for orphans, clear defeat of devils.
frames.concerns: Magic, witches and devil hosting throughout; the dead raised as Paladins conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Kindness to the poor, loyalty, hard work.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic are the basis of the whole world, and the hero's power comes from a demon (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting is the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Persistence, hope and love outlasting hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, devils and fear shown as real powers; magic as the source of strength.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan and stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18-19); honoring those who raised you; persistence.
frames.concerns: Magic (kishuf) and demon alliances are central; Kabbalistic terms (Qliphoth, Sephira) used as fantasy labels (from general knowledge; to verify); tzniut concerns with outfits and gags.

frames.aligns: Love of the stranger, social justice, reconciliation after a historic wrong (the elves).
frames.concerns: Magic and demons; Kabbalistic terms used as fantasy; modesty applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: dismantling prejudice by birth and nation; outsiders included; historic injustice remembered and repaired.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor, the orphan and the stranger; patience (sabr) and effort; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Magic (sihr) is central; the hero allies with a devil (shaytan) and fuses with it; angelic imagery used by the villain; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for outfits and gags.

frames.aligns: Effort and duty; a warrior who fights without hatred; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Some families read the constant fighting as tamasic; the birth-and-rank theme invites discussion families approach in different ways.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts and former enemies; Licht's hatred shown as suffering; craving for power (Lucius, the Dark Triad) leads to ruin.

frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as a fantasy device; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: help others, be industrious, do not murder; self-determination in Asta.

frames.aligns: Worth earned by effort and character, not birth or bloodline; solidarity across peoples; a self-styled savior rejected.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person regardless of birth or power; justice for the excluded; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Violence as the means; the nun gag.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rivalries and duels (Asta and Yuno, ch. 390-391) are friendly; revenge for the elves' massacre is shown as tragic, not honorable.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Magic Knights keep order, but misfits are free to be themselves in the Black Bulls.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family and squad first; service to the kingdom close behind.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Birth-rank is the main injustice; a commoner becomes Wizard King (ch. 391).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A church and old kingdoms honored; worth measured by effort.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Constant war, but characters' quirks and dreams are celebrated.

folkways.japan: Senpai-style mentoring by captains, loyalty to a squad and hard-work (ganbaru) perseverance are common Japanese shonen norms. The church, nuns and the European-fantasy kingdom are borrowed Western settings, and the Hino Country, Yami's homeland, is a Japan-like land seen from outside.

delivery.evidence: Asta and Yuno tell Lucius that a true Wizard King is one everyone admires, and Asta says his imperfect life belongs to him (fan wiki); no review opened addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Asta and his allies state the never-give-up and anti-discrimination themes aloud, while some snobbish rivals are later partly redeemed.

personified.ideology: Effort and loyalty can beat birth

86123.dominant: Progressivism (anti-discrimination), Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (as fantasy setting), Critical theory (class), Patriotism / nationalism (service to the kingdom).

31600.heading: Black Jack
31600.label: From summaries
31600.life_message: Every life is worth fighting for with all one's skill, whatever the law, the price or the odds, yet medicine cannot conquer death, and pride, greed and cruelty are the real diseases.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every life and opposition to euthanasia (CCC 2276-2279) carried by Black Jack against Kiriko; care for the poor; the limits of human power.
frames.concerns: Graphic surgery; occasional horror and supernatural cases; Black Jack's contempt for lawful authority.

frames.aligns: Healing as mercy (the Unmercenary physician saints treated the poor for free); humility before death.
frames.concerns: Gore; ghost stories.

frames.aligns: Sanctity of life; compassion for the poor; pride humbled.
frames.concerns: No God in the picture; gore; supernatural episodes; Pinoko's "wife" gag.

frames.aligns: Life worth saving at any cost; a gruff man whose acts show love.
frames.concerns: Graphic surgery; occasional occult elements.

frames.aligns: Healing and deliverance from despair.
frames.concerns: Ghosts, a cursed mummy and spirits; human skill as the only healer.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pride and reputation are punished; Black Jack ignores his own reputation.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules and licenses yield to conscience and skill.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Serves strangers worldwide; his own family is small (Pinoko) and his father absent.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The poor treated free, the arrogant humbled; status is the enemy.

folkways.japan: Tezuka's target is the hierarchy of Japanese university hospitals, the reticence and sense of duty of 1970s Japan and its postwar memory of war and nuclear weapons; Black Jack stands against those norms rather than within them (Village Voice quote on Vertical's page). The Star System, in which Tezuka reuses characters from his other works, appears throughout (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Each story ends on a moral turn; Tezuka stated the series is about doctors' dilemmas (Japanese Wikipedia); Kiriko is given real reasons for euthanasia.
delivery.note: Reviewers call some stories heavy-handed but say that suits Tezuka's young readers (Manga Bookshelf roundtable).

personified.ideology: A doctor must fight for every life

31600.dominant: Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Duty ethics, Existentialism.

30735.heading: Black Lagoon
30735.label: From summaries
30735.life_message: It holds up no settled good life: in a world without law the strong and the clever survive, but Rock's stubborn empathy argues that a person can keep some humanity, and even change others' fates for the better, without pretending the darkness away.

content.framing: Stylized and often relished as action; atrocities (torture, child killers, terror) shown as horror
Abuse condemned as the root of monsters; fan service and the sex trade shown without judgment

frames.aligns: The dignity of abused children shown through Rock's grief (ch. 15); revenge exposed as madness and mercy as healing in the Roberta arc (ch. 76); Nazis and traffickers condemned.
frames.concerns: Relativism with no moral center; the Rip-Off Church mocks religious life as a front; violence relished; Yukio's suicide (CCC 2280-2283) given tragic honor.

frames.aligns: A world of passions (wrath, avarice) shown as slavery; Rock's tears for Gretel as a glimpse of compassion.
frames.concerns: Wrath and despair made glamorous in Revy; no repentance or grace; the habit worn as a disguise.

frames.aligns: Sin shown with its fruit: abused children become killers, revenge nearly destroys Roberta; loyalty and protection of the weak.
frames.concerns: Profanity, drunkenness and crime as normal life; a church that sells guns; no gospel hope offered.

frames.aligns: An honest picture of a fallen world; Rock's conscience as a remnant of the image of God; ANN's Silverman sees survival and kindness as its themes.
frames.concerns: Gun violence as entertainment (Santos: its commentary amounts to shooting being cool); faith presented as a failure or a con.

frames.aligns: Bondage and trauma shown as real; Roberta's deliverance from her rage through love (ch. 76).
frames.concerns: Holiness concerns with profanity, drinking and the sex trade; the church as a criminal front; despair voiced by the abused.

frames.aligns: Total depravity unsparingly drawn; common grace in Rock's empathy and in Garcia's mercy; human schemes to control fate fail.
frames.concerns: Sin often made stylish; no acknowledgment of God's sovereignty beyond Chang's wry line about God's domain (ch. 116).

frames.aligns: The law's absence shows why order matters (Romans 13); vocation twisted: Rock's company abandons him (ch. 0-1).
frames.concerns: Crime as a calling; graphic violence; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Rock's works of mercy toward Garcia and Feng; social sin (trafficking, war) exposed.
frames.concerns: Holiness concerns on drinking, profanity and violence; no growth toward holiness for most of the cast.

frames.aligns: Moral ambiguity examined seriously in Rock's choices; the cost of revenge (ch. 44-76).
frames.concerns: Gratuitous violence and profanity; religious life parodied. Episcopal and ACNA families will differ.

frames.aligns: Rock prefers talk to guns; the crew's mutual aid.
frames.concerns: Violence as heroic competence is the series' core pleasure; separation from such media.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences shown hard; family love (Garcia and Roberta) as a saving bond.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on graphic violence, profanity, alcohol and tobacco; the sex trade in the background.

frames.aligns: Victims of war, trafficking, racism and state power shown with sympathy; Rock's compassion for the cast-aside.
frames.concerns: Violence as spectacle; Anime Feminist's concern about sexualized framing of women.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences; love saves Roberta.
frames.concerns: FB 22 on entertainment; alcohol and tobacco everywhere; violence as fun; "by beholding we become changed."

frames.aligns: Little beyond loyalty and the exposure of corrupt religion.
frames.concerns: Violence, immorality and drinking against jw.org entertainment counsel; a church as a criminal front.

frames.aligns: Love overcomes Roberta's madness (ch. 76).
frames.concerns: Fear, death and degradation dominate; no spiritual healing.

frames.aligns: Nazis shown as evil and destroyed (ch. 5-8); Benny, a Jewish character, is decent; pikuach nefesh in Rock's rescues.
frames.concerns: Gore, vulgarity and immodesty; nivul peh (foul speech) constant; killing as craft.

frames.aligns: Moral questions argued in earnest; Nazis defeated; mercy (Garcia).
frames.concerns: Violence relished; vulgarity.

frames.aligns: Exposes trafficking, terror and the victims of war; neo-Nazis humiliated and killed (ch. 5-8).
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; sexualized framing of women.

frames.aligns: Grief and injustice behind terror shown, not just hate (Ibraha's son killed, ch. 16-21); protection of the weak.
frames.concerns: A jihadist group as villains (its co-leader an atheist); alcohol, profanity and immodesty throughout; violence for gain.

frames.aligns: Karma's return in the twins' and villains' fates; dharma of protecting the weak in Rock.
frames.concerns: Tamasic violence and intoxication; no turn toward right order.

frames.aligns: Cycles of revenge breed suffering (Roberta, Yukio, the twins); compassion (Rock, Garcia) is the only thing that breaks them.

frames.aligns: Exposes prejudice and the wounds of war across nations.
frames.concerns: Alcohol, violence and the sex trade; no unity or service beyond the crew.

frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere; an honor suicide given tragic beauty.

frames.aligns: Survival on many dynamics; Rock's competence as a negotiator.
frames.concerns: Murder, drugs and harm; The Way to Happiness precepts broken as normal.

frames.aligns: Strong women; critique of state violence (CIA, special forces) and of racism (ch. 102-113); trafficking and child abuse condemned.

frames.aligns: Multicultural cast; critique of power and prejudice; inherent worth of the abused.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence.

frames.aligns: Self-reliant outlaws who reject conventional morality and empty religion; vengeance on those who prey on others.
frames.concerns: Harm to children is the story's deepest evil; Satanist principles forbid harming children.

frames.concerns: Profanity, drinking and crime normalized; a church that is a gun-running front; despair with no deliverance.

frames.aligns: Morality worked out by people without divine command; Rock's empathy and reason; religious hypocrisy exposed.
frames.concerns: Glorified cruelty; the abuse of children; little reason or law prevails.

frames.aligns: Several worldviews argue their case and the story leaves the ending open (ch. 116).
frames.concerns: Certainty in violence on every side; cruelty as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Loyalty among friends; villains often get what they deserve; Rock's hope for better endings.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults are answered with bullets; Revy's code is personal retaliation; the yakuza arc turns on honor (ch. 22-37).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Roanapur has no law but the syndicates' balance; the crew answers to no one.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the crew and one's syndicate over any public.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Syndicates like Hotel Moscow run on military rank; the crew is fairly flat under Dutch.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Cynical, transactional worldview; religion appears as a gun-running church.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Money and staying alive come first for everyone.

folkways.japan: Rock's salaryman background, his estrangement from his parents and the yakuza arc (ch. 22-37) contrast Japanese corporate conformity and giri (duty) with Roanapur's lawlessness; Yukio's honor suicide draws on Japanese tragic ideals that the story mourns rather than praises.

delivery.evidence: Rock and Revy argue morality openly (ch. 9-10, 15), and Rock and Chang argue fate and God (ch. 116); ANN's Matthew Roe says the anime rarely over-explains and leaves viewers to judge; Santos (ANN) thinks it fails to explore its controversial subjects.
delivery.note: Its question of how far an ordinary person sinks is carried by Rock's arc and by debates between characters, with no narrator or arc that settles it.

personified.ideology: Empathy and a stubborn hope for good endings
Nihilism: only money and guns protect you
Killing as the law of the world, learned through abuse

30735.dominant: Nihilism (explored and argued against), Might makes right (explored), Existentialism, Pragmatism.

50375.heading: Black Paradox
50375.label: From summaries
50375.life_message: The wish to die can give way to a reason to live, and every soul is precious; people and societies that treat souls as a resource to be mined bring ruin on themselves.

delivery.note: The story never lectures about suicide or greed; reviewers differ on whether it resolves its ideas (ANN: uneven; Anime Corner: little resolution).

Beauty and money as reasons to live

98148.heading: Black Torch
98148.label: From summaries

frames.concerns: A spirit indwelling a person resembles possession; spirits treated as gods and protectors.

frames.aligns: Kindness and loyalty; protecting the weak; a villain's pride brought low (Proverbs 16:18).

folkways.japan: Draws on the historical Oniwaban (the shogun's spies), ninja family lineages and mononoke folklore, with shrines and torii as living settings; duty to clan and the shame of a disgraced family name are Japanese norms the story treats with sympathy and some doubt.

folkways.japan: The series is Korean in content and creators but ran in a Japanese seinen magazine; it draws on Joseon-era Korea (the amhaeng-eosa inspectors, Chun Hyang, Hong Gildong, Hwanung) and on Confucian ideals of loyalty and upright officials, which the story honors even as its hero breaks them.

delivery.evidence: Bang Ja and Sando voice the case against Munsu's methods and are not mocked; Aji Tae and the corrupt lords are drawn as monstrous.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No honor code; Killy acts without seeking recognition.

Order vs freedom.evidence: A broken order (the Safeguard) is the enemy, but the hope is to restore a working order (the Netsphere), not to escape all order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Almost no kin; duty is to humanity as a whole.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchies of Safeguard levels and AIs, neither endorsed nor overturned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Wholly secular and technological.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Bare survival is the condition of every character.

folkways.japan: Nihei's architectural background and the late-1990s Japanese cyberpunk tradition (Akira, Ghost in the Shell) shape the world; the silent, enduring hero who serves without complaint reflects values common in Japanese stories, while the setting itself has no Japanese locale.

delivery.evidence: Opus notes it avoids manifestos and heavy philosophizing; Thompson notes the sparse dialogue and unanswered questions.
delivery.note: Meaning comes through images of scale and decay and through what Killy does, with almost no speeches.

personified.ideology: Law without purpose; credentials over people
Seizing transcendence for one's own kind

30012.heading: Bleach
30012.label: From summaries
30012.life_message: A good life is spent protecting the people you love and following your own heart even when the authorities, or would-be gods, are wrong; fear of death is part of being human, and it is what gives courage and hope their meaning.

content.framing: Neutral (sword combat as the story's main action); atrocities condemned

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

frames.aligns: Evil is shown but not made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7): Aizen's pride and Yhwach's tyranny fall. Self-giving love (Masaki dies shielding her son; Ukitake gives his life, ch. 616-617). Mercy toward defeated enemies.
frames.concerns: Crosses and knightly orders used as villain costume; God's name taken by the villain (ch. 565); an afterlife without God's judgment; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Aizen's pride, Yhwach's will to power); Ichigo's humility and mercy.
frames.concerns: The Cross is venerated, so crosses on the villains matter; traffic with spirits of the dead; guarding the senses against the gore.

frames.aligns: Clear defeat of the prideful villains; loyalty, courage and protecting family.
frames.concerns: An afterlife run by death gods and reincarnation (Hebrews 9:27; John 14:6); God's name on a villain (Exodus 20:7). Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Aizen as a Satan figure defeated by a messianic Ichigo; sin is depicted, not endorsed.
frames.concerns: A non-Christian afterlife shown as real; misuse of God's name for a villain; Christian imagery on the aggressor army.

frames.aligns: Courage, protection of the weak, good overcoming evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": traffic with the dead, spirits and death gods is the premise; Hell shown as a living force; God's name on a villain. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets good art by non-Christians be valued; total depravity has an echo in Soul Society's own hidden crimes: no side is pure.
frames.concerns: Second-commandment concerns about a "god" figure drawn and dismembered; God's name on a villain; spiritism premise.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Soul Society bears the sword, flawed but needed. No one is saved by their own merit alone.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife; sacred imagery for villains; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy: Ichigo protects ghosts and the weak; people change (Byakuya, Renji).
frames.concerns: Spiritism premise; holiness churches more cautious than UMC families.

frames.aligns: Strong fantasy tradition (Lewis, Sayers): good and evil judged by framing; just war in defending the innocent.
frames.concerns: Crosses and God's name on the villains; Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on other issues.

frames.aligns: Humility, mercy toward beaten enemies, distrust of state power (Central 46 wrong).
frames.concerns: Sword violence is the heroes' tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); a war epic.

frames.aligns: Life continues after death; family love and marriage in the epilogue (ch. 686); agency against tyranny.
frames.concerns: The afterlife differs from the plan of salvation; God's name on a villain; fan service and gore against For the Strength of Youth.

frames.aligns: Critique of unjust institutions and of a hidden genocide; compassion for outsiders (Hollows as lost souls).
frames.concerns: Giselle's villainy tied to being a man in disguise (ANN: "left field transphobia"); Nazi aesthetics for spectacle; women sidelined in later arcs.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, good defeating pride.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so the whole premise (souls living on, death gods, Hell as a present place) conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead (FB 26).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, protection of family.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and contact with the dead are the premise; the cross as a sacred symbol; God's personal name (from YHWH) given to a villain; heroic violence.

frames.aligns: Courage over fear: Ichigo faces fear, and Aizen's closing view says fear of death breeds courage (ch. 686).
frames.concerns: Death, Hollows and Hell shown as real and powerful; dwelling on fear and gore.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; a tyrant who sacrifices his own people is condemned (ch. 603); a destroyed people's memory drives the plot.
frames.concerns: The Tetragrammaton, which is not pronounced, adapted as a villain's name (ch. 565); SS-style guard and a "selection" (Auswahlen) used for spectacle; contact with the dead. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; the Quincy's earlier destruction treated as a real wrong.
frames.concerns: God's name on a villain; Nazi-style aesthetics (ANN); a "selection" that kills the weak and "impure" (ch. 537, 603).

frames.aligns: Critique of genocide and blood-purity ideology (Yhwach killing the "impure," ch. 537); protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Nazi-coded aesthetics without historical framing; the divine name for a villain; Giselle's portrayal.

frames.aligns: Justice against tyranny; mercy to defeated foes; patience under trial; the prideful seeker of godhood brought low.
frames.concerns: A supreme being depicted as a body, killed and absorbed (ch. 614-625); a villain claiming divinity ("The Almighty"); intermediaries controlling souls; lowering the gaze for fan service (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Souls cycle between worlds and return to life; the warrior's dharma to protect; death gods echo Yama's messengers.
frames.concerns: A god-figure reduced to an object; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Hollows as souls trapped by attachment and despair; impermanence; Aizen's and Yhwach's craving for supremacy undone.
frames.concerns: Killing is the main solution, against the first precept; the cosmology is a bureaucracy rather than a path to liberation.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier ideal: courage to defend the oppressed; ego (haumai) shown in Aizen and Yhwach and defeated.
frames.concerns: Heroic violence and a dismembered "god" may be discussed.

frames.concerns: Commitment to nonviolence; blood-purity prejudice is the villains' creed but shown at length.

frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity; a kami-like Soul King treated as a mechanism.

frames.aligns: Death as part of a cycle; spirits and the world of the dead treated as real and natural.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond gore.

frames.aligns: Souls survive death and return to new bodies; personal ability and will win. The Way to Happiness: help others, do not murder.
frames.concerns: Mayuri's experiments and drugging; killing as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Critique of corrupt institutions and of genocide; blood-purity ideology framed as villainous (ch. 537, 603).
frames.concerns: Giselle's portrayal (ANN: "left field transphobia"); Nemu's abuse played partly for comedy; women sidelined; Chizuru's lesbianism as a gag; Nazi aesthetic as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Aizen's closing reflection: a world without fear of death would lack the hope and courage that hold death off (ch. 686); gods exposed as power structures; human choices matter.
frames.concerns: Mayuri's cruelty partly played for fun; violence as the default answer.

frames.aligns: Protective masculinity, loyalty, honor, duty; family and marriage in the ending (ch. 686).
frames.concerns: The defining hero act is defying lawful authority (Rukia's sentence); the "god" at the top is a fraud.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of all souls, including Hollows; justice for the wronged (the Quincy); free search for truth about the gods.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; gender and queer portrayals (Giselle, Chizuru).

frames.aligns: Questioning gods and authority: Soul Society's law is wrong and the Soul King is a prop; individual will and pride celebrated in fighters (Kenpachi, Grimmjow).
frames.concerns: The rebels against "heaven" (Aizen, Yhwach) are the villains and lose; harm to the weak by tyrants is condemned, as the tradition would too.

frames.aligns: Standing up to an unjust sentence (Rukia, v9-21) and to tyrants who crush the weak; a mother's self-giving love (v3); the proud brought low (Luke 1:52).
frames.concerns: Death gods, spirits and Hell treated as real and heroic; God's name taken by a villain (ch. 565); the Cross as villain costume; violence.

frames.aligns: Gods are exposed as structures: the Soul King is a sealed being used as a linchpin (ch. 614-625); human courage and choices win; Aizen's closing view grounds hope in facing death (ch. 686).
frames.concerns: Constant violence; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: The afterlife is shown but its final meaning is left open (Hell's purpose is still a mystery in 2021); the certainties of Aizen and Yhwach are defeated.
frames.concerns: Violence; the villains' total certainty is also what fans admire.

frames.aligns: The dead go on and loved ones can be protected; loyalty to friends and family; karma-like falls for tyrants; a mother's love that saves her son.
frames.concerns: Constant bloodshed; Hell revealed as where great captains are sent (2021 one-shot).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal pride and duels decide much: Kenpachi, Byakuya's honor, Grimmjow's rivalry; Ichigo's mercy toward beaten foes softens it.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The founding act is defying Soul Society's sentence on Rukia (v9-21); order is restored at the end, but conscience over rule is celebrated.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Protecting family and friends is Ichigo's creed; Masaki's sacrifice (v3); Byakuya's choice between law and sister ends with kin winning.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Captains, lieutenants, numbered Espada and noble houses are central and respected, but rank is overturned by a teenager and noble privilege is shown critically.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The setting is spiritual, yet gods are exposed as structures (ch. 614-625) and science (Urahara, Mayuri) is powerful.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and survival dominate the last arc, while style, fashion and personal codes mark nearly every character.

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai and rank deference among Soul Reapers, the noble house as a Japanese aristocratic model, Shinto purification and Buddhist-style death rites, the belief that neglected spirits turn harmful (Drazen), and high school friendship groups are Japanese norms that frame the story; the German, Spanish and Christian elements are borrowed as style.

delivery.evidence: Aizen and Yhwach get long, serious speeches (ch. 178, 686); Kubo said he never thought of Ichigo as a hero (VIZ interview via ComicBook.com, 2023).
delivery.note: Its themes of resolve, loyalty and defiance of corrupt authority come through battles and the villains' arguments, which are partly left standing.

personified.ideology: Protect loved ones and follow your own heart
Human will should take the empty place of heaven
A founder who gives and takes power by blood
The law must be kept, even against family

30012.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, a critique of Might makes right and of Collectivism/authoritarianism, Bushido / honor code, with Buddhist ideas and Shinto folk belief as setting.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Nobles, kings and bosses exist but are mocked; pure-blood prejudice is rejected.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Staz lives for his hobbies; the stakes become life and death.

folkways.japan: Parodies Japanese delinquent (yankii) turf culture and celebrates Japanese otaku media; Fuyumi's white triangular headband is the traditional sign of a yūrei, a Japanese ghost.

delivery.evidence: The moral rides on Staz's vow and on gags; villains such as Braz get motives and partial redemption, while Akim is a monster.
delivery.note: A parody action-comedy; its point about promises and letting go is shown through the quest, not stated.

Cold calculation; the ends justify the means
Honor among rivals; strength by effort

51614.dominant: Pagan/occult (a comic demon world), Might makes right (a world run by the strongest, questioned), Expressive individualism (the otaku hero).

98397.heading: Blood on the Tracks
98397.label: From summaries
98397.life_message: A child is not his parent's possession: a good life begins when you face the truth about the people who shaped you, take back your own self, and can then meet even a parent who harmed you with clear eyes and some mercy.

content.frequency: Recurring undertone; one sexual scene between 14-year-olds
content.framing: Shown as disturbing and confused, not as titillation

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): the abuse is shown from the victim's side as terror. Parents' duty to respect the child as a person (CCC 2221-2224). The son's late care for his mother echoes honoring parents even when they failed (CCC 2218).
frames.concerns: No hope of grace named; a killing and suicidal intent (CCC 2280-2283); incestuous undertones and a sexual scene between minors (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: A clear picture of how a passion (possessive love) grows and devours. The son's final care has a cross-bearing quality (chapter 11 is titled "Cross to Bear").
frames.concerns: No spiritual remedy; long exposure to dread, despair and sexual undertones runs against nepsis (guarding the senses).

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences shown honestly; the cover-up does not hold (v9).
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; under Philippians 4:8 the abuse, killing, suicidal intent and sexual content between minors are a heavy concern. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A realistic fallen family in which hidden sin is exposed; many in this tradition distinguish depicting abuse from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No redemption in Christ; despair and emptiness are long and unanswered. Sexual content with minors and incestuous undertones are a heavy concern even for adult readers.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of bondage.
frames.concerns: Oppressive atmosphere with no deliverance offered; holiness standards weigh the sexual content heavily.

frames.aligns: Depravity even in the most "loving" mother; the fifth commandment's duties run both ways (WLC Q129-130 on superiors' duties). Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace named; Seiichi's killing and suicidal intent (WLC Q136); sexual imagery (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: The fourth commandment shown broken from the parent's side; the law's weight on Seiichi's conscience is crushing.
frames.concerns: No gospel word; conscience decides, with LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Mercy shown late (taking his mother in, v15-17); harm named as harm.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches would weigh the dread, killing and sexual content heavily; the UMC less so.

frames.aligns: Serious literary treatment of sin, guilt and the duties of family, judged by framing.
frames.concerns: Despair long unanswered; sexual content with minors. Practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: The cost of a family cut off from community; no violence made heroic.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes the psychological horror a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family relationships treated as eternally weighty; harm within the family shown as grave.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; abuse, a killing, suicidal intent and sexual content between minors put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: A careful portrayal of child abuse from the victim's view; the mother's own unloved past (v15-16); attention to mental health and the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Suicidal intent against safe-messaging norms; sexual content between minors. Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Harm in the home shown as ruinous; the late care has a healing note.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sustained dread and despair a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Violence and immorality are shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) and sexual content; no hope of God's Kingdom.

frames.aligns: A son who stops seeing himself only through his mother's fear.
frames.concerns: Fear, madness and despair dwelt on at length; members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Kibbud av va-em (honoring parents) is tested to its limit; the son's care at the end echoes it, while halakhic sources also limit a child's duties toward an abusive or ill parent.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the incestuous undertones and the sexual scene a heavy concern; a killing; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Honor of parents and the dignity of the child; teshuvah has only a partial echo.
frames.concerns: Sexual content involving minors; long despair.

frames.aligns: Honest about abuse and mental health; attention to the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Suicidal intent and sexual content with minors; Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Harm and injustice in the family are exposed; the son's care for his aging mother echoes kindness to parents in old age (Qur'an 17:23-24).
frames.concerns: Suicide is forbidden and despair of mercy (Qur'an 39:53) runs long without a faith answer; modesty (haya) makes the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like "tracks" passing from one generation to the next (Seiko's own past, v15-16); the late turn to duty toward a parent.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content under Gita 17; a killing; views vary by community.

frames.aligns: Close to teaching on craving and attachment: Seiko's clinging destroys what she clings to; Seiichi learns that the self he took for granted is fragile (Oshimi, Anime Feminist interview).
frames.concerns: Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sustained dread and the killing a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Attachment (moh) and anger shown as destructive; the late acceptance echoes hukam.
frames.concerns: Despair with no spiritual answer; a killing.

frames.aligns: Family unity valued, and its breakdown shown as tragic.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a concern; despair long unanswered; a killing.

frames.aligns: Ancestral and family bonds taken with full seriousness; the family grave (v14); the hill and the mountain as places of memory.
frames.concerns: Death and impurity (kegare) are pervasive; no shrine or kami involved.

frames.aligns: Harm shown as harm (the Rede); personal responsibility and the wheel of life to death.
frames.concerns: Little hope language; harm to a child.

frames.aligns: "Honor and help your parents" tested and finally lived out; survival chosen over self-destruction (v15).
frames.concerns: Seiko's condition is framed as psychiatric (Wikipedia), which runs against the church's stance on psychiatry. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Takes child abuse, intergenerational trauma and mental health seriously and from the victim's side; refuses easy monsters (Comics Beat).
frames.concerns: Incestuous undertones and a sexual scene between 14-year-olds; suicidal intent shown at length, which safe-messaging guidelines advise care with.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; understanding causes (the mother's own past) rather than blame; a self rebuilt without supernatural help.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and suicidal intent are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: A sober picture of what happens when a family turns inward without support; the son's duty to care for his mother is honored at the end.
frames.concerns: Respect for parents is tested by a portrait of a parent as abuser; despair, and the good, the true and the beautiful often degraded on the page; sexual content between minors.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the child and of the broken mother; honest search for meaning in suffering.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness makes it older-teen or adult reading.

frames.aligns: Self-ownership against a smothering authority ("I Belong to Me," ch. 75); harm to children condemned in the Eleven Rules, as the story condemns it.
frames.concerns: The son's ritual killing of his cousin (v12); the late return to filial care is less in line with self-determination.

frames.aligns: A picture of bondage inside a home and a long road out of it; truth finally told (v9); a son who cares for an aged mother despite the past, a second chance offered late.
frames.concerns: Despair with no hope in God for twenty years; a killing; suicidal intent; incestuous undertones and a sexual scene between minors.

frames.aligns: Harm explained by human causes (the mother's own past, mental illness), not by evil spirits or fate; meaning sought in this life; no faith offered as the answer.
frames.concerns: Cruelty, a killing and suicidal intent are heavy; sexual content between minors.

frames.aligns: Honest about what cannot be known: the dream conversation at the end (v17) and the question of why Seiko acted (v16) are not reduced to a doctrine; no preaching either way.
frames.concerns: Long despair; sexual content between minors; Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty at the end, fairness (the truth comes out), and a man who finally chooses his own path.
frames.concerns: Despair and near-nihilism run long; cruelty to a child; the darkness and the sexual scene put it beyond many families' comfort for teens.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Seiko's concern for face before relatives is part of the harm; the story values the inner dignity of the child over family honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The quiet orderly home is a prison; freedom from the mother is the arc, though it comes at great cost.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin is everything in the plot, but the story shows kin turned inward and harmful; police and courts enter only late (v9-12).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The parent's unchecked power over the child is shown as dangerous.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Mental illness, memory and causes explain events; no religious frame.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The hero's struggle is for a self of his own, more than for safety.

folkways.japan: A 1990s Gunma town, the extended family's weekly visits, the salaryman father, the stay-at-home mother, keeping face before relatives, and the family grave reflect Japanese settings and norms; the "toxic parent" (doku-oya) theme is a recognized Japanese social topic that the story examines from inside.

delivery.evidence: Oshimi drew strictly from Seiichi's perspective (ANN interview) and later gives Seiko's own past (v16); Comics Beat says the book avoids demonizing either character.
delivery.note: The message is carried by atmosphere, point of view and slowly revealed memory, with almost no stated moral.

personified.ideology: Possessive love; the child as part of oneself
Keeping the peace by not seeing
A self struggling to belong to itself

98397.dominant: Existentialism, Confucian ethics (filial duty, explored), Nihilism (explored, then moved past), Buddhist ideas (by echo).

86218.heading: Bloom Into You
86218.label: From summaries
86218.life_message: A good life is lived as your true self, not as the person others expect, and real love lets the other person change and grow rather than freezing them in place.

content.framing: Endorsed; consent in early kisses debated by critics

frames.aligns: Truthfulness and refusing to live a lie; healing from grief; respect for each person; kindness in rejection (Sayaka).
frames.concerns: The central romance is same-sex and is presented as the good life, culminating in premarital sex between teens (ch. 44), against CCC 2357-2359 and teaching on chastity (CCC 2337-2350).

frames.aligns: Humility and honesty about the self; grief and memory of the dead (Mio); a change of heart in Touko.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality; romance and physical intimacy offered as the story's goal. Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on ch. 44.

frames.aligns: Honesty, perseverance, kindness, loyal friendship.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance affirmed as the central good (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII; usually a significant concern); premarital sex between teens (ch. 44). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Being honest about who you are; patience; care for a hurting friend.
frames.concerns: Most churches hold traditional sexual ethics, against the affirmed romance and ch. 44; some affirming congregations would read it differently. No Christian review was found.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual-warfare content, so the "open door" concern is absent. Honesty and growth.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality (AG position papers) against the affirmed romance and ch. 44; holiness and modesty standards.

frames.aligns: Common grace: well-made art by non-Christians may be valued; honest depiction of grief and self-deception.
frames.concerns: Conservative churches (PCA, OPC) hold traditional teaching on marriage; PC(USA) is affirming. WLC Q139 on lascivious books and pictures for ch. 44.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love and conscience; honesty; "put the best construction on everything" in how the friends treat each other.
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS hold traditional teaching on marriage and chastity; ELCA is affirming.

frames.aligns: Love that seeks the other's good; honesty; care for the lonely.
frames.concerns: The UMC has been affirming since 2024; Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene churches hold traditional teaching on sexuality and chastity.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges works by moral vision; honesty, grief and growth.
frames.concerns: The Episcopal Church allows same-sex marriage; ACNA holds traditional teaching. Premarital sex between teens is a concern across the range.

frames.aligns: No violence; humility, honesty, community work (the play).
frames.concerns: Conservative groups hold traditional teaching on marriage and avoid most popular media; romance and intimacy as the story's goal. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Honesty (Article of Faith 13); kindness; developing talents (acting).
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching ("The Family: A Proclamation to the World") and the law of chastity against the affirmed romance and ch. 44.

frames.aligns: Affirms same-sex love and a lasting relationship; an adult queer couple as role models; honesty and dignity.
frames.concerns: Touko's kisses without asking (Bauman's predatory-lesbian critique); teens with little adult support (Friedman).

frames.aligns: Honesty, perseverance, kindness; no spiritualism.
frames.concerns: Marriage between one man and one woman (General Conference statements); same-sex romance usually a significant concern; premarital sex between teens (ch. 44).

frames.aligns: No violence or spiritism; honesty and loyalty.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); homosexual acts considered sinful; premarital sex framed positively.

frames.aligns: Thought shapes experience: Touko's freedom from a false self-image; love over fear.
frames.concerns: Purity and marriage valued; premarital sex (ch. 44). Less public teaching on same-sex relationships (to verify).

frames.aligns: Memory of the dead; honesty ("keep far from falsehood," Exodus 23:7); kind speech in rejection.
frames.concerns: Same-sex acts forbidden (Leviticus 18:22); tzniut and the kissing and ch. 44; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person (the CJLS 2006 rulings opened the way to same-sex commitment ceremonies; views vary by congregation); honesty; grief processed in community.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual activity (ch. 44); modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: LGBTQ inclusion; informed autonomy; honesty and dignity.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's kisses; teen sexual activity worth discussing.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness, patience (sabr), loyalty to friends, kindness in refusing someone.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality; same-sex romance and premarital intimacy (ch. 44) as the central good; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) applies to the intimate scenes.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: living one's own nature rather than another's (Bhagavad Gita 3.35 echoes Touko's arc); duty to family memory; theatre that moves the audience.
frames.concerns: Views on same-sex relationships vary, with traditional views common; teen sexual activity.

frames.aligns: Letting go of a fixed self (Touko's mask); impermanence and grief; compassion in rejection; right speech in honest confession.
frames.concerns: Third precept (avoid harmful sexual conduct): many traditions accept same-sex relationships, views vary by teacher and culture; attachment as a theme.

frames.aligns: Truthful living; equality and dignity; the vice of ego (haumai) behind Touko's facade.
frames.concerns: Sex within marriage; the Akal Takht opposed same-sex marriage (2005), though diaspora views vary.

frames.aligns: Rejection of prejudice; honesty; independent search for truth; unity among friends.
frames.concerns: Teaching reserves sexual relations for marriage between a man and a woman; a "chaste and holy life" (Shoghi Effendi).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) as the story's core value: Touko gives up a false face; respect for the dead (Mio's grave).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no doctrine on same-sex relationships (practice varies, to verify).

frames.aligns: Love and sexuality as positive between consenting partners; largely LGBTQ-affirming; becoming one's true self.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's early kisses ("harm none").

frames.aligns: Self-determinism; honesty; competence (acting).
frames.concerns: Little in the message; The Way to Happiness asks faithfulness to one's sexual partner, which the couple shows.

frames.aligns: Positive, lasting same-sex romance; adult queer couple; a character who feels no romantic attraction treated with respect (Maki); critique of conformity.
frames.concerns: Touko's kisses without permission (Bauman, ANN; Friedman, Okazu); aro/ace readers may feel Yuu's arc closed that reading (Kaiser, Anime Feminist); teen sex scene.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through honest relationships; identity chosen rather than imposed; no supernatural claims.
frames.concerns: Consent and the lack of adult support (Friedman).

frames.aligns: Duty to a shared project, respect for senpai and teachers, perseverance, loyalty.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented to teen readers as the ideal, a concern for many when presented to children; premarital teen sex (ch. 44); the relationship kept from parents.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; welcoming LGBTQ people; free search for truth and meaning.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's kisses.

frames.aligns: Individualism and self-determination; rejection of an imposed identity; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3); LGBTQ-affirming.
frames.concerns: Touko's kisses without permission (Tenet 3).

frames.aligns: Honesty, kindness and loyalty; grief honored; a young person freed from living under someone else's shadow; elders (Riko and Miyako) who counsel the young.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex between teens presented as the fulfillment of love (ch. 44); the large denominations teach marriage between a man and a woman, though members' views vary (Pew 2023-24); no faith in the story.

frames.aligns: Identity and meaning made in this life through honest relationships; no supernatural claims; no religious pressure; equal, chosen love.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's early kisses; a sex scene between 16-year-olds.

frames.aligns: Humility and doubt treated kindly: Yuu's uncertainty about love is never mocked, and the story lets characters work out who they are over time; critics' differing readings of Yuu are possible within the text.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's early kisses; the teen sex scene.

frames.aligns: Loyalty between friends, everyday decency, finding your own path, and a hopeful ending; no preaching.
frames.concerns: The sex scene between 16-year-olds (ch. 44) is beyond what many families want for younger teens; the early kisses without asking.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Inner sincerity over public reputation: Touko gives up the honored image of her sister.

Order vs freedom.evidence: School order is kept and respected, but freedom to choose oneself is the theme.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The student council and friends matter more than blood family, which is mostly background.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai roles invert as Yuu comes to lead Touko (Japanese Wikipedia).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular; customs kept as setting.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Identity and love are the stakes; survival is never in question.

folkways.japan: A Japanese public co-ed high school, the student council, senpai-kohai etiquette, a school trip to Kyoto and the family grave set the scene; the yuri genre and its Class S history are the Japanese tradition the series answers (Wikipedia; Henderson, Anime Feminist).

delivery.evidence: Nakatani says she avoided a story about the social obstacles to same-sex love and focused on the characters' flaws (Wikipedia, Production). The play inside the story states the theme openly (choose to be yourself).
delivery.note: The message is carried by the characters' inner lives and by the school play, which mirrors Touko's choice; the adult couple and Maki are drawn to make the point that love is real and that a life without romance can be full.

personified.ideology: Living as someone else versus becoming yourself

164708.heading: Blooming Love
164708.label: From summaries
164708.life_message: Two people who are each "half-fledged" can grow into skilled, whole people by honoring each other's craft, helping where the other is weak, and choosing each other's good over their own comfort.

folkways.japan: Wadaiko making as a family trade handed down by a grandfather, the shokunin (master craftsman) ideal, art-university entrance exams with cram school, and the Yakushima cedar forests (vol. 5) are Japanese settings; the story draws on Japanese respect for craft (monozukuri) and presents it warmly.

delivery.evidence: Sportskeeda describes a slow, character-focused romance about personal growth; the lesson (help each other where you are weak) is shown in shared projects, not stated in lectures.

86890.heading: Blue Giant
86890.label: From summaries
86890.life_message: Love what you do with your whole heart, practice every day, and play with honest feeling; greatness is built from stubborn effort, humility before criticism, and the people who believe in you.

content.framing: Neutral (part of jazz-bar life); not glamorized

frames.aligns: Beauty pursued with discipline, as John Paul II's Letter to Artists (1999) praises; Masayuki's self-giving love; honoring father and family (CCC 2214-2220); humility as the root of growth.
frames.concerns: Yui's heavy drinking (CCC 2290) is shown without comment; the goal of being the greatest can feed pride.

frames.aligns: Daily ascetic-like practice by the river; patience in failure; love of brother and father.
frames.concerns: Ambition to be the best in the world could become vainglory; bar culture.

frames.aligns: Diligence (Proverbs 22:29, a man skilled in his work); a brother's sacrifice; no sexual content.
frames.concerns: Drinking in jazz clubs and a teacher who drinks heavily; a teen who smokes. Philippians 4:8 test passes on most counts.

frames.aligns: Using a gift with all one's heart; mentors who invest in the young; forgiveness and encouragement within the band.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond bar settings; success is pursued for its own sake, with no reference to God.

frames.aligns: Passionate, full-volume expression; music that moves people to tears; perseverance.

frames.aligns: Vocation and common grace: excellence in a God-given art by people who do not know him; diligence and humility.

folkways.japan: Dai's solitary daily practice reflects the Japanese ideal of mastering a craft through long repetition, and his surname deliberately recalls Miyamoto Musashi. delivery.evidence: Dai states his goal openly and gives one short speech on letting beginners into jazz (v5-6); the critics he faces are drawn fairly and often proved right. Reviewers describe the music conveyed through faces and layout rather than lectures (ANN; Publishers Weekly).

folkways.japan: Senpai-free meritocracy is the program's deliberate break with Japanese team culture, where Blue Lock's premise holds that Japanese players are too team-minded to produce selfish strikers (Wikipedia); the rich heir escaping a family firm is a familiar Japanese motif.

106130.heading: Blue Lock

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pride and the hunger to "devour" rivals are honored, and Rin's rage at Sae fuels his game; but disputes are settled on the pitch, and Kuon's cheating is condemned.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The individual striker over team harmony (ch. 1-3); freedom is pursued through a harsh, rule-bound program.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin ties appear mostly as wounds (the Itoshi brothers, Kaiser's father); friendship is secondary to ego (Nagi leaves Reo).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank is everywhere (ranking screens, NEL bids, "emperor" titles) but earned by results; seniority is critiqued.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith; Isagi grows through analysis and "formulas"; team harmony is presented as the cause of failure (ch. 1).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Find what only you can do is a strong self-expression value; the survival contest with lifetime bans keeps it near the middle.

folkways.japan: The series is an argument with Japanese norms; Kaneshiro says frustration with Japanese society shaped its focus on ego. Team harmony (wa), seniority and self-effacement are the values it pushes against, so readers from more individualist cultures may find its "ego" less radical than Japanese readers do.

delivery.evidence: Ego states the thesis in direct speeches; Common Sense Media says self-centered ego themes overshadow the positives; The Daily Campus calls it propaganda for hyper-competition. The Side-B arc (vol. 39) is the first sustained voice for the other side.
delivery.note: The teamwork view is voiced mostly by players who are eliminated, though the story refines "ego" into self-knowledge and lets rivals combine.

personified.ideology: Japan needs egoists; cooperation is weakness
Team play; Blue Lock as inhumane

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Dorm honor, duels and family name (Airu's guarding of the Inuzuka house) drive many conflicts; the story moves toward dignity for all.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules are bent constantly in secret, but the heroes change the rules through the student government rather than tearing them down.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and dorm loyalty give way to a wider civic loyalty to the whole school and both nations.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Prefects, nobles and dorm leaders form strong hierarchies; the story moves toward equality between nations and sexes but keeps leaders and ranks.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The romance is a personal choice pursued at real social cost; security comes second.

folkways.japan: A Japanese shōnen boarding-school comedy: senior-junior ranks, a powerful student council and prefect system, the sports festival, cultural festival, school trip, and Valentine's customs. The two invented nations borrow a Japanese-style East (Touwa: kendo, naginata, family houses) and a European-style West (nobility, debutante balls), and the feud loosely echoes East-West prejudice.

delivery.evidence: Early volumes carry the theme lightly (ANN reviewers found the feud thinly developed in vol. 1); TV Tropes' YMMV page says the message grows heavier near the end, with Westerners on the class trip drawn as racists easily beaten. The main segregationist, Reon, is given a sympathetic backstory and redemption.
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice message rides on a romantic comedy and becomes open politics in the election and class-trip arcs (ch. 79-108).

folkways.japan: The ninja village with its Hokage, council of elders and feudal lord, the master-disciple bond (Sasuke and Boruto), duty to the group and the honor of the village reflect Japanese historical and shōnen-manga norms; the Daikokuten dimension is named after a Japanese god of fortune (from general knowledge; to verify).

33468.heading: Bunny Drop
33468.label: From summaries
33468.life_message: Family is made by choosing to care for someone day after day, not by blood or by what relatives think proper; the series carries that idea to an ending in which the girl and the man who raised her choose to marry, which most readers rejected.

frames.concerns: The ending turns a father-daughter bond into marriage; for legal adoption canon law even makes marriage invalid (canon 1094); Rin never legally became his daughter, but the relationship the story built is a father's.

frames.aligns: Sacrificial love for an orphaned child; humility as Daikichi gives up his career path.
frames.concerns: Confuses the order of the household: the one who stood as father becomes a husband.

frames.aligns: Care for the fatherless (James 1:27); a man who lays down his comfort for a child.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Daikichi rejects the relatives' concern with face to protect a child's dignity (vol. 1).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Personal choice over family convention, from adoption to marriage.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin and household are the whole world: funeral, grandparents, neighbor families (vols. 1-7).

folkways.japan: Family embarrassment over a child born outside marriage, the koseki-style concern with surnames and adoption (vol. 2), and the price a salaryman pays for leaving the long-hours track reflect Japanese norms; the series sides with the child against family face. Carlson links the ending to the old pattern, from The Tale of Genji, of a man raising a girl who later becomes his wife.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe quiet, awkward slice-of-life with thoughts shown rather than lectures (Gaffney, vol. 7). The relatives who object to Rin are drawn as cold; Daikichi's own hesitation about the romance is shown (vol. 9), but no character argues the case against it at length (Carlson).
delivery.note: The message is carried by everyday scenes, not speeches; the ending is presented as natural and the objections to it are left to the reader.

folkways.japan: The black-company backstory, the ideal of diligent craftsmanship, gratitude to benefactors and gods, and the slow-life (surō raifu) isekai genre reflect Japanese settings and norms; the story draws on them warmly and sets itself against exploitative work. Described here as context.

folkways.japan: A Japanese middle-school class trip (shuugaku ryokou), class presidents, club ranks, deference to teachers and a delinquent rising to lead reflect Japanese school norms; Weekly Shonen Magazine's fan-service conventions shape the art.

111233.heading: Call of the Night (Yofukashi no Uta)
111233.label: From summaries
111233.life_message: A good life is one you choose for yourself. Freedom, honesty about your feelings and real connection matter more than fitting in, and love means staying with someone even when it costs you.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Anko's revenge for her family is the series' main honor-style drive, and she gives it up (ch. 155). Insults and slights are handled with jokes and talk.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Leaving school, curfew and home routine is presented as liberation (ANN's This Week in Anime); the night is a space without rules.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Birth families are weak or absent (Ko's mother, Mahiru's parents); loyalty goes to chosen friends and a found community of night people.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Vampire society is loose, without strong ranks; adults earn no deference by position.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion or inherited custom guides life; choices are personal.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, tolerance of difference and quality of life (sleep, pleasure, honest feeling) are the story's goods (Aftermath).

folkways.japan: School refusal (futoko), late-night convenience-store culture, hostess work and long working hours are Japanese social context; Ko's escape reads partly as a response to Japanese school conformity and group pressure, which the story critiques by showing a kinder world outside it.

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime calls the show a "pseudo-moral argument in favor of truancy"; reviewers otherwise praise its quiet, introspective tone (Aftermath).
delivery.note: Its case for freedom and honest feeling comes through mood and character arcs rather than speeches, while school and parents are mostly absent rather than argued against.

personified.ideology: Freedom and self-discovery outside school norms

111233.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Hedonism (explored, then tempered).

folkways.japan: The salaryman protagonist's politeness and caution, the love of home cooking, convenience-store and drugstore brands, bathing culture and food offerings to gods (shinsen, omiyage) are distinctly Japanese; the "slow life" isekai genre is a response to Japanese overwork culture.

delivery.evidence: The kingdom's motives are shown through Mukohda's suspicions and the fan wiki's later reveal rather than argued; Anime Feminist describes a light comedy that pokes fun at its own genre. The gods' greed is satirized but never preached against.
delivery.note: Its preference for a modest, comfortable life is carried by Mukohda's choices and cooking, not by speeches.

folkways.japan: Elementary school life, White Day and Valentine customs, a Shinto shrine maiden, a single father who cooks, and respectful sibling and family roles reflect Japanese settings; the teacher-student romance draws on a romantic trope common in Japanese fiction (fan wiki), which many Western readers do not share.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Escape from slavery and from a state that hunts a child; the village is a free, small community.

folkways.japan: A European-style fantasy (Greco-Roman, Viking and 17th-century elements, per ANN's Rebecca Silverman) drawn in the dark-fantasy line of Berserk and Vinland Saga; the found-family and self-sacrifice ideals, the guilt over surviving and the debt to the dead (Julian's hundred lives) also run through Japanese shonen storytelling.

delivery.evidence: Mira states the moral of ch. 1 aloud, but the rest is carried by events. Villains get some reasons: Elstri fears for the kingdom, the Rummir Empress would sacrifice a child for peace (Wikipedia), Lacrima grieves her brother; Arkos is drawn as pure cruelty, as Kuramori intends (Shonen Jump+ villain interview, via fan wiki).
delivery.note: The message rides on sacrifices and choices rather than speeches.
