105778.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
105778.label: From summaries
105778.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, a dog, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

content.framing: Mixed: Denji's lust played for comedy and pathos; coercion and manipulation shown as harmful but rarely judged

frames.aligns: Care for the poor and human dignity against being used as a tool (Makima, Public Safety); sacrificial love among friends; manipulation exposed as evil; mercy to a wounded enemy (ch. 229).

frames.concerns: Demonic power shown as the hero's strength; sexual content involving teens (ch. 167-168); profanity; despair. Holiness and Pentecostal families would see the devils as spiritually real.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Aki's duty-and-revenge path ends with him as the Gun Fiend (ch. 79); Denji answers Makima not with vengeance but by eating her as an act of love and raising Nayuta (ch. 96-97).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Total control is the villain's creed (ch. 84); the good is choosing your own wants. Public Safety treats workers as expendable.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family carries the warmth; institutions and crowds (the Church, mobs, ch. 140-155) are threats.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Those who seek control lose (Makima, Barem, Yoru); authority appears mostly as exploitation.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion is imagery and a youth cult, not living faith; salvation-like moments come through human love and a meal.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Denji's dreams are basic: jam on bread, a bed, a girlfriend (ch. 1); poverty frames the story, while the goal of choosing one's own wants pulls the position up.

folkways.japan: Public Safety's disposable workers and death as a workplace hazard echo critiques of Japanese overwork culture, and Part 2's fame culture, fan clubs and hero worship reflect Japanese online and idol culture; the story uses these as targets rather than models.

delivery.evidence: Morals are never stated; ideas come through absurd events and characters' choices. Makima's case for control and the Church's case for a world without evil are given real force before they fail (ch. 84, 141).
delivery.note: Its ideas come through absurd, violent events and the characters' choices rather than stated morals.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Flio shrugs off the kingdom's insult and seeks no revenge (ch. 1, 18); Balirossa's wish to restore her family's honor is gently mocked (ch. 8).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Flio wants to be left alone by king and Dark One alike; he moves his whole house to stay out of the war (ch. 9).

Civic vs kin.evidence: His wife and household come first, but he also defends towns and plans schools (ch. 18-19; vol. 13).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Demon society ranks by strength and Rys's tribe submits to the strong, but Flio treats servants, demons and nobles as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Tribal customs and magic sit beside practical trade and education.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A comfortable, chosen life is the stated goal; survival is never in doubt.

folkways.japan: The 'slow life' isekai ideal, escape from a demanding kingdom that treats people as tools (read by many as an image of overwork), the hot-spring trip, the store-keeping merchant hero and a devoted wife figure reflect Japanese web-novel genre norms.

delivery.evidence: Coexistence is shown through the household and Flio's choices rather than speeches; the war-hungry side (the old king, the Blonde Hero, Yuigarde) is played as comic incompetence, while Gholl's reluctant demon rule and the wyverns' different view of life and death get a fairer hearing (vols. 9-10).
delivery.note: The message is clear and gentle: peace and family beat conquest. It is carried by domestic comedy, with occasional serious turns (Rys injured, Wyne's loss, the twins).

folkways.japan: Exam-ranked schooling, class units that are punished together, senpai-kohai hierarchy, the student council's authority and the fear of public shame reflect Japanese school culture; the story pushes these to an extreme to critique them, while its hero quietly rejects the group harmony the system asks for.

delivery.evidence: Kinugasa says each class's approach has problems and none is absolutely correct; rivals (Ryuen, Sakayanagi, Ichinose) are given real strengths.
delivery.note: The story shows rather than tells; Ayanokoji's unreliable narration (Wikipedia) leaves the reader to judge him.

30583.heading: Claymore

frames.concerns: "Harm none" and the constant violence; exploitation of women's bodies.

frames.aligns: Exposure of experimentation on people and of a hidden controlling power; "do not harm a person of good will" (The Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Killing as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Critique of an institution that uses girls' bodies as weapons; women at the center of the action; prejudice overcome (Rabona).
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist argues the series undercuts its heroines: sexualized trauma, nudity, women drawn as childlike (Priscilla, Miata), queer-coded women tied to vice, shock deaths; the "awakening as climax" premise.

frames.aligns: Human bonds and choice over a monstrous body; truth and inquiry (Miria) against a lying authority; the Yoma have a made, natural cause (v15).
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown at length; the black card needs a mental-health conversation.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, sacrifice and honor among comrades; a faith community as refuge; distrust of an unaccountable secret power.
frames.concerns: Gore and nudity; little place for family life; some conservatives may find the gender framing at odds with traditional roles.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the exploited and feared; justice against a secret power; a community that welcomes those it once excluded.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; how women's suffering is framed (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Art that challenges authority: women made into tools rebel against a hidden power and win; self-determination over obedience. The Satanic Temple's compassion and justice tenets fit the warriors' mutual care.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (orphans made into weapons, the threat to the child Clare) is shown as evil, as the Eleven Rules also hold; a sympathetic church.

frames.aligns: Deliverance from an institution that owns and uses its warriors, an Exodus-like breaking of bondage (the revolt, v20-23); hope and endurance through long suffering (the seven hidden years); protecting the weak; a church that learns to receive the outcast.
frames.concerns: Revenge as a starting motive; demon flesh and the "witch" label; uncensored nudity; constant gore; the spirit of the dead in the finale.

frames.aligns: The monsters have a man-made cause uncovered by investigation (Miria, v15); a manipulative secret authority is exposed; goodness comes from loyalty and empathy, not command; the fictional church is a refuge, not the answer.
frames.concerns: Glorified carnage and the sexualized treatment of women (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: No preachy certainty: Rabona's faith is shown with both prejudice and kindness; Teresa's return is left as a mystery the reader can read many ways; ethics grounded in care for comrades.
frames.concerns: Violence as the only tool; the treatment of women's suffering.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fairness (the liars fall), protection by a loved one who died (Teresa within Clare), and a lonely hero finding her place among friends.
frames.concerns: Gore, nudity and the death of many sympathetic heroines are heavy for younger teens.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal vendetta drives Clare and Ophelia, and Ophelia's ends in ruin (likely v8). The story moves from revenge toward protecting others; warriors' pride in rank is real but not the final value.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Organization's rules, ranks and executions are the enemy; deserters and rebels are the heroes (v15-23). The freed warriors choose their own paths at the end.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Blood kin are mostly dead; loyalty goes to a chosen band of comrades and to promises to the dead (Teresa), more than to the whole community. Rabona shows a wider civic duty.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The rank system (1 to 47) is the Organization's tool; the lowest-ranked warrior becomes the hero; Miria leads by trust, not rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Monsters have a man-made cause; truth comes by investigation (Miria). A fictional faith is treated with respect and its holy city becomes a refuge, but faith does not solve the plot.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, endurance and protecting comrades come first in a world of constant threat.

folkways.japan: The setting is a European-style fantasy (a Chartres-like cathedral, a Scottish sword name, Catholic-sounding names, per the MyAnimeList feature). Group loyalty, endurance and quiet self-sacrifice (Teresa's faint smile) reflect values common in Japanese shonen storytelling; the medieval Christian look is borrowed scenery rather than a message about Christianity.

delivery.evidence: The Organization's motives are revealed through Rubel and Miria's investigation (v15-16) rather than speeches; Isley and Priscilla get sympathetic backstories (Extra Scene 3-4, v14). No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of humanity and institutional exploitation emerge through plot reveals and characters' choices rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and humanity kept despite a monstrous body
People as weapons; ends justify means
Faith community moving from exclusion to hospitality
Power without restraint, born of trauma

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rejection hurts Mikoto inwardly; Haiba takes blame to protect his ex (vols. 15-16); no feuds.

Order vs freedom.evidence: School rules against the relationship are evaded throughout.

folkways.japan: Hiding a forbidden relationship to protect a teacher's job and the school's name, the shoujo "suspension bridge effect" romance, and the family grave reflect Japanese school norms and genre conventions; Japanese schools treat teacher-student relationships as serious misconduct (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: The premise and the episodic comedy carry the message; no character is reported to argue against the relationship except as a rule to dodge (MyAnimeList reviews; ciatr).
delivery.note: The school's ban on teacher-student relationships appears only as something to hide from, not as a view the story weighs (to verify in print).

Despair, then a reason to live

folkways.japan: The yankī delinquent subculture, bōsōzoku biker gangs, rival high schools, senpai-kohai rank and graduation as the end of youth are Japanese settings; the story celebrates the subculture's loyalty code while showing the yakuza as a dead end.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Teens act on their own judgment; institutions barely help, and adult authorities are often the danger (the Kito family; the teacher, ch. 170-191).

30021.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata, 2003-2006)
30021.label: From summaries
30021.life_message: No one may make himself judge of who deserves to live: a life spent seizing that power ends in lies, isolation and a meaningless death. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin (Galatians 6:7); deception exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: A human claiming divinity is punished, but no gospel answer is given; the "Mu" ending; death gods. Profanity and coerced suicide fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the engaging plot and its discussions of morality and justice; Christian writers read Light as a man seizing God's throne and falling.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of spiritual themes, violence and language, and of Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Private judgment and killing are the story's target: Light's vigilante "justice" ends in exposure and death (ch. 103-107). Soichiro and the task force, who stand for rule of law, duty and honesty, are the moral center.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Law and due process are endorsed over one man's will. L's surveillance and confinement of suspects (Misa, ch. 33-35) are questioned, so order is honored but not without limits.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rules are meant to apply to all, including family: Soichiro serves the investigation even as it points at his son. Light risks his father and sister (vols. 8-9), a betrayal of kin the story condemns as part of his corruption.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light's claim to be "god of the new world" (ch. 1-2) is the root wrong; no person is above the law. The police chain of command and the Wammy's House succession (Near, Mello) are shown neutrally.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious language belongs to the villain and his cult (Mikami, ch. 83; the Kira worshippers, ch. 108). The "Mu" rule offers a naturalist note, and the duel is won by reason and investigation.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Crime, safety and deterrence are the central question; a frightened public accepts a killer who promises security. Ohba's takeaway, "let's give it our all while we're alive," adds a modest self-expression note.

folkways.japan: Capital punishment, a powerful police bureaucracy and the public's quiet approval of Kira reflect debates in Japan, which keeps the death penalty; Wikipedia cites Jolyon Baraka Thomas reading the cults against the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack. Soichiro's quiet devotion to duty echoes Japanese workplace norms, and the film director Kaneko called the idea of spirits living in written words "very Japanese" (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Light and L argue openly about justice; Light's final speech (ch. 105) states his case in full before the story rejects it. ANN's Briana Lawrence: two sides that both believe in justice (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Ohba said he had no particular theme in mind (Wikipedia); the verdict comes through Light's fall rather than a stated lesson.

personified.ideology: Justice by results; one genius may judge and kill
Rule of law, duty and honesty

87216.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
87216.label: From summaries
87216.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duty and samurai-style service are honored, but personal vendetta is not: Tanjiro mourns the demons he kills, and mercy toward Akaza and Gyutaro (ch. 96, 154-156) is part of the story's ethic. Defending family drives the plot more than defending one's name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Demon Slayer Corps has ranks, supply, doctors and discipline (Pragmatic lens). Duty, training and obeying the Corps are celebrated; Muzan's lawless rule by fear is the counter-example (ch. 52).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the central value: a brother guarding his sister, the Corps as a family-like body, Rui's forced "fake family" as its opposite. The epilogue honors descendants and lineage (ch. 205).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hashira ranks and deference to Kagaya Ubuyashiki are presented with reverence; his servant leadership and self-sacrifice (ch. 137-138) are shown as heroic. Inherited Breathing styles and passing the will down tie worth to lineage and rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Buddhist and Shinto motifs are sincere: the blind monk Gyomei, the fire-god kagura dance, spirits of the dead meeting the dying (ch. 66, 156, 163, 179, 200), a rebirth-style epilogue (ch. 205). Doma's cult, not faith itself, is exposed.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Life is lived for others: protect the weak, keep promises, accept early death (the "Mark"). Hard training and self-sacrifice (Rengoku, ch. 66) are the highest goods.

folkways.japan: The Taisho-era setting, Confucian filial piety, samurai ideals of service and death, and Shinto and Buddhist imagery are Japanese traditional values the story treats as true; many readers from other cultures will see these as the setting's norms more than a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: Tallon (Christian Research Journal): "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about compassion and duty are spoken in Tanjiro's lines and shown through the demons' backstories.

folkways.japan: Japanese police procedure, school life, hot springs, festivals and regional rivalries (Tokyo and Osaka detectives) are the setting; the confession scene restores social order, and the yearly school trip and karate tournaments reflect Japanese youth culture. Its rationalism draws on the Western detective canon.

delivery.evidence: Conan states his rule against letting culprits die and repeatedly lectures killers that murder is never justified (DCW); The Escapist notes the anime treats killing as serious. Culprits' grievances are heard in full before the verdict.

folkways.japan: Written in 1972 for a boys' weekly, it blends Western demonology and Christian myth (via Dante and Doré, Nagai's childhood influences) with Japanese monster tradition; The Anime Encyclopedia found the mix of Japanese and European mythology messy (via Wikipedia). Its anti-war intent reflects the period of the Vietnam War and Cold War nuclear fear (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Characters deliver long speeches on human nature and the coming end (TCJ calls it preachy; a MangaUpdates reader notes drawn-out exposition); Nagai stated the anti-war message directly (Wikipedia). delivery.note: The warning is spoken aloud by Ryo and the narration and enacted by the mob in v5; the theology (Satan sympathetic, God as aggressor) is carried by the ending more than by argument.

folkways.japan: Ritual apology (shazai), including the bowing press-conference apology by public figures, is a recognizable feature of Japanese public life (from general knowledge; to verify); World Literature Today links the book to a 2013 filmed idol apology. The school setting, transfer student and neighborhood gossip are everyday Japanese settings; the Devil is a Western, Christian-derived figure rather than a Japanese yokai.

delivery.evidence: The apology satire is carried by the plot and by Ito's comic afterword on public apologies (The Beat; Wikipedia); no character argues for or against it.

31133.heading: Dorohedoro
31133.label: From summaries
31133.life_message: A good life is a shared meal, a loyal partner and a job you can keep. The world has no fair rulers, so you stick with your own people, keep your word to them, and laugh at the horror.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hospitality and friendship; the abusive powerful (Chidaruma) are humbled; forgiveness between old enemies.
frames.concerns: Killing is rarely framed as wrong, so evil is often made attractive through comedy (Inter Mirifica 7); devils shown as benign or desirable; inverted crosses as decor (CCC 2115-2117 on the occult); nudity (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Loyalty and shared meals; the proud devil ruler brought low (ch. 167).
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so friendly devils, devil exams and inverted crosses are a serious concern; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore a concern too.

frames.concerns: Demons and Hell played as comedy and reward; occult imagery throughout (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); killing without consequence. Views vary by congregation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are answered personally: Caiman hunts the sorcerer who cursed him (ch. 1 on); En's family avenges attacks on it; the Hole's dead take revenge as Hole-kun. There are no courts.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The lawless Hole and its free-for-all life are the norm; En's order is enforced by fear, not celebrated as law.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Partners and crews come first: Shin and Noi, Caiman and Nikaido, En's "family." Strangers are often fair game.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks are real (devils, En, his cleaners) and shown with affection, but the top devil is humbled (ch. 167) and humans and sorcerers mix at the Hungry Bug.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No sacred tradition guides life; Hell and magic are mechanics; science (Vaux, Kasukabe) and craft solve problems.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in a harsh world, but also food, parties, odd fashion and casual tolerance of difference (Turkey, ch. 167).

folkways.japan: The food culture (gyoza, the restaurant as home), oyabun-style crime "families," and the folk idea that the grudge of the unquieted dead becomes a vengeful spirit are Japanese elements; the devils and inverted crosses borrow Western occult imagery as style rather than belief.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Loveridge says it revels in absurdity; WSWS faults its weak social analysis; Anime Feminist stresses heart and whimsy. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series gives sorcerers, humans and devils each sympathetic and cruel members, and states no message outright.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and finding yourself through friends
Power as amusement; nothing is serious
Grievance of the exploited turned to slaughter

35293.heading: Doubt
35293.label: From summaries

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge for fathers' and parents' shame and ruin drives both villains; liars are punished by death.

Order vs freedom.evidence: A trapped group under a game's rules; order is imposed by the killer.

folkways.japan: Offline meetings (ofu-kai) of online friends, the loan-guarantor debt that ruins Mitsuki's father, media scandals that shame a family into suicide, and the rabbit-and-wolf game are drawn from Japanese settings; the death-game genre follows Battle Royale (Publishers Weekly).

delivery.evidence: The rule 'the liar must die' is stated by the villains; the book exposes everyone's lie but gives the moral to no hero (Slings & Arrows says the plot both carries and undercuts it).
delivery.note: A plot-driven thriller; the theme of lies and trust is carried by the game's structure, not by speeches.

35293.dominant: Nihilism (explored), Duty ethics (critiqued: an absolute rule against lying turned murderous).

108919.heading: Doughnuts Under a Crescent Moon
108919.label: From summaries

98416.heading: Dr. STONE
98416.label: From summaries
98416.life_message: A good life is spent learning, building and sharing knowledge so that every person can live. Progress is slow, earned step by step through work and cooperation, and it is passed down from parents to children.

frames.aligns: Faith and reason are not at odds in Catholic teaching (Fides et Ratio), and the series honors reason, work and the dignity of every life (Senku revives everyone; the purge is condemned). Mercy to enemies; honor for a father (CCC 2214-2220). Evil is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: A world with no God where science carries the hope of salvation; Dulin (Christian Research Journal) warns science can become an idol. Revival nudity and the harem arc (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Love for parents and ancestors, memory of the dead (Senku at Byakuya's grave, ch. 45), mercy to enemies, humility in learning.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the nudity and harem panels a concern. The story's only "liturgy," the priestess's tales, is turned into data, which may feel like a flattening of the sacred.

frames.aligns: Hard work, honesty, compassion, rescuing the sick (ch. 35-43), clear wrong in Tsukasa's purge and Ibara's tyranny.
frames.concerns: No acknowledgment of God; humans save themselves. Philippians 4:8 applied to the nudity, harem and teens brewing alcohol. Each congregation decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Dulin (Christian Research Journal) admires Senku's creativity in rebuilding for others and says Christians can serve God as scientists. Beneath the Tangles praises Senku's refusal to revive only the "best" people. Depicts wrong without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Dulin: Senku's motive is not distinctly Christian, and science can claim devotion that belongs to God. Fan service (SLJ).

frames.aligns: Little occult content: "sorcery" and petrification are explained as science, not spirits (ch. 17-19, 227-231). Clear right and wrong.
frames.concerns: A wholly naturalist worldview with no spiritual realm; a priestess tradition demythologized. Modesty standards and the harem arc.

frames.aligns: Common grace: the series celebrates real knowledge of creation and cultural work (the cultural mandate, Genesis 1:28). Depravity echoes in Ibara and in Tsukasa's view of corrupt adults.
frames.concerns: Humanity rebuilds itself with no reference to God's providence. WLC Q139 makes the harem and nudity panels a concern.

frames.aligns: Vocation: building, farming and healing as service to neighbor. The left-hand kingdom of reason and order is treated seriously; tyranny is resisted.
frames.concerns: No gospel and no God; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA about the fan service.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (healing Ruri, feeding the village), education for all, social holiness. Wesley valued science and medicine (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not tend to the knowledge or love of God; holiness churches more cautious about nudity and alcohol.

frames.aligns: A tradition of science and faith together; good and evil framed clearly; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: The absence of God; fan service.

frames.aligns: Senku avoids killing, wins wars by bluff and invention (ch. 53-83), and forgives enemies; a mutual-aid village.
frames.concerns: Progress through technology is the story's goal, at odds with Old Order separation and plain living; violence still used. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Learning and "the glory of God is intelligence" (D&C 93:36); family bonds across generations (Byakuya's records for his son); work and self-reliance.
frames.concerns: Revival nudity and the harem arc; teens brewing alcohol (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Science and faith compatible; care for the sick; rejection of eugenic culling and purges; justice for Ibara's subjects.
frames.concerns: Few women among the inventors (Common Sense Media); "gorilla" jokes; harem arc.

frames.aligns: Health, education and medicine are valued in the tradition; nothing spiritist; the dead do not walk.
frames.concerns: Teens brewing and drinking alcohol; nudity; no Creator, and petrification explained by alien machines. "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18).

frames.aligns: Little violence or spiritism; love of family, honesty, hard work.
frames.concerns: The story's hope is a human-built "Kingdom of Science" that will fix the world, against the teaching that only God's Kingdom will. Alcohol use by teens; nudity. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Goodness, cooperation and courage win; fear is overcome.
frames.concerns: The heroic turning point is a drug cure for disease (sulfa for Ruri's pneumonia, ch. 35-43); material medicine is shown as the means of healing, against the teaching on spiritual healing. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love of learning, honoring parents (Exodus 20:12), preserving a tradition across generations (the Hundred Tales as a kind of oral record), saving life above all (pikuach nefesh).
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the nudity and harem arc a concern; many Haredi homes restrict secular media; no God. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Learning, saving life, honoring the dead and ancestors, tikkun olam echoed in rebuilding the world.
frames.concerns: Fan service applied through family modesty values. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy, education, tikkun olam, rejection of eugenic culling; no stereotype concerns reported.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond fan service. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Seeking knowledge ('ilm) is praised in the tradition; justice against tyrants; mercy; care for the sick.
frames.concerns: Teens brewing and drinking alcohol; revival nudity and the harem arc (Qur'an 24:30-31, lowering the gaze); creation and the end of the world explained with no reference to God.

frames.aligns: Knowledge (jnana) and duty (dharma) as paths; devotion to a teacher and father; a hero who avoids killing.
frames.concerns: A purely material account of the world; some families apply the Gita's sattvic test to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Compassion, patience, investigation of cause and effect; Senku avoids killing where he can.
frames.concerns: Progress and craving for more (Ryusui's openly stated greed) are celebrated; the eight-precept view of entertainment; intoxicants made and drunk.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni), sharing (vand chakna), service to all (seva); tyranny opposed; equality of all people versus Tsukasa's "pure" selection.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and fan service; ego in Senku and Ryusui (the five vices). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Harmony of science and religion and the unity of humankind are core teachings; Senku's science is shared, serves everyone and rejects selective survival.
frames.concerns: Science shown without religion, which Bahá'í writings warn can drift into materialism; fan service.

frames.aligns: Gratitude to ancestors and founders, nature restored and beautiful (Boichi's untouched Japan), sincerity (makoto) in Senku's work; the village priestess is treated with respect.
frames.concerns: The priestess tradition is explained rather than kept as sacred; little else to raise. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for nature and lineage; "harm none" echoed in Senku's non-lethal tactics.
frames.concerns: "Sorcery" is unmasked as ignorance of science (ch. 17-19); Tsukasa's nature-first world is the villain's. No stereotyped witches. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: be industrious, be competent, safeguard and improve the environment, do not murder (Tsukasa's purge condemned).
frames.concerns: Gen Asagiri as a "mentalist" manipulator is a comic figure. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Science, education and STEM; against eugenic culling and authoritarian rule; Common Sense Media: a lot of positive messages (teamwork, scientific progress).
frames.concerns: Male-gaze art (SLJ); Ibara's harem used as plot; "gorilla" jokes; few women among the inventors (Common Sense Media); Anime Feminist's early worry about female characters.

frames.aligns: Reason, evidence, cooperation and human dignity, with no supernatural; knowledge shared freely; religion's mysteries explained naturally but without contempt; free inquiry.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; chemistry projects need safety talk.

frames.aligns: Respect for fathers, founders and inherited knowledge; earned authority; free trade and private initiative (Ryusui); utopian purges and tyrannies fail.
frames.concerns: Progress framed as the highest good; village tradition superseded; fan service.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person (all seven billion revived), free search for truth, democratic cooperation, justice against tyrants.
frames.concerns: Gender jokes; harem arc. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The Satanic Temple's tenet that beliefs should conform to the best scientific understanding fits Senku closely; skepticism of authority; rejection of tyranny; individual excellence.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; harm to the vulnerable (Ibara) condemned. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Deliverance from bondage: Ibara's island is freed (ch. 101-138); education and self-improvement for a whole village; healing the sick; every person worth saving, against Tsukasa's chosen few; enemies forgiven.
frames.concerns: No acknowledgment of God; humans save themselves; teens brewing alcohol; fan service in the harem arc. Holiness families may be more cautious. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Characters question, test and prove claims; "sorcery" and a sacred myth are explained as science without contempt; goodness comes from human care; meaning is built in this life; humans save themselves.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond fan service and lab safety.

frames.aligns: Wonder and humility before what is unknown: even Why-Man does not know who made it, and Senku answers with curiosity (ch. 231); no preaching for or against belief.
frames.concerns: The story is sure that science is the answer to every mystery it raises; the priestess tradition is explained away.

frames.aligns: Friendship, fairness and second chances; a hopeful ending with a wedding (ch. 232); enemies become friends.
frames.concerns: Spirit and tradition are explained away, which some spiritually minded families may not like; the fan service.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Senku answers insults with sarcasm, not vendetta; enemies are pardoned (Tsukasa, Hyoga, Xeno). Worth comes from what you contribute.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Kingdom of Science runs on voluntary cooperation and trade; Ibara's rule-bound tyranny (no new inventions, no leaving the island) is the counter-example (ch. 101-138).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin love drives key characters (Byakuya and Senku, Tsukasa and Mirai), but the goal is reviving all of humanity, strangers and enemies included.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senku leads and the village has a chief, but rank is earned by skill; elitism (Hyoga, Xeno) is defeated.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Sorcery becomes science (ch. 17-19); the priestess's tales become records (ch. 44-52); the petrifier is a machine (ch. 227-231).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival needs dominate the early story; later the joy of discovery and personal passion take center stage.

folkways.japan: The work ethic of steady effort, school-club-style teamwork, respect for teachers and the shonen ideal of friendship reflect Japanese norms; the secular, practical outlook also fits Japan's high secular-rational position on value surveys. The village festival, the chief's bout and the priestess are drawn from Japanese folk settings.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists the value of scientific progress as a theme; Beneath the Tangles notes Senku's stated belief that doing right leads to good results. No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The pro-science message is spoken openly in Senku's lines and the Science Corner asides, while rival visions get a sympathetic hearing in Tsukasa and a thinner one in Ibara.

personified.ideology: "Pure youth" primitivism and purge of corrupt adults
Village priestess tradition and oral memory

30229.heading: Dragon Head
30229.label: From summaries
30229.life_message: Fear, more than disaster, is what destroys people; facing it honestly and staying with one another, rather than numbing it, worshipping it or preying on the weak, is the only way to stay human, even with no answers.

content.category: Sexuality and romance (incl. fan service, manga art vs anime)

frames.concerns: The story dwells on fear, matter, injury and death as overwhelming realities.

frames.aligns: Endurance through a long dark road; hope that does not give up; protecting the weak; leaders who abuse power condemned.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: With courts gone, Teru must fight Nobuo and Nimura himself (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Collapse is a nightmare, but every attempt to impose order (the Izu mob, the drugged shelters) is worse.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty narrows to Teru and Ako; families are dead; strangers are dangerous.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Authority figures (a violent teacher, Nimura, officials) are untrustworthy.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A modern disaster world; rituals appear only as madness; science is abused for control.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Bare survival is the whole story (AniList Survival 100%).

folkways.japan: Earthquake, volcano, a vanished Mount Fuji and a Shinkansen school trip tap Japanese disaster fears; the collapse of teachers, the Self-Defense Forces and town officials mirrors 1990s distrust of institutions.

delivery.evidence: The bad answers to fear (worship, drugs, mob rule, suicide) are each given a character or group with reasons; Teru's monologues state his resolve, which Thompson finds unconvincing.
delivery.note: The book argues through what happens to people, not through lectures; the meaning of the disaster is never given.

185129.heading: Drama Queen
185129.label: From summaries
185129.life_message: Hatred of a whole people, fed by grievance and the story we tell about our own suffering, passes from person to person and wounds everyone, haters included; no one understands a conflict without the whole truth.

content.framing: Explored from inside the killers' view; the story frames hatred as a cycle

frames.concerns: Murder and cannibalism by the leads, framed with black humor; underage drunkenness; judgment slow to come and the ending unconfirmed.

frames.aligns: Anger and resentment (the passions) shown consuming Kitami and Nomamoto.
frames.concerns: Graphic killing and eating of bodies; guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Vengeance shown as a trap (Romans 12:19) if the ending judges it; prejudice exposed.
frames.concerns: Villain leads; gore and body disposal; drunkenness by a teenager (Ephesians 5:18); Philippians 4:8 test.

frames.aligns: Opens talk about prejudice against outsiders and loving the stranger (Leviticus 19:34).

frames.aligns: Hatred and bitterness shown as a destroying force.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: unequal privilege, poverty and prejudice all examined.
frames.concerns: Much harm, little mercy so far.

frames.aligns: Good and evil grow more complex as aliens are humanized.
frames.concerns: Cannibalism and gore; teen drinking for laughs.

frames.aligns: Violence answering violence is shown never ending.
frames.concerns: Revenge killing is the leads' project throughout; outside media.

frames.aligns: Warns against contention and hatred of others.
frames.concerns: Violent, disturbing content; underage drinking (Word of Wisdom; For the Strength of Youth).

frames.aligns: An allegory of anti-immigrant hatred and its cycle; aliens given backstories (ComicBook.com).
frames.concerns: Early chapters let xenophobic rhetoric stand unanswered (Anime Senpai); the "partner" line.

frames.aligns: Hatred shown as corrupting.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": graphic murder and cannibalism; drinking.

frames.aligns: Shows human societies unable to end hatred.
frames.concerns: Violence God hates (Psalm 11:5) is central and repeated; drunkenness.

frames.aligns: Hatred as a false belief that multiplies harm.
frames.concerns: Fear-inducing, degrading images throughout.

frames.aligns: Revenge forbidden (Leviticus 19:18); the stranger to be loved.

frames.aligns: Echoes of how scapegoating of minorities escalates.

frames.aligns: Confronting hatred of the outsider; the cost of prejudice to the prejudiced.
frames.concerns: Readers need help seeing the leads as cautionary, not models.

frames.aligns: Justice sought for a wrongful killing; prejudice examined (49:13 on peoples made to know one another).

frames.aligns: Hatred as the root of suffering is the stated theme ("hate brings pain," publisher text).

frames.aligns: Equality of all people; vengeance shown as ruinous.

185129.dominant: Patriotism / nationalism (critiqued, as anti-alien nativism), Critical theory (privilege and immigration satire), Strength rules (critiqued), Absurdism and Nihilism (black comedy).

folkways.japan: A Japanese seinen artist's view of Victorian England: Joe Suwa replaces Stoker's Dr. Seward as a Japanese photographer, Renfield becomes a karakuri (Edo-period mechanical doll) (Taliesin), and Sakamoto's practice of visiting a shrine for the lives lost in his work (Wikipedia) reflects Japanese custom. delivery.evidence: The prejudice of the school is shown through Mina's experience; the VIZ blurb states the theme of a group that eclipses gender, nationality and station; Taliesin notes that unity is not yet shown in vol. 2. Sakamoto speaks of a mission to revive Stoker's message (ANN interview).

43801.heading: Drifters
43801.label: From summaries
43801.life_message: War is the stage on which people show what they are worth, and the story sides with warriors who keep a code, free the enslaved and protect the weak, against those who use power to persecute or exterminate.

content.framing: Endorsed when the Drifters fight; cruelty by Orte and the Ends condemned

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Drifters act freely, then rally under Nobunaga's plans and take over a state (v3-4).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Clan loyalty mixed with new bonds across races and eras.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Military rank and command matter; Nobunaga plans as a lord; equality of races is the goal.

folkways.japan: The Shimazu clan's ferocity at Sekigahara, Sengoku-period lordship, head-taking and respectful burial of heads, the Genpei War's Yoichi and Yoshitsune, the Shinsengumi and WWII Japanese aviators reflect Japanese military history and the warrior ideal; the story admires the ideal while laughing at its excesses.

delivery.evidence: The Black King and Seimei hold opposed views of humanity and the Black King is given his reasons (fan wiki); Orte's knights are drawn as pure villains (TV Tropes lists Aram as a Complete Monster).

97675.heading: Drifting Dragons
97675.label: From summaries

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pride in the trade and an old rivalry (Mika and Cujo, v6), but disputes are settled by work, not feuds; a "Showdown" (ch. 34) is the exception.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Free nomadic life in the sky; ship discipline and a captain.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The crew is a family against an ostracizing world (Wikipedia).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ship roles and a captain, but rookies are taught and listened to.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Practical craft knowledge and ecology alongside clan traditions (the Taruka, the Molatao).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A miss means hunger and no repairs; but the crew lives for the joy of the hunt and the meal.

folkways.japan: The crew's craft pride, the care in preparing and thanking for food, and the whaling-like trade echo Japanese work and food culture; the European-styled port towns and airships draw on Miyazaki-like steampunk fantasy.

delivery.evidence: Values come through daily work and meals; the Slayers are an opposing ideology given a captain and a contract (v7-9, v14), but no review on delivery was opened (to verify).
delivery.note: The series argues by showing: the Quin Zaza eats and uses what it kills, the Slayers waste it, and the reader is left to weigh them.

personified.ideology: eat what you hunt; passion and skill
kill for profit by any means

97675.dominant: Communitarianism (the crew as family), Environmentalism (no waste, no overhunting), Pragmatism.

folkways.japan: The story is set almost wholly outside Japan (South America, Australia, China, the Middle East); Kenji, the brother of a yakuza boss, brings a Japanese underworld code. The seinen frankness about sex and violence reflects its adult magazine.

folkways.japan: The student council, senpai-kohai year ranks, club budgets, school ghost stories (nanafushigi), a hot-spring trip and rice-ball (onigiri) sales are standard Japanese school settings, and four-panel gag comedy is a long-running Japanese form; the series follows a line of student-council gag manga such as Seitokai Yakuindomo.

delivery.note: Hope and friendship are shown through Mavis's choices; Otaku USA found some dialogue sappy.

personified.ideology: Hard choices: sacrifice one to save many

85319.dominant: Communitarianism (the guild as family), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (magic world).

100456.heading: Farming Life in Another World
100456.label: From summaries
100456.life_message: Patient, honest work on the land and an open door to strangers can turn a wilderness into a peaceful, plentiful home; a life lost to overwork is answered by a slow, good life among family and neighbors.

content.framing: Endorsed (plural marriage and many children); pressure on Hiraku played as comedy

frames.aligns: Dignity of work and care for creation (Laborem Exercens); hospitality to refugees and strangers; openness to children; peacemaking.
frames.concerns: Plural marriage presented as ideal (CCC 2387); sex pressed on Hiraku as a joke; idol statues; a God who errs.

frames.aligns: Simple labor, hospitality and thanksgiving for the harvest.
frames.concerns: Plural marriage; sensual scenes; carved gods given offerings.

frames.aligns: Hard work (Proverbs 10:4), generosity and kindness to strangers.
frames.concerns: Polygamy as the happy ending; sexual jokes and partial nudity; idols and offerings (Exodus 20:4); wine as a main pleasure.

frames.aligns: Stewardship, generosity and welcome; Family Friendly Gaming praises its story and home-building.
frames.concerns: Family Friendly Gaming flags revealing clothing, lust, the breeding schedule and idol-making; a fallible God.

frames.aligns: A peaceful, prosperous community built by blessing and labor.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on sexual content and drinking; angels and demons as housemates; offerings to carved gods.

frames.aligns: The cultural mandate: subduing and cultivating the earth (Genesis 1:28); common grace in honest trade.
frames.concerns: Polygamy against creation order (Genesis 2:24); images of gods (Second Commandment); sexual humor.

frames.aligns: The farmer's vocation honored; serving the neighbor through daily work.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment (plural marriage, sexual jokes); First Commandment (idol statues). LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Doing good to all who come; works of mercy toward refugees.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches object to drinking, plural marriage and sexual jokes; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Pastoral idyll, hospitality and thanksgiving for the harvest.
frames.concerns: Plural marriage; sexual comedy. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on how much it matters.

frames.aligns: Farming, mutual aid and a nonviolent village that turns enemies into neighbors echo Anabaptist ideals.
frames.concerns: Plural marriage and immodesty; worldly media; images of gods.

frames.aligns: Self-reliance, work, gardens and large families.
frames.concerns: Plural marriage (long discontinued in the Church); immodesty; alcohol (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Welcome of refugees and every species; creation care; peace over war.
frames.concerns: Women valued for bearing children; consent played as a joke.

frames.aligns: Garden life, health restored, rest from overwork.
frames.concerns: Alcohol central to village life (temperance teaching); polygamy; spirits and idols.

frames.aligns: Paradise-earth farming imagery; peace among peoples.
frames.concerns: Polygamy, spirits, angels and demons as friends, idol statues, magic.

frames.aligns: Health restored; harmony and supply; fear of the forest overcome.
frames.concerns: Sensual content; drinking.

frames.aligns: Blessing of the land and hospitality (hachnasat orchim); honest trade.
frames.concerns: Avodah zarah: statues of gods with offerings; tzniut; plural marriage beyond any halakhic frame.

frames.aligns: Care for land, workers and the stranger (Leviticus 19:33-34).
frames.concerns: Plural marriage; idol statues; sexual comedy.

frames.aligns: Inclusion and welcome; peace and fair dealing.
frames.concerns: Gender roles in the household; consent played as comedy.

frames.aligns: Honest work and hospitality; peace with neighbors.
frames.concerns: Statues of gods with offerings (shirk); more than four wives; alcohol central; nudity scenes.

frames.aligns: Grihastha (householder) life, abundance from work, offerings of gratitude.
frames.concerns: Modesty; sensual humor.

frames.aligns: Right livelihood and peaceful coexistence; compassion to all beings.
frames.concerns: Fifth precept (wine central); sensual craving as a running joke.

frames.aligns: Kirat karni (honest work) and vand chakna (sharing).
frames.concerns: Plural marriage; alcohol; idols.

frames.aligns: Unity of diverse peoples; work as worship.
frames.concerns: Monogamy principle; alcohol forbidden.

frames.aligns: Gratitude for the harvest, offerings at a shrine, harmony with the forest and its spirits.

frames.aligns: Living by the seasons and the land; many gods honored with offerings.
frames.concerns: Pressure on Hiraku breaks consent ideals.

frames.aligns: Building a thriving group (third dynamic); productive work.
frames.concerns: Faithfulness model.

frames.aligns: Diverse community, refugees welcomed, sustainability.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Starts as survival in the Forest of Death and becomes leisure, festivals and comfort.

folkways.japan: The slow-life (nonbiri) isekai is a response to Japanese overwork culture (the hero's first death; the author's own fatigue, Otaku USA), and the village under a respected household head echoes rural ie (household) customs, harvest festivals and shrine offerings.

delivery.evidence: Episodic daily-life chapters; Anime UK News says each chapter reads like a diary entry with almost no conflict. Anime Feminist found the opening's apology from God heavy-handed.
delivery.note: The message rides on the slow growth of the village rather than on argument; no rival way of life is given a voice.

personified.ideology: Slow, honest work and an open door
Rumor and fear of the unknown

100456.dominant: Communitarianism (the village as family), Traditionalism (land, household, children), Hedonism (food, wine, comfort), Pacifism / nonviolence (conflicts ended by welcome).

86310.heading: Fire Force
86310.label: From summaries
86310.life_message: A good life is the hero's life: you keep hope against despair, protect people even when they call you a devil, and treat your team as a family. Faith is honored when it is sincere and serves people; institutions that use faith to control people are exposed.

content.framing: Endorsed as comedy; defended in ch. 280-282

frames.aligns: Evil (the Evangelist, Rekka) is framed as evil; hope over despair; the sincere nun and prayers for the dead are shown with respect.
frames.concerns: A church modeled on Catholic rites is revealed as founded for evil; a human becomes creator and fashions a god for people (ch. 298-302). The Lure gags make sexual humiliation of a teen comic, against Inter Mirifica 7 and CCC 2521-2524 on modesty.

frames.aligns: Prayer for the departed; the struggle against despair (akedia).
frames.concerns: Church imagery used for an evil institution; the hero as world-creator; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the fan service the larger concern.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; protecting others; the exposure of religious hypocrisy.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 applied to the fan-service gags; a human taking God's place in the finale (Isaiah 45:7, 18). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Hope against despair; hypocrisy and false teachers exposed (Matthew 7:15); sincere faith honored in Iris. Geeks Under Grace praises its themes of family and protecting others.
frames.concerns: Geeks Under Grace finds the church modeled too closely on reality and the nun's sexualization irritating; a human creator-savior; heavy fan service.

frames.aligns: Spiritual-warfare imagery: an apocalyptic being and its cult are defeated.
frames.concerns: Media as an open door: fire-spirit powers, an otherworld (Adolla), communion with an evil being for power ("Grace"), and a hero who becomes god are shown positively or neutrally. Fan service against holiness standards.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in human cruelty; idolatry of a false church exposed; common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 for the Lure gags; the story traces all gods to a despair entity and ends with a human making a god, against the Creator-creature distinction (WSC Q4).

frames.aligns: Exposing a church that controls through fear echoes Reformation critique; the firefighter's vocation as service.
frames.concerns: A human creator in the finale; fan service (LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA).

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (prayers and care for victims); social holiness against corrupt power.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used in the name of the Lord Jesus applies most to the Lure gags; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: institutional corruption is critiqued while personal faith is honored, in a tradition at home with fantasy.
frames.concerns: Fan service of a teen; the creator-hero finale as theology.

frames.aligns: Suspicion of a state church allied with empire matches Anabaptist history; mutual aid in the companies.
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' main tool (Matthew 5:39); fan service; conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a corrupted church that keeps truth hidden; family reunion (Shinra, Sho and their mother join hands in the finale); hope.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the Lure gags; a human remaking creation.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutional religion that serves power; care for victims; sincere faith not mocked.
frames.concerns: Treatment of a teenage girl in the fan service (ComicBook.com; The Back Catalogue); fatalism preached by a church.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a church-state alliance can echo the Adventist reading of Revelation (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so souls passing to another realm and a human reviving the dead conflict with teaching; fan service against FB 22.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a corrupt religious establishment may resonate with Witness teaching on false religion (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic (fire powers, Adolla, communion with a being), violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality as comedy are the jw.org tests.

frames.aligns: Thought shapes reality in the story (Adolla as collective imagination; the hero remakes the world by imagining it); fear of death reduced at the end.
frames.concerns: Fear, fire and death shown as overwhelming forces through most of the series.

frames.aligns: Exposure of idolatry and false prophets; protection of life (pikuach nefesh).
frames.concerns: A human as creator who makes a god to be worshipped (avodah zarah); tzniut makes the fan service a major concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a manipulative cult; protection of life; family reunion.
frames.concerns: Fan service of a teen; a human creator figure.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in rebuilding a burnt world; critique of institutions that oppress.
frames.concerns: Treatment of a teenage girl in the gags.

frames.aligns: Hope over despair; justice against oppressors; exposure of false religious leaders.
frames.concerns: A human becomes creator and makes a god to be worshipped, against tawhid; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) weighs heavily with the Lure gags.

frames.aligns: Fire as sacred, cosmic destruction and re-creation, a hero acting from duty; deities are not mocked.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the tamasic category to the gags and horror.

frames.aligns: Adolla as a collective mind shaped by human despair or hope; the finale ends the cycle of despair and salvation and lessens fear of death (fan wiki).
frames.concerns: Killing is routine; right speech and what feeds the mind weigh on the gags.

frames.aligns: Courage in defense of the oppressed; ego and cruelty condemned in villains.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) shown as comedy (one of the five vices).

frames.aligns: Religion that divides and controls is critiqued; service and unity of former rivals; the faith has no clergy, matching the critique of a priestly class (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: The chaste and holy life counsel weighs on the gags; a human creator figure.

frames.aligns: Prayer for the dead echoes purification rites; sun and fire imagery; Amaterasu named.
frames.concerns: The name Amaterasu is given to a power plant with a person trapped inside; sun worship shown as a cover for evil.

frames.aligns: Fire and sun as powerful symbols; no witch stereotypes (Inca dresses as a mischievous witch at the end).
frames.concerns: The sun-worshipping religion is the corrupt one, though the story blames its founders, not sun reverence.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: do not murder, help others; villains who harm are condemned.
frames.concerns: Killing as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Critique of church-state-corporate power; found family; a non-powered leader (Obi).
frames.concerns: Repeated sexual-humiliation gags with a 17-year-old (ComicBook.com; The Back Catalogue); ch. 280-282 frames her exposure as empowering sex appeal.

frames.aligns: Religion used for control is exposed; religion described as a human collective creation (Ohkubo); hope as a human choice.
frames.concerns: The finale resolves through a supernatural creator-hero; fan service of a teen as exploitation.

frames.aligns: Heroism, duty, loyalty, team as family, protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Established religion portrayed as founded on a lie; fan service of a teen.

frames.aligns: Free search for meaning; worth of every person (even Infernals get a prayer); critique of dogma used for control.
frames.concerns: Treatment of a teenage girl in the gags; violence.

frames.aligns: A hero branded a devil is the true protector; established religion is exposed as a tool of control; rebellion against corrupt authority is justified (Company 8 as outlaws).
frames.concerns: The story ends in self-sacrifice for the group and a benevolent new god figure.

frames.aligns: Hope that refuses despair; protecting the weak; deliverance from a lying, oppressive establishment; a family reunited; a sincere woman of prayer whose faith protects her friends.
frames.concerns: A teenage girl groped and stripped for laughs; supernatural powers drawn from an otherworldly being; the story traces faith to despair and ends with a human making a god.

frames.aligns: Religion shown as a human collective creation (Ohkubo) and as a tool of control when institutions misuse it; skeptics and believers both act from compassion; hope is a human choice.
frames.concerns: The resolution is supernatural, and the hero gives people a god because they need one; a skeptic (Hibana) is drawn harshly at first; teen fan service.

frames.aligns: Sincere believers, doubters and fanatics all have voices; humility about where gods come from; doubt is not punished.
frames.concerns: A firm in-story answer about the origin of all religion; heavy fan service of a teen.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to a team, family reunited, protecting people, karma-like justice for villains, and hope against despair; a personal spiritual sense (prayer for the dead) respected.
frames.concerns: Teen fan service and groping jokes; constant violence and horror.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Shinra seeks recognition as a hero after being called a devil; Arthur's knight's code and Asakusa's pride (ch. 48); Tamaki answers public shaming by fighting on (ch. 280).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Disciplined companies with captains, but the heroes defy corrupt orders and become outlaws (about ch. 175-197).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Team as family (Ohkubo); the Kusakabe brothers and their mother join hands to win the finale; the epilogue serves the whole world.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks exist, but Obi, a non-powered captain, leads by care; the church hierarchy is exposed.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The inherited state religion is shown as founded on a lie; personal faith is respected; the resolution is supernatural.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hope and choosing one's own path weigh against a world built around fear and fatalism.

folkways.japan: The firefighter company as family, senpai-captain respect, the Edo-style Asakusa company and the fan-service gags of weekly shonen magazines reflect Japanese norms; Ohkubo modeled the setting on Meiji and Taisho Japan (MyAnimeList, 2019). The church's Western Christian look is an outside model used as setting, which Geeks Under Grace reads as too close to real Christianity.

delivery.evidence: Sincere believers, skeptics and fanatics each speak, and Ohkubo frames religion as a collective human creation (Anime Corner); the church's leaders and its fanatic officer are drawn as plain villains.
delivery.note: The message about hope and faith comes through battles and revelations rather than lectures, but the final arc states its view of gods and death directly.

personified.ideology: Hope and heroism; faith has worth whatever its object

86310.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist/New Age.

87170.heading: Fire Punch
87170.label: From summaries
87170.life_message: In a cruel world people survive by playing roles and believing stories, including gods they invent; revenge and false worship destroy, and what is left worth having is the plain choice to live and to love another person.

content.framing: Sexual violence condemned, but used as the backdrop of a cruel world

frames.aligns: Self-giving to feed the hungry; human dignity against slavery and trafficking; revenge shown to destroy the avenger; Doma's remorse.
frames.concerns: Religion shown only as manipulation; sexual abuse of a child (ch. 2) and an incestuous relationship (ch. 1); suicide attempts with no hope beyond this life; Togata's identity affirmed against Church teaching on the body (Dignitas Infinita, 2024). Inter Mirifica 7 allows depicting evil to aid understanding, not to make it attractive.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and enslaves; a false savior exposed; endurance of suffering.
frames.concerns: A man worshipped as god is the plot engine, with no true sacred to contrast; incest themes; Togata's transition theme; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the imagery itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; slavery and abuse condemned; a false god exposed as false.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and incest themes throughout; suicide; a world without a true God; trans character affirmed. Soul liberty means families decide; many would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Exposes how people create gods to serve their needs (an idolatry theme some evangelicals discuss); sacrificial love; revenge's cost.

frames.aligns: False religion and bondage shown as harms; slaves set free.

frames.aligns: Total depravity on vivid display; idol-making as the human default (Calvin's "idol factory"); common grace lets some value its honesty.
frames.concerns: WLC Q136 on self-murder (suicide attempts); Q139 on lascivious pictures; incest; no redemption beyond human acts.

frames.aligns: Agni cannot save himself or others; false gods fail; self-giving to feed others echoes vocation.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment (incest, sexual violence); despair and suicide; LCMS and ELCA families may differ on Togata.

frames.aligns: Social holiness critique of slavery and trafficking; mercy to the hungry.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches avoid this level of sexual violence, nudity and despair; UMC families vary on Togata.

frames.aligns: Honest picture of sin, suffering and false religion; dignity of the enslaved; repentance (Doma).
frames.concerns: Sexual violence involving children; incest; suicide. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on Togata.

frames.aligns: Doma's late pacifism and care for orphans; revenge shown as ruin.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; violence as the main action; the pacifist community is slaughtered by the hero.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; family love (Agni and Luna).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on sexual content, graphic violence and degrading media; the law of chastity; false prophets.

frames.aligns: Liberation of slaves; a trans character treated with sympathy; critique of religious manipulation.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence against children and women used heavily; despair; little hope offered.

frames.aligns: Exposure of false worship; freedom from bondage.
frames.concerns: FB 22 on entertainment; "by beholding we become changed"; graphic violence and sexual content.

frames.aligns: False religion exposed as human-made.
frames.concerns: Gore, sexual immorality including abuse and incest, suicide and a man worshipped as god, all against jw.org entertainment counsel.

frames.aligns: Endurance; refusal to be defined by suffering.
frames.concerns: Bodily suffering, death and horror are the substance of the story; sensual and abusive content.

frames.aligns: Idolatry exposed; pikuach nefesh echoed in feeding the starving; slavery condemned (Exodus).
frames.concerns: Arayot (incest and sexual violence); kavod ha-met (desecrated bodies); tzniut; suicide.

frames.aligns: Critique of idolatry and tyranny; teshuvah in Doma.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence, incest and gore; despair.

frames.aligns: Social justice: slavery and abuse condemned; inclusion of a trans character.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and incest; nihilism.

frames.aligns: Shirk exposed (a man worshipped as god); freeing slaves; feeding the hungry.
frames.concerns: Zina and incest; sexual violence; nudity; suicide; Togata's transition.

frames.aligns: Agni's name recalls the Vedic fire god; karma-like consequences of revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Imposed orders (Behemdorg, Agnism) are tyrannies; freedom brings chaos but is preferred.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Agni's loyalty is to his sister above any community; strangers matter less until late.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchies of rulers, priests and masters are condemned; the freed slaves are equals, until a new cult forms.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Traditions and religions are shown as human inventions; survival logic rules.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A survival world of famine, cold and slavery; self-expression (Togata's film) is a luxury that also harms.

folkways.japan: A Jump+ web manga that borrows from Western and Korean film rather than Japanese tradition; Japanese elements are few (the blessing and cult structure echo new-religion movements only loosely, from general knowledge; to verify). Its frankness and genre shifts fit the web platform's freedom from magazine limits.

delivery.evidence: The story rarely states a moral; villains such as Doma and Judah are given reasons and inner lives, while Sulya and Jack are flatter.
delivery.note: Fujimoto changes genre almost every volume and undercuts each apparent message; readers have to draw their own conclusions.

personified.ideology: Revenge, then the will to live

87170.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism, Postmodernism (film and fiction), critique of invented religion and authoritarian rule.

159142.heading: Firefly Wedding

Civic vs kin.evidence: Personal and kin loyalty over law; the island operates outside the state; a pardon, not justice, frees Shinpei.

folkways.japan: Meiji-era aristocracy and arranged marriage, red-light districts and the oiran system, retainer shame and punishment, and the firefly as an image of brief life (and of souls in Japanese folk belief, from general knowledge; to verify) reflect Japanese history and imagery; the story turns against the family-first marriage system rather than drawing on it.

delivery.evidence: The story shows rather than tells; Satoko voices objections to Shinpei's killing and he changes, but the narrative also enjoys his violence (But Why Tho; Aftermath).

159142.dominant: Expressive individualism (choosing her own love), Feminism and Traditionalism (a woman against the marriage system), Duty ethics (family duty weighed), Might makes right (explored through Shinpei).

folkways.japan: Japanese settings: an aging, unequal society, Buddhist funerary temples, Pure Land imagery (Gokuraku Jōdo), sacred camphor trees and a culture of quiet self-sacrifice for others; the story questions that self-sacrifice when the poor are made to bear it.

delivery.evidence: Both the pro- and anti-transfloration sides are shown as self-interested; VIZ's vol. 5 blurb says the heroes question whether they are on the right side (VIZ).

35806.heading: Franken Fran
35806.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: Ero-guro (erotic-grotesque) is an established strand of Japanese horror art, and the rural mansion, wartime-scientist backstory and episodic monster-of-the-week format draw on that tradition and on Osamu Tezuka's Black Jack, described here as context.

folkways.japan: Arakawa set the story in a European-style country, but its themes draw on Japanese history and life: the dispossession of the Ainu in Hokkaido, interviews with WWII veterans, and her parents' farming ethic of working for what you eat (Wikipedia; The Mary Sue). Respect for teachers (Izumi) and senior officers is Japanese in feel.

delivery.evidence: Arakawa set out to put social issues in the story and presents the Ishval war from many viewpoints (Wikipedia; The Mary Sue). Villains get motives (Hohenheim's history, Scar's grief); Father's pride is the clearest moral.
delivery.note: The themes are stated by characters (equivalent exchange, the all-is-one teaching, the meaning of family) but carried mostly by plot and consequences rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Equivalent exchange, then humility and love beyond exchange

folkways.japan: Middle-school life, 2000s keitai (phone) culture, a new religious movement built around a child oracle (echoing Japan's many new religions; from general knowledge; to verify) and the yandere archetype reflect Japanese settings; the death-game genre it helped shape (alongside *Battle Royale*) is a Japanese form.

frames.aligns: Bondage to debt and the oppression of the poor condemned, as the prophets condemn those who "sell the poor for a pair of shoes" (Amos 2:6); Ishida's self-giving love.
frames.concerns: Gambling as the world of the story; despair with no faith to carry people through; swearing and cruelty.

frames.aligns: Problems are solved by reasoning, testing the rules and reading people; no supernatural rescue; exploitation exposed.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.aligns: Honest about how hard trust is; no preaching in either direction; characters wrestle with doubt.
frames.concerns: Bleak at times.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fairness and karma-like payback for some villains (Tonegawa).
frames.concerns: Despair runs deep and the biggest villain wins this round.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Face and apology matter: Tonegawa must kneel on a burning plate to apologize (ch. ~135-137); Kaiji plays E-Card to avenge his dead friends.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The games run beyond the law (outside the Coast Guard patrol zone, SKJAM); there is no legal order to appeal to.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kaiji seeks allies among strangers; Ishida gambles for his family (fan wiki).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A steep hierarchy of the rich over debtors, and the story sides with those below (AniList Class Struggle).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Probability and strategy, not faith or custom, decide fates (MangaUpdates Strategic Minds).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Debt, unemployment and survival dominate (MangaUpdates Debt/s, Unemployment).

folkways.japan: Set in 1990s recession Japan, it reflects the post-bubble "lost generation": unemployment, loan sharks and the shame of debt in a society that prizes steady work. Kneeling apology (dogeza) and loss of face are Japanese forms the story turns into punishments.

delivery.evidence: E-Card is an open allegory of Emperor, Citizen and Slave (Wikipedia); a talkative, grandiose narrator explains the stakes with wild metaphors (Daryl Surat of Otaku USA, via Wikipedia); Tonegawa and Hyodo deliver lectures that Fukumoto calls cruel truths.
delivery.note: The class message is stated in the games' design and in villains' speeches, but the villains are given strong arguments about personal responsibility, so the story does not simply preach one side. Whether the English edition's narration reads as heavy-handed was not checked.

personified.ideology: Desperate underdog relying on wits and, slowly, on trust
Winners deserve to win; debtors are to blame for themselves
The rich may use the poor for amusement
Self-sacrifice for family and a friend

33572.dominant: Strength rules (critiqued), Marxism (class struggle explored), Existentialism, Pragmatism.

54903.heading: GANGSTA.
54903.label: From summaries
54903.life_message: In a city that treats some people as disposable, loyalty to the few who stand by you, and refusing to treat anyone as less than human, keeps you alive and decent, but the cost is high and the world does not change easily.

content.framing: Neutral (killing as work); cruelty and massacre condemned
Mixed: forced prostitution and abuse condemned; adult sex work treated as a job

folkways.japan: The Western-styled mafia city is a stylized import; the loyalty within a crew and the outlaw with a code echo Japanese ninkyo (chivalrous gangster) fiction, and the discrimination theme speaks to disability more than to any Japanese setting.

delivery.evidence: The anti-discrimination theme is carried by the setting (tags, the Three Laws, massacres) rather than speeches; Otaku USA calls the stories simplified revenge fantasy; anti-Twilight villains get little inner life in sources opened.
delivery.note: The message is shown through who suffers and who protects whom; the heroes are not idealized, and the creator has spoken about the theme only outside the book (Real Sound).

Pragmatic power that uses the weak
