30564.heading: Gantz
30564.label: From summaries
30564.life_message: A good life is found in caring for particular people (a girlfriend, a little brother, a friend) and protecting them, even in a universe that shows no sign of caring back; selfishness and cruelty are common and ugly, and self-giving love is rare and costly.

content.framing: Neutral to shown with consequences; massacres condemned
Mixed: sexual assault shown as vile; fan service and casual sex not framed critically

frames.aligns: Kato's self-giving love for strangers and his brother (John 15:13); the dignity of victims; remorse after killing (Sakurai); critique of bystander indifference (ch. 1).
frames.concerns: The final being dismisses humanity with no answer from faith (v36); fan service and sexual content involving minors run against Inter Mirifica 7 (evil not made attractive) and CCC 2523-2525 on modesty.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (lust, wrath, despair) on every page; Kurono's slow change toward love.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the nudity and gore a heavy concern; holy images (Buddha, Kannon) as monsters; a cosmos without God.

frames.aligns: Clear moral contrast between Kato and the Osaka team; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 is the common test, and the nudity, sex scenes and profanity fail it for most families; a godless cosmology goes unanswered. Each congregation is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Many distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it: massacres and sexual predators are shown as vile; hunger for purpose in a purposeless game can open faith conversations.
frames.concerns: Fan service is presented for enjoyment, not as sin; hope rests on human love without God. Some families favor separation from such media.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice, clear evil in the massacres.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a cosmos ruled by indifferent powers, souls treated as data, graphic sexual content. Holiness standards make it a strong concern.

frames.aligns: Depravity shown in raw form (bystanders, bullies, the Osaka team); common grace lets adults value serious work by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists lascivious books and pictures among sins against the seventh commandment; the sexual content weighs heavily; providence replaced by indifferent beings.

frames.aligns: No one can save themselves in the game; Kato's free self-giving reads as neighbor-love.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered; entertainment is judged by conscience, and LCMS and WELS families are much more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Kato); social holiness against bullying and abuse.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used in the name of Jesus; holiness churches would avoid the sexual content entirely; UMC families more open.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges dark works by framing; massacre and predation are framed as evil.
frames.concerns: The godless cosmology goes unchallenged; fan service is not framed as wrong. Episcopal and ACNA families would both treat it as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Kato tries not to kill where he can (TV Tropes); remorse after killing (Sakurai).
frames.concerns: Violence as the way to survive and win (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family care (Kato and Ayumu); love between Kurono and Tae; agency against an arbitrary game.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the 18+ rating, nudity and sex put it far outside youth guidance; souls called worthless clash with the plan of salvation.

frames.aligns: Critique of bystander apathy, bullying and abuse; empathy for the giants as a people fleeing a dying world (v36).
frames.concerns: Objectification of women; sexual violence used as plot; a shooter in racial disguise (ch. 123).

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice; care for family.
frames.concerns: The dead return as copies and souls are reborn, against teaching on the state of the dead; Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the explicit content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love of family, protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel asks whether entertainment features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality are central; reincarnating souls conflict with teaching on death.

frames.aligns: Love is what carries Kurono through.
frames.concerns: The story dwells on fear, death, bodily destruction and sensuality and treats matter as all there is; members guard thought against these.

frames.aligns: Saving a life (the opening rescue); protecting a younger brother; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the nudity, sex and profanity a heavy concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media entirely; denial of God unanswered.

frames.aligns: Saving life; critique of bystanders; dignity of victims.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content and stereotyped women; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Bystander ethics; tikkun olam echoes in Kato; empathy for the giants.
frames.concerns: Exploitation and objectification of women; sexual violence as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) under trial; protecting kin; saving life (Qur'an 5:32).
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the nudity and sex a heavy concern; denial of God; souls treated as data.

frames.aligns: Souls exist and are reborn (v36; TV Tropes), an echo of rebirth; duty to protect family; craving and violence lead to ruin.
frames.concerns: Souls called meaningless, with no dharma or moksha; Buddhist statues as monsters; many families would place the gore and sex in the Gita's tamasic category.

frames.aligns: Rebirth of souls (v36); suffering and craving as the human condition; Kurono's turn from selfishness to compassion; mercy toward the aliens (v35).
frames.concerns: A Kannon and Buddha statues are killer aliens and a priest is helpless (ch. 62-94); killing for points breaks the first precept; the sex and gore weigh on mindful consumption.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) in the Osaka team and Nishi lead to ruin; Kato's courage echoes the saint-soldier ideal.
frames.concerns: Lust is shown so often and so explicitly that it reads as appealing; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Service and sacrifice (Kato); the world's peoples facing a common threat.
frames.concerns: The call to a chaste and holy life warns against degrading art; constant conflict; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Yokai-themed aliens in the Osaka arc draw on folklore; sincerity in Kato.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity (kegare) everywhere; temple statues as monsters.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and for the giants' families; no stereotyped witches.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against constant killing; sexual exploitation without consent.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts "Do not murder" and "Safeguard and improve your environment"; massacres condemned.
frames.concerns: Killing for points; no content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Critique of bystander apathy, bullying, abuse and media spectacle; empathy for the aliens as refugees (v36).
frames.concerns: Objectification of women and sexual assault as plot (Otaku USA on Kishimoto); sexual content involving minors; a massacre in racial disguise.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by people in an indifferent universe; no prayer saves anyone; love and courage need no god.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown for shock; the final being also asserts that souls exist and are reborn, which a naturalist would reject.

frames.aligns: Courage, protective masculinity, loyalty, duty to a younger brother; decadence punished (the Osaka team).
frames.concerns: Media that degrades the good and beautiful; sexual content; contempt for institutions.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including the giants; justice for abuse victims.
frames.concerns: Objectification and sexual violence; age-appropriateness makes this adult reading.

frames.aligns: Art that challenges authority: Gantz is an arbitrary master, and the being's indifference matches a non-theistic view; individuals make their own meaning.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules condemn harm to children and unwanted sexual advances, both of which appear (Takeshi, Ayumu, Sakurai; assaults).

frames.aligns: Kato's sacrificial love and protection of his little brother; captives rescued from an alien city where humans are farmed (v31-35); a deliverance story at the end.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content and sexual violence, including against minors; a cosmos that calls humanity dust with no caring God; despair; a massacre staged in racial disguise (ch. 123).

frames.aligns: Meaning built in this life by human love and effort; the priest's prayers fail and no god intervenes (v6-8); the godlike being is shown as arrogant and indifferent.
frames.concerns: The being asserts souls exist and are reborn (v36; fiction, noted); exploitation and sexual violence used for shock.

frames.aligns: The mystery of Gantz is never fully explained; humility before a vast universe; no sermon for faith or against it until the end.
frames.concerns: A long final lecture with firm cosmic claims; bleakness; contempt for human worth voiced by the being.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, protecting family and friends; the heroes come home (ch. 383).
frames.concerns: Gore, cruelty and sexual content far heavier than most families want; long stretches of despair.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge and status drive several characters (Sakurai's revenge killings, v10; Nishi's school massacre, v26) but are shown as ugly; Kurono and Kato fight for others, not for face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Gantz's order is arbitrary and the state is absent (Shinjuku, ch. 123-125); survival is left to individuals and small teams.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The deepest loyalties are particular: Kato and his brother, Kurono and Tae. Kato's rescue of a stranger (ch. 1) is the civic counterweight.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teams sort by points and experience, but leadership is earned (Kurono, v13-14) rather than inherited.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as monsters (temple statues) or helpless prayer; the final explanation is technological and denies that humanity matters (v36).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is the whole game; staying alive comes first, with little room for self-expression.

folkways.japan: Bystander shame on a Tokyo subway platform, school bullying, the idol industry (Reika), yokai folklore in the Osaka arc and a Buddhist temple are contemporary Japanese settings rather than a message about Japan. The cluster match is loose, because the story's values are mostly set by an extreme survival game.

delivery.evidence: Most themes come through events; the final arc states its cosmology through a long speech by the being behind Gantz (v36). A MyAnimeList reviewer finds no meaningful philosophy; Yokogao Magazine reads it as a study of the human condition.
delivery.note: Oku says he uses grotesque and erotic scenes, surprise and humor to keep readers engaged (Gigazine, 2016), so the message is often secondary to the spectacle.

personified.ideology: Meaning found through love and loyalty
Humanity is insignificant; order without care

30564.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored), Naturalism, Secular humanism, Absurdism.

71733.heading: Gate: Where the JSDF Fought
71733.label: From summaries

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and survival dominate; otaku leisure as Itami's quiet counterpoint.

folkways.japan: The JSDF's constitutional limits, the Diet's question time, the media's role, otaku culture (Akihabara, doujinshi) and postwar wariness of militarism are all Japanese; Martin reads the manga as an example of casual "pop nationalism" in recent Japanese culture.

delivery.evidence: THEM: opposition politicians and foreign leaders are caricatures and the JSDF near flawless; ANN's Silverman calls it possibly too political and open to reading as glorifying the military; Martin finds the manga follows the JSDF's official self-image.
delivery.note: The case for the JSDF is made openly through Diet hearings, diplomats' speeches (ch. 30) and battle outcomes; the novels' web version was more nationalistic still (Wikipedia).

personified.ideology: Apostle of a war god; killing judged by its reasons

45578.heading: GE: Good Ending
45578.label: From summaries
45578.life_message: Love worth having is honest: stop calculating, face your own feelings and the other person's wounds, and choose each other freely; manipulation, pressure and exposing someone's private life do lasting harm.

content.framing: Condemned (abuse and assault); slaps played as drama

folkways.japan: The samurai code, the Shinsengumi and the Bakumatsu-era unequal treaties, the senpai and teacher bond (sensei), Edo nostalgia, Kabuki-cho nightlife and Shonen Jump fan culture are Japanese material that the series both honors and parodies; Gintoki's personal code is a modern reworking of bushido.

146983.heading: Goodbye, Eri
146983.label: From summaries
146983.life_message: Grief, love and memory are all things we partly make up, and that is not a lie but a way to go on: a person can choose to live, and remembering someone at their best, while knowing it is edited, can be an act of love.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (deaths); explosions played as dark comedy
Shown with consequences; both suicide plans abandoned

34632.heading: Goodnight Punpun
34632.label: From summaries
34632.life_message: The series does not promote a single picture of a good life. It shows how neglect, abuse and isolation damage children, and it suggests that ordinary survival, with work and a few human ties, is what is left after the dream of rescue through one perfect love fails.

frames.aligns: Takes suffering, guilt and the need for repentance seriously; the mother's deathbed apology (ch. 67); a child chosen over abortion (ch. 121); the dignity of a wounded person who keeps living; sin is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Asano's relativism; no hope beyond human ties; an abortion weighed without moral comment, though Sachi keeps her child (ch. 105-121; CCC 2270-2275); the abuser is never held to account (ch. 144); a comic "God." Sex outside marriage, sexual abuse and repeated suicide on the page are a heavy depiction concern (CCC 2280-2283, 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Close to a study of the passions (despair, lust, self-love) and of a soul without spiritual guidance; their cost is never hidden.
frames.concerns: Despair is left without any answer of grace or repentance in the tradition's terms; a comic "God" figure. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual imagery and suicide scenes a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Honest about the emptiness of a life without hope; sin's consequences are not hidden.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: a person crushed by guilt with no word of forgiveness, shown honestly.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about suffering and guilt in the line of serious literary fiction; pastoral approach to suicide; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Relativism; an abortion weighed without moral comment; no answer of grace. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on how much adult literary content they allow.

frames.aligns: Community care as the missing thing; the killing leads only to ruin; no violence shown as heroic.
frames.concerns: A world with no church or community to catch anyone, and no answer beyond private survival. Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as the thing that matters most, shown by its absence; repentance and forgiveness (the mother).
frames.concerns: No plan of salvation or hope beyond survival; relativism; an abortion weighed without moral comment (Sachi keeps the child, ch. 121). For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the sexual content, profanity and suicide put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: The cost of broken homes and unhealthy lives is shown, not admired.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond survival; an abortion weighed without moral comment; a comic "God." Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence are shown as harmful, not admired; cults shown as deadly.

frames.aligns: Love and friendship (Sachi) are what save Punpun's life.

frames.aligns: Honest treatment of mental illness, abuse and family violence; a male abuse survivor taken seriously; compassion for the broken.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; teshuvah; the dignity of the wounded.

frames.aligns: Honest about abuse, cruelty and exploitation as harm; compassion for the broken.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect across a family; the duty of parents (dharma) shown by its failure.

frames.concerns: No path beyond suffering is shown. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and suicide scenes a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Sincerity and its absence; ordinary life and community repair after impurity and loss.

frames.aligns: Sexual harm and family breakdown shown as damaging; friendship as service.

frames.aligns: Survival as the core urge across the dynamics (self, family, groups); a person who keeps living; cults that harm members shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Depression framed through trauma; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede); no stereotyped witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Little hope offered. The Rede ("harm none") underlines the abuse and killing.

frames.aligns: Serious treatment of depression, family violence and a male abuse survivor; no glamorized fan service; critique of cult control.
frames.concerns: Women written as damaged rescuers; the protagonist's sexual coercion (ch. 64, 79, 104) only partly answered; Midori is never held to account. Suicide shown repeatedly, including Aiko's hanging (ch. 139), which safe-messaging guidelines advise against.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; human connection and ordinary work as what keeps a person going; critique of cults and magical thinking.
frames.concerns: Little model of recovery. Cruelty and the suicide scenes are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: Shows the cost of broken families and absent fathers; no glamour in the sex or violence; responsibility shown by its failure.
frames.concerns: Relativism; an abortion weighed without moral comment; a protagonist who abandons his responsibilities. Content that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful is a depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Life lived now, with no afterlife; critique of cults and of messianic hope; harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, framed as harm.
frames.concerns: Little self-determination shown; Punpun is mostly passive. Harm to children shown on the page is the depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the wounded; compassion; honest search for meaning without a given answer.
frames.concerns: Women as damaged rescuers; little community repair. Age-appropriateness makes it adult reading.

frames.aligns: The story tells the truth about neglect, abuse and broken homes, condemns adults who harm children, and honors a dying mother's apology (ch. 67) and a friend who steps in to save a life (ch. 143).
frames.concerns: No hope beyond bare survival; God appears only as a mocking inner voice that Punpun renounces (ch. 141); an abortion weighed without comment, though Sachi keeps her child (ch. 105, 121); suicide (ch. 139), sexual content and the sexual abuse of a 15-year-old by an adult (ch. 50) are on the page.

frames.aligns: Cults are shown as deadly (Aiko's mother; the Pegasus group, ch. 134-136); no supernatural rescue comes; Punpun rejects the "God" in his head (ch. 141); what keeps a person going is work, time and a few human ties.
frames.concerns: Graded on harm: repeated suicide scenes against safe-messaging guidance, the protagonist's sexual coercion and the abuse of a minor (ch. 50).

frames.aligns: The author says the world has many values and none is simply right; the story raises questions rather than answering them, and the ending is left open.
frames.concerns: Its bleakness and the suicide and abuse scenes make it adult reading.

frames.aligns: Everyday decency survives in Sachi's friendship and a mother's late apology, and life goes on for the next generation (ch. 144-147).
frames.concerns: Despair dominates; suicide (ch. 139), self-harm (ch. 141), the abuse of a minor (ch. 50) and sexual content put it well beyond children's age.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No act of revenge or defense of honor is celebrated: Punpun's killing of Aiko's mother (ch. 113-114) leads only to flight and loss, and Asano has said he does not consider Punpun a good person.

Order vs freedom.evidence: No institution rescues anyone, and Asano's frame is pluralist: "the world has many different values, but none of them are 'right.'" The story neither celebrates rules nor romanticizes freedom; the Kagoshima escape fails.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are broken (the father's violence, ch. 1; Aiko's cult mother; Midori's abuse, ch. 50). What helps is a friend who intervenes (Sachi finds Punpun, ch. 143) and a mother's late apology (ch. 67).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Adult power over children is the main form of power, and it is shown as harmful (Socio-cultural lens). No leader or elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as a comic inner "God" voice and as cults that fail to save (Aiko's stepmother; Pegasus's group). The ending rests on ordinary secular survival: a job, time, a few ties.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The ending values plain survival and work, but Sachi's creative ambition and the story's tolerance for many values pull toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The pressure to appear normal, social withdrawal, silence about family violence and the I-novel tradition of confession are Japanese context the essay notes; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

delivery.evidence: Asano (ANN interview, 2018) says the work offers no answers, only questions.
delivery.note: The series avoids stated morals and leaves most of its verdicts open.

personified.ideology: Frank friendship and creative work as a reason to go on

folkways.japan: Japanese university circle culture (clubs built around socializing), senior-junior (senpai-kohai) hierarchy, drinking parties (nomikai) with games and pressure to drink, an Izu Peninsula seaside town, and pressure to inherit a family inn (ryokan). The legal drinking age of 20 is why the anime ages the first-years up (TV Tropes).

delivery.note: The message about friendship and the sea is carried by situations, not speeches; the rare serious moments (Palau, the diving scenes) speak for themselves.

folkways.japan: Bosozoku biker gangs, yankee delinquency, senpai-kohai rank, yakuza heirs, juvenile detention and the Shonan surf coast reflect late-Showa and early-Heisei Japan; the honor code draws on the yankee subculture's version of loyalty and manliness, which the ending partly questions.

folkways.japan: Okinawa as a holiday island, Tokyo's canals and the memory of Imperial Army weapons research shape the setting; TV Tropes reads it as a warning about Japan's wartime past. Ito works in the Japanese horror line of Kazuo Umezu and Hideshi Hino (Wikipedia), and Amigara Fault draws its name from Amida Buddha.

delivery.evidence: No speeches about war or science; the warning sits in the backstory (ch. 6-7) and the imagery. Ito said the idea came from wanting a shark that could also attack on land, after Jaws (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Gyo is built to disturb rather than to argue; any message is carried by image and consequence.

folkways.japan: Built on Japanese school club culture: senpai and kohai, club managers, the national high school tournament, school-trip training camps and Miyagi local pride. Its message works inside these norms: respect and discipline serve the team, while the story pushes back on tyrannical seniority (Kageyama's past).

delivery.evidence: Coaches and players state the lessons, but rival teams are drawn with their own philosophies and are respected, and Karasuno loses.

folkways.japan: Post-disaster Japan after earthquakes and tsunamis, Kojiki myth names, school life, and Ishiguro's unease about Japanese governance before the 2020 Olympics shape the setting (Wikipedia); the gender theme is written against Japanese manga's tradition of comic body-swaps.

86720.heading: Helck

folkways.japan: Yakuza office life, hostess clubs, salaryman careers, a riverside homeless camp, family grave visits and the Dolls' Festival title reflect Japanese settings; the gratitude and diligence Anzu learns echo widely shared Japanese values.

folkways.japan: Freeter life, black-company overwork, the old one-story house (hiraya) in Asagaya, a hometown in Yamagata to return to, and an elderly woman living alone on her pension are all recognizably Japanese; the series sets itself against workplace conformity while honoring family and neighborhood ties.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe a character-driven series with no easy answers in which people grow unevenly and sometimes regress (Yatta-Tachi); ambitious characters (Yomogi, Natsumi) are treated sympathetically, not as foils to mock.

folkways.japan: A Japanese artist's view of ancient Greece in the tradition of Tezuka's historical epics; the focus on loyalty to a lord, the outsider who serves, and death without sentiment echoes Japanese war and samurai stories, though no Japanese setting appears.

30936.heading: Homunculus
30936.label: From summaries
30936.life_message: The series does not hold up a model of a good life. It shows people hiding guilt and trauma behind masks (money, rank, surgery, lies) and asks whether a man with no true self under his masks can heal anyone; its answer is bleak, since Nakoshi's "cures" wound others and end in his own ruin, while the one person who finds a real self is Ito.

content.framing: Ambiguous: exploitation shown, but one act with a minor framed as a "cure"

frames.aligns: Lies, vanity and the refusal to know oneself lead to ruin; the yakuza boss's confession and act of reparation echo contrition and penance.
frames.concerns: The sexual use of a minor is framed as a cure, against CCC 2389 on abuse of the young; mutilation of the body (CCC 2297); no hope beyond the self; suicide (CCC 2280-2283) shown without comment.

frames.aligns: A study of the passions (vanity, lust, self-love) and of a soul without a true face; their cost is shown.
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace; the self dissolves rather than being healed; watchfulness of the senses (nepsis) weighs heavily against the sexual imagery and body horror.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences (lies, lust, self-harm) are not hidden.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ; a minor's sexual exploitation not clearly condemned; skull drilling as a path to truth. Philippians 4:8 test: sexual content, gore and suicide. Congregations are self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A picture of a fallen self that cannot remake itself; masks and lies exposed. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: The Yukari scene is presented as healing; no gospel answer; explicitness is high even for families who engage culture (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: Shows a man opening himself to unseen forces and being destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: ESP and a "sixth sense" gained by drilling the skull may be read as an "open door"; no spiritual answer; sexual content. Holiness standards make the depiction a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The heart's deceitfulness has a strong echo: the homunculi may be Nakoshi's own projections. Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace; the Yukari scene; self-mutilation. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: A man curved in on himself (incurvatus in se), shown to his ruin.
frames.concerns: No word of forgiveness; the abuse of a minor framed ambiguously. LCMS and WELS families are typically far more cautious than ELCA families about the content.

frames.aligns: The yakuza boss's turn from violence; Ito's remorse.
frames.concerns: No grace named; sexual exploitation of a minor; holiness churches avoid such media and UMC families would treat it as adult reading only.

frames.aligns: Works are judged by how they frame good and evil; the story shows vanity and lies destroying a man.
frames.concerns: The Yukari scene's framing; no hope offered; firmly adult literary reading. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.

frames.aligns: Violence leads to ruin; the yakuza boss leaves violence behind.
frames.concerns: A world with no community to catch anyone; mutilation and sexual content. Old Order groups would avoid it; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Repentance and restitution (the yakuza boss).
frames.concerns: Sexual exploitation of a minor; self-mutilation; sexual content; no hope beyond the self. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; this falls outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Trauma taken seriously; a sympathetic arc for a gender-questioning character (Ito, per Looper); homelessness shown humanely.
frames.concerns: A minor's sexual exploitation framed as healing; women as objects of the hero's need; suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Self-destroying living is shown as destroying.
frames.concerns: No hope; sexual content; body horror. "By beholding we become changed" and Fundamental Belief 22 make it a heavy concern; health teaching weighs the self-mutilation.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: A psychic "sixth sense" may be weighed as spiritism; sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.concerns: Trauma, disease and mutilation presented as the deepest reality; surgery as the path to insight. "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.concerns: Sexual activity between an adult and a 17-year-old framed as rescue rather than clearly as abuse; reviewers call it a rape scene; women as objects of the protagonist's need; suicide by hanging.

frames.concerns: Unethical human experiments are the premise and not clearly condemned; cruelty to the vulnerable; no humane resolution.

frames.concerns: The worth and dignity of Yukari and Nanako are violated; adult reading only.

frames.aligns: Self-determination and the rejection of social masks; skepticism toward the supernatural.
frames.concerns: Harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Church of Satan's Eleven Rules and the Satanic Temple's tenets condemn, are framed ambiguously.

frames.aligns: Lies and pride destroy; the homeless are shown with dignity; the yakuza boss's confession.
frames.concerns: A minor's sexual exploitation framed as healing; occult-like "sixth sense"; suicide and self-harm with no hope offered; no deliverance.

frames.aligns: A skeptical scientist; the supernatural left in doubt (the visions may be projections); no faith answer imposed.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation of the vulnerable, including a minor, framed ambiguously; a pseudoscientific procedure never clearly debunked.

frames.aligns: Open about what is real: the story never settles whether the homunculi exist; no preaching either way.
frames.concerns: Ambiguity extends to the abuse of a minor, which is not clearly named as harm; bleak and cruel.

frames.aligns: Lies catch up with people; the homeless look after each other (Ita-san).
frames.concerns: Despair, cruelty and the harm to a teenager go unanswered; content far beyond what most families want.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The yakuza code of finger-cutting is shown as guilt in disguise; the boss's last cut is atonement, not honor, and he leaves the gang (Japanese Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions (hospital, gang, family) fail; Nakoshi lives outside all rules in his car; the story neither celebrates order nor endorses his freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families harm (Ito's father, Yukari's parents); the homeless park is the nearest thing to community (Ita-san).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank (banker, doctor, yakuza boss) is shown as a mask over trauma; no elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; the frame is scientific and psychoanalytic (Ito's experiments).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story is about the self and its expression (surgery, identity, Ito's transition), set among the homeless struggling to survive.

folkways.japan: Yakuza finger-cutting (yubitsume), burusera shops and the sale of schoolgirls' images, manual-style parenting and exam pressure, appearance culture and the homeless of Shinjuku after the bubble economy are Japanese settings the story uses; it criticizes more than endorses them.

delivery.evidence: Ito explains psychoanalytic theory on the page (Wikipedia); MyAnimeList reviewers split between finding it profound and finding it pretentious; the story never settles whether the visions are real (Looper).
delivery.note: Ideas about trauma and the self are spelled out in dialogue, but the plot leaves the central question (are the homunculi real?) open.

personified.ideology: Scientific skepticism about the mind and the occult
A self made of surface: money, surgery, lies

98171.heading: How a Realist Hero Rebuilt the Kingdom

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal honor and vengeance (Gaius) are faulted, but loyalty and face in court politics still matter.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Order, planning and a strong crown are the good; rebellion is crushed.

folkways.japan: The hero applies Japanese and Western modern governance (roads, broadcasting, idols, technocrats) to a European-style fantasy kingdom. Respect for capable ministers, harmony in the court and duty over personal wishes reflect Japanese and Confucian norms; the polygamous royal household is a genre convention of harem isekai.

delivery.evidence: Souma and his ministers explain policy at length (ANN notes info-dumps in the novel); idealists like Maria are given a hearing but shown their contradictions (v9); villains (Gaius, Julius, the Papal State) are proud or scheming.

98171.dominant: Pragmatism (realist statecraft), Utilitarianism (hard choices for the greater good), Patriotism / nationalism (the country's survival first), Confucian ethics (the benevolent ruler and the gathering of talents).

folkways.japan: Set among Tokyo university students: the light music club, part-time jobs, the Coming of Age Ceremony at twenty and its kimono, and job-hunting season (shūkatsu). 30026.heading: Hunter x Hunter
30026.label: From summaries
30026.life_message: A good life is a chosen adventure shared with friends. The story questions whether humans are better than the "monsters" they hunt, and it shows that strength, revenge and even goodness can become destructive when they turn obsessive.

frames.aligns: The passions (wrath, pride) destroy Gon and the King until humility enters; a repentance-like change in Meruem.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge for kin drives Kurapika and Gon, and both pay heavily for it (ch. 64-119; likely ch. 305-309). Hisoka's duels are personal. The story counts the cost of honor rather than celebrating it.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen friendship outranks blood (Killua leaves his family), but loyalty to kin still matters (Killua protecting Alluka, ch. 319-339). The Hunter Association is a flawed civic body.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A secular world: Nen is a learnable system with rules; religion is personal (Netero's prayers) and in the background.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A deadly, food-chain world, but the heroes pursue chosen adventures for their own sake.

folkways.japan: Mentor-student respect (Wing, Biscuit, Netero), board-game culture (gungi, modeled on shogi-type games), the shonen tournament structure and Buddhist imagery around Netero reflect Japanese norms. delivery.evidence: Even monsters get a full hearing (Meruem, Pitou); Thompson praises the rules and puzzles rather than any message; no review opened calls it preachy.

folkways.japan: The "redo my youth" web-novel genre, the shachiku (company-slave) burnout of Japanese office life, school trips, summer festivals and meeting a partner's parents are Japanese settings. folkways.japan: Built from Japanese tradition: a Shinto shrine family and shrine maidens, Buddhist monks and sutras, yokai folklore, the Sengoku warring-states era, and motifs from the 19th-century novel Nansō Satomi Hakkenden (Wikipedia). delivery.evidence: The theme is carried by the Jewel itself and by what characters do with shards; villains such as Naraku, Kagura and Sesshomaru get motives and some sympathy; Takahashi balances drama with comedy (Wikipedia, citing Manga Life).

folkways.japan: Cohabitation before marriage, still less common in Japan than in the West, is shown as an ordinary urban choice; seasonal customs (New Year, hanami), formal visits to announce an engagement and the photo wedding (a common lower-cost choice) reflect Japanese practice.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman calls it a beautiful example of "showing versus telling"; MrAJCosplay notes conflicts are handled calmly, not dramatically.
delivery.note: Contentment is carried by small daily episodes rather than stated; the move to marriage arrives without a lecture.

110140.dominant: Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Traditionalism (contentment in daily life; cohabitation growing into marriage).

31706.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Part 7–Steel Ball Run
31706.label: From summaries
31706.life_message: A good life is the honest pursuit of one's own fulfillment and growth through hardship and friendship: getting from minus to zero by one's own effort, not by power taken from others. No nation, and no sacred object, justifies sacrificing the powerless.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friendship and personal loyalty outweigh national duty; Gyro returns home to his family's land only in death.

33009.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
33009.label: From summaries
33009.life_message: A good life is chosen, not fated: loyalty to family and friends, courage under unjust power, and sacrifice for the weak are worth more than the peace of a destiny imposed from above, and hope in an unknown future is part of being human.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): Pucci's scheme fails and his "Heaven" is shown as false. The story sides with free will against fate, close to CCC 1730-1742; Jolyne's death for Emporio echoes John 15:13. Concern for prisoners echoes Matthew 25:36.
frames.concerns: A priest as the main villain who claims Christ was fated to the cross (ch. 140s) and loves DIO as God (TV Tropes). Fatalism differs from Providence, which works through free creatures (CCC 302-308). Masturbation reference (ch. 1); gore; a reincarnation-like ending (CCC 1013).

frames.aligns: Freedom (autexousion) and synergy over fate; a counterfeit "Heaven" exposed; self-sacrificial love.
frames.concerns: A cleric turned servant of a demonic figure; Christ's passion recast as blind fate; a universe remade without God; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs the gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: Evil is clearly framed as evil and defeated; a religious leader whose faith is false (Matthew 7:15-20); self-sacrifice; justice for the falsely accused.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: constant gore, a masturbation reference (ch. 1), strong language. A priest-villain misusing Scripture. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a story that rejects a counterfeit heaven built by a false shepherd and honors self-giving love (ch. 155). Depicts without endorsing.
frames.concerns: Pucci's "happiness" is peace without God; the story offers no gospel alternative, only human hope. Sexual material and gore (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a demonic figure's plan defeated.
frames.concerns: Souls pulled from bodies, a baby grown from absorbed souls (ch. 73-81), devotion to a vampire as to God, and the 14 phrases recited to bond with DIO's bone (ch. 95): many would see an "open door" to spiritual darkness.

frames.aligns: A rich talking point: Pucci's "gravity" is impersonal fatalism, while the Westminster Confession (3.1) says God's decree does no violence to the will of creatures. Common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 on lascivious material (ch. 1, the DIO-Pucci flashback); gore; a pastor figure using Scripture to justify murder.

frames.aligns: Bondage of the will is about sin, not blind fate; the story honors gift-like sacrifice and friendship. A father's vocation (Jotaro).
frames.concerns: A priest villain; Christ's cross called fate rather than free self-giving; sexual material. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace and free response fit the story's rejection of fate; social holiness toward the falsely imprisoned and abused.
frames.concerns: Gore, language, sexual material; holiness churches more cautious than UMC (General Rules on diversions).

frames.aligns: Imaginative fiction judged by framing (Lewis's tradition): a counterfeit heaven (compare The Great Divorce) defeated by love. Article 17 cautions against the despair a misused doctrine of predestination can bring, which is Pucci's path.
frames.concerns: Clergy as villain; gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a church official who serves another master; suffering of prisoners; Jolyne's sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool, ending with the killing of the villain (ch. 157-158) (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Moral agency is central to the plan of salvation (2 Nephi 2:27), and the story defends agency against a forced, foreknown fate; family across generations; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: the masturbation reference, sexual material and gore do not invite the Spirit for many families; a resetting universe.

frames.aligns: Critique of prisons and of racist violence (ch. 128); a female lead; a clergyman who abuses pastoral power is exposed.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; slurs in the manga; Anasui's murder of his girlfriend treated lightly as backstory (ch. 59).

frames.aligns: Free will and the great controversy between good and evil; a false "Heaven" exposed.
frames.concerns: The state of the dead: souls taken out as discs, a ghost room and the dead returning in a new universe conflict with Fundamental Belief 26; "by beholding we become changed" weighs the gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: A religious leader who uses God's name for evil is condemned.
frames.concerns: Spiritism-like content (souls extracted, the dead returning), constant violence (Psalm 11:5), sexual material; Jesus said to die on a cross; jw.org counsel on entertainment weighs these heavily.

frames.aligns: Fear is overcome; Pucci's "gravity" as a mental law resisted.
frames.concerns: Fear, decay and death shown as overwhelming and real; body horror; time and matter as all-powerful.

frames.aligns: "All is foreseen, yet freedom is given" (Avot 3:15) and Rambam on free will (Hilchot Teshuvah 5) fit the heroes' stand; racism and lynching condemned.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: the masturbation reference, strip search, sexual material, language; gore. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Free will against fate; justice for the wrongly imprisoned; racism condemned.
frames.concerns: Sexual material and gore. A Christian cleric as villain is not a Jewish concern in itself; no antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in the critique of prisons and racism; a woman as hero.
frames.concerns: Violence; slurs in the manga. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Pucci's love of DIO as of God is a form of shirk, and he is defeated; justice for the oppressed; mercy and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Qadar (divine decree) is a pillar of faith, but Pucci's version removes human responsibility; Jesus said to be crucified (Qur'an 4:157 differs); sexual material; the summoning of souls.

frames.aligns: Cyclical time and a universe that ends and begins again echo the kalpas; karma: Pucci's actions return to him; the Gita's call to act rightly whatever the outcome.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, cruelty); the reset is achieved by a villain, not by dharma.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment drive Pucci; release from fear comes not from knowing the future but from compassion and right action; cycles of time.
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) against constant killing; the final killing of the villain.

frames.aligns: Hukam (divine order) is accepted in Sikh teaching through humility, not ego; Pucci shows haumai (ego) disguised as acceptance. Defending the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence and sexual material; a vision of the divine will imposed by force.

frames.aligns: Free will and the unity of humankind: racist violence (ch. 128) is shown as evil; a false religious leader is exposed.
frames.concerns: Constant violence; sexual material ("chaste and holy life").

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the heroes; gratitude (Emporio's debt to Jolyne and Weather, ch. 157-158); renewal after the reset.
frames.concerns: Death, blood and corpses (kegare) are constant.

frames.aligns: Cycles of time and rebirth; a moon-timed working (the new moon at Cape Canaveral) framed as power, not evil in itself; the self-directed will.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" set against constant violence.

frames.aligns: Self-determinism against an imposed fate; personal responsibility; The Way to Happiness: do not murder.
frames.concerns: Memories and abilities ripped out as discs; constant killing by heroes and villains.

frames.concerns: Anasui's murder of his girlfriend treated as backstory while he courts Jolyne (ch. 59); a slur in the manga; the DIO-Pucci bed scene with a young Pucci.

frames.concerns: The supernatural is central as fiction; heavy violence.

frames.aligns: Father-daughter love and duty (Jotaro, Jolyne); loyalty, sacrifice and courage; evil punished.
frames.concerns: A priest as villain; heroes are convicts; masturbation reference and sexual material; strong language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of prisoners and outsiders; free search for meaning; religion used for harm critiqued.
frames.concerns: Violence; slurs.

frames.aligns: A religious authority who claims to know what is best for all humanity is defeated; individual will and self-determination win.
frames.concerns: Proportional retaliation (Church of Satan) and compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1) would read the final killing differently.

frames.aligns: Deliverance of the falsely imprisoned; a Klan lynching condemned as evil (ch. 128); a false shepherd exposed; sacrifice for the weak; hope that does not give up.
frames.concerns: The lynching and racist language are shown on the page; gore and sexual material; souls and spirits used as power; revenge as Weather's drive.

frames.aligns: A clergyman's promise of "Heaven" is exposed as manipulation; human will and loyalty, not divine plan, win; no conversion arc.
frames.concerns: Heavy violence; fate and rebirth are real inside the fiction.

frames.aligns: Fate and freedom are argued, not preached; the ending leaves the mystery of rebirth open; certainty is the villain's flaw.
frames.concerns: Gore and a bleak final act.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, family and friends; karma-like justice for Pucci; loved ones meeting again in a new world.
frames.concerns: Gore and the deaths of almost everyone may be heavy for many families.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are settled personally, not by courts: Ermes's revenge for her sister (v6), Weather's vow against Pucci (ch. 133-137). The court is rigged (ch. 1-12).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Prison order is oppressive and the villain's ideal is a total order of fate; freedom of choice is the story's prize.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Bloodline and father-daughter loyalty drive the plot (ch. 11, 75, 154); a found family of inmates; civic institutions fail.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Guards' and the chaplain's authority are abused; a child, Emporio, wins.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious authority is the villain's; the heroes choose for themselves. The bloodline legacy remains honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in prison comes first; Jolyne's style and self-possession lean toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The Joestar bloodline and inherited duty, and the gratitude Emporio owes (on), reflect Japanese norms. A Catholic priest as a stylish villain fits a Japanese pop-culture habit of borrowing Christian imagery without Christian doctrine. Araki's idea of a universe that returns to its origin is his own artistic framing (bunkoban afterword), set in a carefully researched American prison.

delivery.evidence: Pucci argues his theology of fate in long speeches (ch. 140s, 157); the story answers through the heroes' choices and sacrifices rather than counter-sermons. Araki's afterword describes the ending as a cycle returning to its origin.
delivery.note: The villain states the ideas; the heroes answer with actions.

personified.ideology: Accepting a known fate is happiness; God's will as irresistible "gravity"
Will and hope against fate; sacrifice for others
Choice and justice can change fate
Victim of racism and fate who answers with vengeance

33009.dominant: Existentialism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Collectivism/authoritarianism and Stoic-style fatalism (critiqued through Pucci), Christian (explored through a villain), Critical theory and Feminism (explored).

47915.heading: Judge
47915.label: From summaries
47915.life_message: Revenge dressed up as judgment destroys everyone it touches, the avenger included; guilt that is hidden instead of confessed curdles into cruelty, and the one person who refused to be corrupted is the one who walks free.

frames.aligns: Envy, pride and greed shown destroying lives; a corrupt court exposed; Rina's mother's integrity rewarded; vengeance condemned by its fruits (Romans 12:19).
frames.concerns: No confession, grace or forgiveness; Kazu's suicide (CCC 2280-2283) not reflected on; the game's sin labels include homosexual orientation as "lust," which Catholic teaching distinguishes from acts (CCC 2358).

frames.aligns: The passions (envy, wrath, lust) named and shown enslaving; hidden sin festering instead of confessed.
frames.concerns: Dark mood with no repentance or healing; violence and despair.

frames.aligns: "Be sure your sin will find you out" (Numbers 32:23); bribery and injustice exposed; integrity rewarded.
frames.concerns: No gospel, only judgment and death; gore; suicide; attempted assault.

frames.aligns: Opens talk on sin, guilt, and who has the right to judge (Matthew 7:1-2).
frames.concerns: Bleak and hopeless; the twist rewards cleverness over conscience until the last page.

frames.aligns: Sin exposed; justice for the corrupt.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on gore, despair and sexual menace; no spiritual victory.

frames.aligns: Total depravity on display under pressure; human courts corrupted (Westminster on the civil magistrate).
frames.concerns: Ninth-commandment deceit and murder by vote; no grace offered.

frames.aligns: The law exposes sin: every mask is an accusation.
frames.concerns: Only law, no gospel; the story ends in condemnation.

frames.aligns: Conscience and guilt taken seriously; social injustice (a bribed court) condemned.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and suicide with little hope.

frames.aligns: A morality play built on the seven deadly sins; justice and corruption.
frames.concerns: Cruelty dominates; no redemption.

frames.aligns: Refusing to kill would be the faithful choice; revenge plainly destroys the avenger.
frames.concerns: Killing is the game's rule and most characters comply; worldly violent media.

frames.aligns: Honesty, accountability and the corrosive effect of hidden sin.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on violent, fear-centered media; suicide; attempted assault.

frames.aligns: Critique of a corrupt justice system and of scapegoating by vote.
frames.concerns: Kazu's orientation listed as a sin and never challenged (MyAnimeList review); unchallenged sexist claims; cruelty.

frames.aligns: Judgment and accountability as a theme.
frames.concerns: Fear and violence as entertainment (FB 22 on entertainment).

frames.aligns: Bribery and lies exposed.
frames.concerns: Violent entertainment (Psalm 11:5); death-game premise.

frames.aligns: Guilt confronted rather than buried.
frames.concerns: Dwells on fear, death and despair.

frames.aligns: A bribed judge condemned (Exodus 23:8, a bribe blinds the clear-sighted); revenge (nekamah) shown destroying the avenger.
frames.concerns: Bloodshed and suicide; immodest seduction scenes; bittul Torah.

frames.aligns: Integrity in judges (Deuteronomy 16:19-20); lo tikom (do not take revenge).
frames.concerns: Violence; suicide.

frames.aligns: Ethical dilemma about collective judgment and corrupt courts.
frames.concerns: Cruelty; Kazu's orientation treated as a sin label.

frames.aligns: Accountability for sins; bribery of judges condemned (Quran 2:188); justice even against one's kin (4:135).
frames.concerns: Humans taking life unjustly (5:32); suicide; seduction scenes.

frames.aligns: Karma: every captive's deeds, and their families', return to them.
frames.concerns: Tamasic violence and despair.

frames.aligns: Envy and craving lead to suffering; hatred answered with hatred never ends (Dhammapada 5).
frames.concerns: Killing as the game's rule (first precept); suicide.

frames.aligns: The five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) mirror the masks.
frames.concerns: Violence; no remembrance of God (naam).

frames.aligns: Justice and truthfulness tested; corruption exposed.
frames.concerns: Violence and division; backbiting and deceit throughout.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) versus deceit tested; impurity of hidden wrongdoing.
frames.concerns: Death and blood throughout (kegare).

frames.aligns: "Harm returns": the avenger is harmed in turn.
frames.concerns: Harm-centered plot.

frames.aligns: Hidden wrongs (overts) come to light and destroy those who carry them.
frames.concerns: Murder and suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Shows how a corrupt system and coercion turn people on each other.
frames.concerns: A gay character labeled with a sin and never defended (MyAnimeList review); unchallenged sexist claims; attempted assault.

frames.aligns: Moral reasoning under pressure; integrity (Rina's mother) vindicated.
frames.concerns: Cruelty as spectacle; little room for reason or empathy to win.

frames.aligns: Sin, guilt and responsibility taken seriously; corruption punished; honesty rewarded.
frames.concerns: Nihilistic mood; gore; teenagers plotting murder.

frames.aligns: Questions who may judge whom; justice versus vengeance.
frames.concerns: Cruelty; a gay character labeled sinful.

frames.aligns: Self-preservation; distrust of corrupt authority; responsibility for one's own acts.
frames.concerns: Hiro's revenge harms innocent relatives, against the Satanic Temple's tenets on harm and justice.

frames.aligns: A justice system that lets a killer go free for money exposed; the one family that refused to be bought survives (Proverbs 17:23).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: A courtroom frame where votes replace duels, but tie-breaker fights to the death (vol. 4-5) and revenge for a brother are honor logic.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Captors impose absolute rules; failing to vote kills everyone (The Fandom Post, vol. 1).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Relatives are the leverage and the motive: captives fight for trapped family (vol. 4-5); Hiro avenges a brother.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Unseen captors hold total power; the judge's rank protects him until the end.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Medieval sin symbolism in a modern, secular setting.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Pure survival (AniList Survival; MangaUpdates Play or Die Situation).

folkways.japan: Death-game fiction is a popular Japanese thriller form (Tonogai's own Doubt; Battle Royale), and Japan's lay-judge (saiban-in) system, introduced in 2009 just before serialization, put ordinary citizens on criminal trials (from general knowledge; to verify). Public shame and family responsibility for a member's wrongdoing are familiar themes, described here as context.

delivery.evidence: The sin masks carry the theme without speeches; The Fandom Post notes no moralizing in vols. 1 and 3; the final reveal explains everyone's motives in a closing monologue (MyAnimeList reviews).
delivery.note: The story states its moral only through outcomes: the corrupt and the vengeful are destroyed, the honest family survives. Kazu's "sin" label is never contested inside the story.

personified.ideology: Guilt hidden, then turned into revenge
Kindness under a label of sin

47915.dominant: Nihilism (explored), Utilitarianism (the vote), Christian (the seven sins as structure), Existentialism (guilt and choice under pressure).

105469.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen 0

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, a bullied boy finding friends; a cult leader's fraud exposed.

frames.aligns: A clear deceiver defeated; sacrificial love; trauma turned to service.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rika's revenge on bullies (ch. 0-1) is shown as the curse's danger, not as justice; Yuta fights to protect friends, not to answer insults (ch. 0-4).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Gojo bends the higher-ups' order to save Yuta (ch. 0-1), while the class trains under discipline (ch. 0-2).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Yuta's bond to one person (Rika) is loosened into care for his class and for strangers; Geto's in-group loyalty to sorcerers is condemned (ch. 0-3 to 0-4).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Geto's ranking of sorcerers over "monkeys" is the villain's creed; teacher authority is warm but real.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Japanese spirit lore is used respectfully as story physics, but organized religion appears as Geto's fraud.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival under threat dominates, but the ending's message is to live a full life (Rika's farewell, ch. 0-4).

folkways.japan: The school class, teacher-student bonds and the training montage reflect Japanese school and shonen norms; the vengeful-spirit figure of Sugawara no Michizane and the idea of pacifying a restless spirit come from Japanese religious history rather than from the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: The love-as-curse twist is explained by Gojo once and then shown (Wikipedia); Geto's ideology gets little room in four chapters, and Otaquest wished the supporting cast had more (Wikipedia). Akutami says there was no specific theme in mind (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message about letting go is carried by the plot twist and Rika's farewell rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Sorcerers are superior; non-sorcerers should be exterminated
Love that releases; live to protect others
Possessive love that will not let go
Raise and protect the next generation

198372.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen Modulo
198372.label: From summaries
198372.life_message: Living as neighbors with people who are strange to you takes patience, listening and sacrifice; peace is made by people willing to lose rather than win the wrong way, and the old cycle of fear and revenge can be ended.

content.framing: Mixed: battle action shown as thrilling; cruelty and murder condemned; one revenge killing approved
Shown with consequences; sacrifice honored and then undone

frames.aligns: Welcoming the stranger and refugee (CCC 2241; Fratelli Tutti); child trafficking condemned (ch. 1); self-giving love (John 15:13) in Yuka and Usami; Tsurugi refuses a victory he judges wrong.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, shikigami and a cursed ring as the heroes' tools (CCC 2117 on magic); a ritual that rewrites human souls; Dabura's revenge beheading left unjudged (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Peacemaking over vengeance; Usami offers his life for his people (ch. 13); reverence for the sacred respected (ch. 7, 25).
frames.concerns: Curses and spirits worked by sorcerers as real powers; Maru's ritual remakes souls, a power the tradition reserves to God; violence.

frames.aligns: Love for the outsider (Leviticus 19:34); evil men who sell children punished; sibling devotion and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and curses at the core (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a soul-altering ritual saves the day; battle violence and a severed head (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Hospitality to aliens and refugees opens talk about neighbor love; Tsurugi's humility; no mockery of faith.
frames.concerns: Heroes wield curses and shikigami, beyond Tolkien-style magic for many families; salvation by a technique, not by grace.

frames.aligns: Resisting hatred between peoples; protecting children from exploiters.
frames.concerns: Curses, possessing spirits (Rika in the ring, ch. 17-18), a soul-eating curse (Mahito, ch. 22) and sacred beasts worshipped for millennia are the world's core, not background.

frames.aligns: Civil authority used carefully for peace (Romans 13); human dignity across peoples; sin shown in fear and greed (ch. 9, 13).
frames.concerns: Occult framework; a humanly engineered remaking of souls as the answer; justice by duel.

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms themes: diplomats, councils and sorcerers each claim authority; vocation as service (Usami, Mino).
frames.concerns: Curse-based powers; Dabura's revenge killing approved; violence.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: building a just peace for displaced people; works of mercy (Yuka and Cross with a lost child, ch. 7).
frames.concerns: Violence as the way disputes are settled (duels); occult framing of powers.

frames.aligns: Patient diplomacy and reasoned dialogue; respect for another people's sacred things.
frames.concerns: Sorcery as the heroes' tools; a severed head shown in triumph (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Tsurugi lays down his sword and accepts defeat (ch. 21); Dura dies pleading for peace (ch. 9); the vote for coexistence (ch. 10).
frames.concerns: Disputes settled by champions' duels; heroes are trained fighters; Dabura's vengeance is applauded; worldly media and occult content.

frames.aligns: Family legacy and love; respect for others' beliefs (Articles of Faith 11); service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Violent battles and spirit-like curses; For the Strength of Youth on violent media.

frames.aligns: Refugee welcome, xenophobia and a fear-driven shooting (ch. 13) open talk on immigration and justice; land taken for resources exposed (ch. 9).
frames.concerns: Battle violence; women barred from power in Rumelian culture is noted but not challenged by the story.

frames.aligns: Welcome to a displaced people; peace over war.
frames.concerns: Curses and spirits as real powers; violence; 'by beholding we become changed.'

frames.aligns: Seeking peace between peoples; children protected.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirits at the core (spiritism counsel on jw.org); battle violence.

frames.aligns: Fear of strangers replaced by understanding; healing in the end (ch. 24).
frames.concerns: Curses born of human negative emotion and disease (Yuka's tumor) dwell on fear and matter.

frames.aligns: 'Love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19); pikuach nefesh in rescuing children.
frames.concerns: Kishuf (sorcery) is the basis of power (Deuteronomy 18); souls altered by a ritual; violence.

frames.aligns: Loving the stranger; justice for a displaced people; Usami's readiness to die for others.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and violence.

frames.aligns: Welcome of the refugee and tikkun olam; a vote for peace; the exploitation of children condemned.
frames.concerns: Battle violence; the Rumelian gender rule left unchallenged.

frames.aligns: Hospitality to the traveller and refugee; justice and mercy; protecting the weak; no mockery of faith.
frames.concerns: Sihr-like cursed techniques and spirits shown positively; souls reshaped by a creature; revenge killing approved.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protectors; Yuka's wish for rebirth (ch. 15); respect for sacred beings; duty kept at cost.
frames.concerns: Curses and dark techniques as weapons; ahimsa tested by duels.

frames.aligns: Curses born of human negative emotion echo teaching on how hatred breeds suffering; the curses 'rest in peace' (ch. 24); Tsurugi lets go of winning.
frames.concerns: First precept: conflicts settled by force; Dabura's revenge.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak; courage; dignity of all peoples (sarbat da bhala).
frames.concerns: Sorcery is central, against the rejection of magic and superstition; vengeance.

frames.aligns: Unity of peoples; consultation and a council vote choose peace (ch. 10, 25).
frames.concerns: Violence settles much of the conflict; duels.

frames.concerns: Violence; mind-confusing powers.

frames.concerns: Rumelian rule that only men may wield power is treated as concern rather than challenged; coexistence arrives by magic, not politics (ComicBook.com).

frames.concerns: A magic fix replaces human politics at the end; violence.

frames.concerns: Violence and a revenge killing.

frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice and the common good rank above self-interest throughout.

frames.concerns: Violence; the ending settles every question neatly.

frames.concerns: Frequent battle violence and a terminal illness for younger readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duels of champions and a warrior's code settle disputes (ch. 9, 13); Dabura's revenge restores his people's honor (ch. 24); heroes also choose humility over face (ch. 21).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Careful rules and diplomacy are honored, but cover-ups are criticized and Yuji acts on his own (ch. 12, 20).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Sibling love drives the heroes; the larger aim is peace with strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Clan inheritance, ranked sorcerers and a men-only warrior caste exist; the story gently questions each (ch. 1, 11, 12).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Rituals and sacred beasts are respected; diplomacy, votes and science-fiction technology sit beside them.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A war for living space and resources frames the plot; personal wishes (Yuka's ring, Maru's amusement park) are small but real.

folkways.japan: Clan inheritance (the Gojo and Zen'in families), deference to elders and committees, a government that manages public fear, Japan's postwar stance on nuclear weapons (ch. 14) and the memory of hidden Christians and the fumi-e (ch. 7) reflect Japanese settings; the refugee theme reads, in a French critic's view, as an echo of Japan's own debates over immigration.

delivery.evidence: Dura states the neighbor ideal in a speech (ch. 9); the pro-war Osuki and the fearful Yakumaru are drawn thinly, but Cross's resentment and Dabura's code get real backstories (ch. 8-9, 18).
delivery.note: The coexistence theme is argued through characters on both sides and a vote, not lectures; the final peace comes by a supernatural ritual rather than persuasion.

personified.ideology: Resentment of those who wronged his people
Take land and resources by force

198372.dominant: Communitarianism (neighbors across peoples), Pagan/occult (the jujutsu curse system), Pragmatism (diplomacy), Bushido / honor code and Pacifism / nonviolence in tension.

101517.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami)
101517.label: From summaries
101517.life_message: A good life is spent using whatever strength you have to help others, so that no one, including you, dies alone; you do not have to be the strongest, only one part of something larger.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love: Yuji, Nanami, Gojo and Choso give their lives for others (ch. 120, 236, 259); Yuji refuses to treat anyone as disposable; confession of guilt (ch. 165); cruelty and nihilism defeated.
frames.concerns: Fantasy magic is judged by framing, and here sorcery, summoning and possession are the heroes' craft (CCC 2115-2117); a cult cheers a child's death (ch. 76); Mei Mei's conduct goes unjudged (ch. 133).

frames.aligns: Struggle against evil; repentance-like grief after Shibuya (ch. 126-133); honor for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so demon-like curses and possession used as a skill system turn spiritual warfare into a tool. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore a concern.

frames.aligns: Responsibility after failure; courage; loyalty; Yuji's refusal to abandon others.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, summoning and spirits as the heroes' tools (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); suicide references (ch. 55, 114). Congregations differ; some accept fantasy magic, many are cautious with spells and spirits.

frames.aligns: Clear evil fought at cost; mentors who sacrifice; the Higuruma arc read as human justice failing and grace needed (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Occult mechanics and possession; despair. Some churches treat the magic like Tolkien-style fantasy, others avoid spirit-contact stories.

frames.aligns: Courage and self-sacrifice; evil is real and must be fought.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": curses, possession, body-stealing and summoned spirits are the engine of the story and the heroes' means.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is vivid: every institution and most adults fail. Common grace: self-sacrifice and loyalty still shine.
frames.concerns: Occult framework; suicide references (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: the story is heavy on law (judgment, guilt, Higuruma's court) and shows grace mainly as forgiveness between brothers (Yuji and Choso, ch. 259).
frames.concerns: Occult themes. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; protecting the weak; grace-like second chances (Choso).
frames.concerns: Occult content; gore. Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imaginative tradition can read the curses as fantasy judged by framing; sacrifice and duty; critique of corrupt hierarchy.
frames.concerns: Occult and gore. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.

frames.aligns: Critique of power and of using people as tools; self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Violence is the story's means of salvation; occult content.

frames.aligns: Service, family loyalty, agency and accountability (Yuji's confession, ch. 165).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on graphic violence and occult content.

frames.aligns: Critique of corrupt institutions and hereditary privilege; empathy for outcasts (Junpei, Choso); Maki's escape from a sexist clan.
frames.concerns: Women sidelined in the second half (ANN review); gore.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice; care for the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; spirits of the dead and occult framing conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Loyalty and courage.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and violence (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Psalm 11:5) are the heroes' tools throughout.

frames.aligns: Fear and hatred as the source of evil (curses are born of negative emotion) and overcome by courage.
frames.concerns: Constant bodily harm and death.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh (saving life above all); mourning and honoring the dead; justice and confession (ch. 165).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and necromancy (Deuteronomy 18); desecration of corpses (Kenjaku, Yuta in Gojo's body, ch. 261) against kavod hamet.

frames.aligns: Saving life; teshuvah (Yuji and Higuruma accept guilt); critique of corrupt authority.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and necromancy; gore.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; protecting the vulnerable; questioning corrupt authority.
frames.concerns: Gore and occult content left to family values.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice, protecting the weak; justice.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) and jinn-like spirits as the heroes' tools; desecration of bodies.

frames.aligns: Karma, rebirth (Kenjaku's thousand-year cycle; the reincarnated twin, ch. 255), dharma-like duty (Nanami).
frames.concerns: Constant violence; Indian deity names used for shikigami without their meaning (Mahoraga).

frames.aligns: Suffering born of negative emotion (curses); impermanence; Buddhist lore (Tengen spreading Buddhism, ch. 74; a monk's remains as Prison Realm, ch. 90); compassion over hatred.
frames.concerns: Killing constant (first precept); Buddhist imagery mostly aesthetic (rubric anchor in this guide).

frames.aligns: Courage to protect the weak (the saint-soldier ideal); seva; honesty.
frames.concerns: Sorcery; gore.

frames.aligns: Service and unity; justice.
frames.concerns: Teaching against degrading entertainment applies to the gore; sorcery.

frames.aligns: Curses, spirits and purification echo kami and kegare; respect for the dead; exorcism of malevolent spirits.
frames.concerns: Blood and death everywhere with little purification.

frames.aligns: Magic as a craft with rules and costs (binding vows); personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against constant harm.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: care for others, courage; overcoming suppressive people (Mahito, Kenjaku).
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" against constant killing.

frames.aligns: Critique of hereditary privilege, corrupt elders and sexist clans (Maki, ch. 148-150).
frames.concerns: Nobara sidelined after a cruel twist and other women given less arc (ANN review); a mother's body used by a male villain to bear a child (ch. 143, 208).

frames.aligns: No supernatural rescue; meaning built by people helping people; Akutami says no one holds the ultimate truth (ComicBook.com); cults exposed (ch. 76-78).
frames.concerns: Gore; despair in Shibuya.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, honoring mentors, family love (Yuji and his grandfather; Megumi and Tsumiki).
frames.concerns: Elders and tradition mostly villainous (ch. 10, 148-150); occult framework.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of every person (Yuji's refusal to call anyone disposable); justice against corrupt authority.
frames.concerns: Gore.

frames.aligns: Challenges corrupt authority (the higher-ups); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); rejection of cults.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice over self-preservation; Sukuna's pure self-indulgence is condemned.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak, endurance through grief, elders' wisdom (Yuji's grandfather), standing up to a corrupt authority, second chances (Choso).
frames.concerns: Sorcery, curses and possession as the heroes' power, which Holiness and Pentecostal families may see as spiritually real; constant gore; despair in Shibuya.

frames.aligns: Problems solved by effort, rules and teamwork; cults that worship a god-figure are shown as cruel (ch. 76) or as a con (ch. 78); no faith answer; Akutami's no-one-holds-the-truth stance.
frames.concerns: Curses and spirits are fantasy furniture and do not lower the grade; gore.

frames.aligns: Villains' views (Geto, Mahito, Sukuna) are heard; Akutami says if no one is really right, no one is wrong either (ComicBook.com); no doctrine about what lies beyond (Gojo's afterlife scene is left ambiguous, ch. 236).
frames.concerns: Little at the level of message.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, everyday decency, protection by those who came before (Gojo's and Nanami's words guide Yuji, ch. 141), and a fair ending for Sukuna.
frames.concerns: Despair and cruelty in Shibuya; many beloved characters die.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge is tempting but Yuji acts to protect, not avenge; clan honor is shown as cruelty (ch. 148-150).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Jujutsu Society's rules are kept but its elders defied (ch. 10, 137).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Bonds to friends, teachers and found brothers outweigh institutions; Megumi acts for his sister (ch. 211-219).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Clan hierarchy and grade rankings critiqued; anyone can help.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Curses are explained by rules and energy; religious cults are exploitative (ch. 76-78).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Constant survival stakes; Yuji's aim is a meaningful death and helping others rather than self-expression.

folkways.japan: Curses drawn from yōkai and onryō folklore, Buddhist-derived jujutsu lore, high-school seniority and old clans echo Japanese settings and norms; the story's critique of hidebound elders and hereditary privilege is its own message.

delivery.evidence: Mentors state lessons (Nanami on duty, ch. 19 and 31; Yuji's grandfather, ch. 1), while villains like Geto and Mahito get full arguments (ch. 77-78, 30); Akutami says no character holds the ultimate truth.
delivery.note: Lessons are spoken by mentors and tested in fights; villains' worldviews are given space before they lose.

personified.ideology: Strength and pleasure are all that matter
Souls are only shapes; nothing has meaning

101517.dominant: Existentialism, Pagan/occult, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

86635.heading: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War
86635.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: The elite-academy setting, senpai-kohai etiquette, the student council's authority, Valentine's and White Day customs, Christmas Eve as a couples' holiday, conglomerate dynasties and the Kaguya-hime folktale are Japanese norms the story treats as setting; the pressure of reputation (Ishigami's shunning) reflects Japanese school culture as the story portrays it.

folkways.japan: The "King game" is a real Japanese party game of dares; the cell-phone novel boom of the late 2000s, school-class seating numbers, the shame of public popularity votes, and group conformity in class life are the setting. 46765.heading: Kingdom
46765.label: From summaries
46765.life_message: A worthy life is lived for a great dream larger than oneself: courage, loyalty to comrades and a just king, and the will to rise from nothing, spent in a war the story frames as the price of a lasting peace.

frames.concerns: Peace imposed by conquest; authoritarian unity.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Honor, face and revenge drive generals and clans; duels and oaths matter.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Unity and order under a just king are the goal.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the unit and state, but clans and noble families still matter.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Strong military and royal hierarchy, softened by merit-based rise.
