folkways.japan: A Japanese seinen retelling of Chinese history in the tradition of historical war epics; the warrior-loyalty ideal, the stress on comrades and the rise of a commoner by merit read in a Japanese key (compare the samurai epic), and Hara's years in a corporate team shaped his view of leadership (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Zheng states his dream of unifying to end war, and Hara says he chose to portray him as an enlightened ruler (VIZ Q&A). Enemy generals like Li Mu and Pang Nuan are given their own philosophies; Lu Buwei is a strong opponent.
delivery.note: The story argues openly for unification through speeches and the hero's rise, while keeping many sides sympathetic.

personified.ideology: Unification to end war; a ruler of law

46765.dominant: Patriotism / nationalism (unification), Classical virtue ethics, Authoritarianism (benevolent form), Bushido / honor code, Strength rules (explored), Utilitarianism.

folkways.japan: A Japanese-styled ship culture (dormitories, festivals, hot springs, kanji everywhere, hand rails and emergency drills), a ship-first ethic and a hidden council of elders reflect Japanese settings and norms; Nihei says it may carry some of Japan's essence but is not a copy of modern Japan (Barnes & Noble, 2016).

85702.heading: Konosuba: God's Blessing on This Wonderful World!

folkways.japan: Parodies the Japanese isekai boom and gamer otaku culture: the hikikomori (shut-in) NEET hero, chūnibyō ("eighth-grader syndrome") posing in the Crimson Magic Clan, Japanese hot-spring and bathhouse comedy, and fantasy borrowed from Dragon Quest and other Japanese role-playing games.

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 1) reads it as parody where the jokes come from taking fantasy at face value; no lesson is stated, and sincere heroes (Mitsurugi) and fanatics (the Axis Church) are drawn as cartoons.
delivery.note: Values come through gags and the occasional sincere moment (ch. 53, 74-79, 102-103) rather than speeches.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Reiko's worth is inherent and claimed quietly; no one avenges slights except Miyuki, whose revenge is abandoned (anime ep. 12).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters reinvent themselves; the city's only "order" is a corporate simulation that collapses.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Neighbors and coworkers matter more than blood family; Yaomay flees, then reconciles with, her mother.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A two-person office of near-equals; the Hebinuma family's corporate power is the menace.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science-fiction mechanisms explain everything; religion is absent; old customs survive as nostalgia.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being one's own self, not a copy, is the central value.

folkways.japan: A Japanese company man (Kudou transferred from the Japan branch) in a Hong Kong setting seen through Japanese nostalgia for the Showa-era city; reserve about feelings, workplace senpai-kohai roles and grief kept private reflect Japanese norms. Anime Feminist notes the nostalgia may carry echoes of Japan's imperial past in Hong Kong.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it a languid, mood-driven mystery; the themes come through Reiko's discoveries and small daily scenes, and the one argued position (Yulong's) is answered by Reiko's refusal, not by a lecture.
delivery.note: The message about selfhood and regret is carried by mood, mystery and symbol (eyesight, glasses, the goldfish, the looping summer) rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: You are yourself, not a copy; live now
Clinging to a lost love and a lost city
The copy should die so the original can be free

folkways.japan: High school club culture (bukatsu), senpai-kohai seniority, team harmony and the Winter Cup as a national dream are Japanese norms shown positively; Teiko's elite program reflects concern about results-only youth sport, while Kagami's American upbringing adds a more individual, playground style.

74489.label: From summaries

Order vs freedom.evidence: Obedience to Kongo versus Phos's search for truth; neither is clearly endorsed.

folkways.japan: The manga industry's contest and serialization system, school refusal (futoko), the shared grief after the Kyoto Animation attack and the ideal of mastery through diligent practice are Japanese context; the story treats the last as true and the others as setting.

folkways.japan: A Japanese story borrowing Western Christian imagery (the Vatican, exorcists, the Seven Deadly Sins) as many manga do; the overworked child-weapon who apologizes and promises to do better and the setting in a Japanese studio and high school (Part 4) reflect Japanese school and shonen norms. Japan is about one percent Christian (from general knowledge; to verify), so the Church is read largely as a foreign institution.

delivery.evidence: Characters state the thesis (Dante's advice, ch. 1; the boy's speech to Lucifer, ch. 97), but churchmen like Daniel and Heisenberg are given reasons, demons are given backstories, and the boy's faith is never mocked.

folkways.japan: Parodies the Japanese web-novel 'villainess' genre, where a noble daughter's public broken engagement and loss of face start the story; the reincarnated 'heroine' Terenezza turns the usual isekai setup into the villain's role.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers describe the noble villains as cartoonish targets (A.V. Club; ANN ep. 12 calls Terenezza too stupid to see her plan fail); the moral (slavery is wrong, abusers deserve punishment) is never argued against.

31211.heading: Me and the Devil Blues: The Unreal Life of Robert Johnson

folkways.japan: The story is set entirely in the American South; Japanese context is in the telling: a Japanese seinen artist's reimagining of an American legend, Japanese body language noted by Brienza, and the readership of a men's magazine. Described, not judged.

folkways.japan: The family temple a son is expected to inherit, and the idea of training the mind in daily life, reflect Japanese Buddhism, where temple priests commonly marry and pass temples down in families (from general knowledge; to verify), which makes Medaka's no-romance rule a story device rather than a general Japanese practice. folkways.japan: Japanese youth sport culture (club hierarchies, badge tests, rinks run by former athletes, parents watching from the stands), senpai-kohai respect, gratitude and repayment of kindness, and an underdog "gekokujo" (overturning rank) theme; the story draws on these norms while questioning how much pressure adults put on children.

delivery.evidence: Jun Yodaka's win-at-all-costs view is given real weight and real success; Inori's mother's caution is treated as love; Koichi's counsel in ch. 60 is the most openly stated lesson.
delivery.note: The message is carried by training, competition and character backstories rather than speeches, with a few explicit talks from mentors.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Totalitarian order, secret police and indoctrination are the antagonists; freedom of conscience is honored.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to family and to friends is tested against loyalty to nation; the story sides with people over the state.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Racial hierarchy is condemned; mixed-race and Jewish characters are the sympathetic center.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Political dogma is the danger; a journalist's evidence and memory are the hope; religious tradition appears mainly as identity.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Wartime survival, flight and hiding dominate; self-expression (Ogi's poems) is punished.

folkways.japan: Tezuka puts Japan's own wartime alliance with Germany, its Kenpeitai and its militarist schools in view, alongside the real Kobe Jewish community and the Sorge spy case; Col. Honda's seppuku and his killing of his son draw on the samurai honor code, shown as tragedy.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call the anti-war message strong but carried by characters and history (Experiments in Manga); the frame story and the closing question about "justice" state it outright (BookDragon; Wikipedia). Nazi ideology is shown from inside a sympathetic child, while Hitler himself is a caricature (TV Tropes).
delivery.note: The message is mostly dramatized, but the ending steps forward to state it, and the cycle-of-revenge coda is the story's argument made plain.

frames.concerns: Sexual content and fan service throughout; consent as a joke; sexual content involving a minor (ch. 92-97).

frames.aligns: Prejudice exposed as irrational; liminals win rights through law and acceptance.
frames.concerns: Objectification and non-consent as comedy; a minor sexualized.

frames.concerns: Constant sexual content; consent as a joke; a minor sexualized.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Kimihito answers insults with patience; tribal honor customs (centaur riding, ch. 4) are treated as quaint.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules of the exchange act are constantly broken for comedy; desire drives the plot.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The household is kin; the exchange program is civic, and Kimihito serves both.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Bodies, desires and personal comfort dominate; survival is never at stake.

folkways.japan: The yokai-like monster girls, the seinen harem genre, the host-family system, the shrine maiden job and the government bureaucracy reflect Japanese settings and genre norms; the integration plot echoes Japanese debates about foreign residents and visas.

delivery.evidence: The racist couple are cartoon villains with no case (ch. 2, 9); prejudice is never given a fair hearing. The anti-prejudice message is carried by situations, not speeches.
delivery.note: Acceptance is the stated theme, but the sexual comedy dominates almost every chapter.

66213.dominant: Hedonism (affirmed), Communitarianism (found family), acceptance of the outsider through Progressivism and Liberalism (explored).

30001.heading: Monster
30001.label: From summaries
30001.life_message: Every life has equal worth, even a monster's: a good person keeps saving lives rather than taking one, and a name, a memory and someone who cares are what keep a person human.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every life (CCC 2258) in Tenma's choice and in saving Johan; evil depicted but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); conversion of Eva and Lunge. Matthew Tan reads it as communion against isolation (Humanum Review).
frames.concerns: Many suicides and suicide games; Tenma's resolve to kill; dread with no explicit grace.

frames.aligns: Repentance in many lives; Tenma's humility and self-giving; evil as personal and deceiving.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against long dread, murder and despair; Antichrist imagery used as a thriller motif.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a hero who will not take vengeance (Romans 12:19); the worth of the outcast (immigrants, orphans).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the murders, drinking and suicide content; T+ and TV-MA ratings. Views vary by family.

frames.aligns: Gaheret (Beneath the Tangles) reads Johan as a real, personal evil that works through people's own flaws, powerful but not all-powerful.
frames.concerns: Rescue in the story is human and medical, not explicitly in Christ; the open ending.

frames.aligns: Real, personal evil that tempts and deceives; deliverance from despair (Nina).
frames.concerns: An Antichrist motif with no spiritual battle; picture books used for mind control; a dark open ending. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Total depravity in how easily people are drawn to Johan; common grace in Tenma's mercy and in skilled art; providence-like irony in the ending.
frames.concerns: Long violence and despair; little lascivious content.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Tenma's guilt and the grace of being forgiven by those he wronged; vocation as a physician.
frames.concerns: Little beyond the dread; LCMS and WELS families may weigh the suicide content more.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and social holiness (care for immigrants and orphans; Tenma keeps treating patients while on the run, from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Drinking and gun violence; holiness churches more cautious under the General Rules.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: a serious literary thriller that condemns cruelty and honors mercy.
frames.concerns: Little beyond the dark mood.

frames.aligns: Tenma never kills; the climax is healing an enemy; a critique of state violence (Kinderheim) and nationalism (neo-Nazis).
frames.concerns: Tenma carries a gun and intends to kill; heavy violence; conservative groups avoid popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency over upbringing; the worth of souls (D&C 18:10); family and identity restored (Nina).
frames.concerns: Alcohol, suicide themes, nude photos (anime). Does it invite the Spirit (For the Strength of Youth)?

frames.aligns: Equal worth across class and nationality (immigrants, orphans); critique of xenophobia, neo-Nazis and abusive institutions.
frames.concerns: Few women in power; little on structural repair.

frames.aligns: The sanctity of life and a healer as hero fit the health-ministry tradition; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": long murder, alcohol and despair content; Antichrist motif used as suspense.

frames.aligns: Exposes nationalism, political power and violence as destructive; values life.
frames.concerns: Constant violence (Psalm 11:5); mind control through picture books; surgery is central (members accept surgery without transfusion; not raised by the story).

frames.aligns: Love overcoming hatred; truth exposing error.
frames.concerns: Surgery and medicine save lives at the core of the story; fear, disease, injury and death fill it.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh: saving a life overrides almost everything; "whoever saves one life saves a world" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5); teshuvah for Eva and Lunge; neo-Nazis condemned.
frames.concerns: Time on secular entertainment; immodest images (anime); Haredi homes may restrict it. A "new Hitler" plot needs care.

frames.aligns: Sanctity of life; memory and names as a moral duty; neo-Nazis and genocidal plans condemned.
frames.concerns: Little; no antisemitic tropes reported (to verify).

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in healing; anti-racism; equal dignity.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.aligns: "Whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32); Turkish immigrants shown as victims of hate, not as villains; mercy and justice.
frames.concerns: Alcohol throughout; immodest images (anime); suicide content.

frames.aligns: Ahimsa and the dharma of the healer; karma-like consequences of one choice; the self beyond a name.
frames.concerns: Little beyond the violence.

frames.aligns: Compassion without exception; craving and ignorance as roots of harm; Johan's "nameless" emptiness read against non-self.
frames.concerns: Killing on many pages; Johan's nihilism could be confused with emptiness (sunyata), which it is not.

frames.aligns: Sarbat da bhala (the welfare of all); seva in Tenma's service; ego (haumai) in the hospital director.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.aligns: Oneness of humanity against racism and nationalism; service as worship; low glorification of violence.
frames.concerns: Drinking; dread.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in Tenma; gratitude and purity of heart.

frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.concerns: A psychotherapist and a criminal psychologist are sympathetic helpers and therapy heals, which the church's opposition to psychiatry rejects (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.concerns: Women mostly in supporting roles; some critics (Brienza, ANN) find the ending unsatisfying.

frames.aligns: The inherent worth of every person without appeal to the supernatural; science and medicine as service; eugenics and mind control condemned; choice over upbringing.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.concerns: An outlaw hero for most of the story; little faith content.

frames.aligns: The first principle, the "inherent worth and dignity of every person," is the hero's motto; justice and compassion; a free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.concerns: Tenma's mercy to a man who harms others conflicts with "responsibility to the responsible" (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak (orphans, abused children, immigrants targeted by neo-Nazis); mercy instead of revenge (Romans 12:19); redemption for Eva, Lunge and others; a man who endures false accusation and keeps doing good.
frames.concerns: Drinking, suicide and long despair; no explicit faith; Revelation imagery used for suspense.

frames.aligns: Goodness grounded in empathy and a doctor's oath, not command; eugenics, cults of personality and mind control condemned; problems solved by investigation and medicine.
frames.concerns: Revelation epigraphs and devil imagery are framing, not doctrine; little to raise.

frames.aligns: Johan's nature and the final page are left open; several worldviews get a fair hearing (Tenma, Eva, Lunge, Johan); no preaching.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.aligns: Every life matters; names, memory and family; karma-like justice for abusers; hope for survivors.
frames.concerns: Dark mood and many deaths.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Tenma refuses revenge and the code of honor; dignity of every person is the motto.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rule of law is valued (Lunge's procedure, Tenma clearing his name) while secret-police order is condemned.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Tenma serves strangers of every nationality; kin ties are often broken or abusive.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The hospital's ranking of patients is the original sin of the story (ch. 1).

folkways.japan: A Japanese doctor abroad, his sense of duty and humility, and Urasawa's reading of German medicine are the Japanese threads; the setting and social issues are European (reunification, neo-Nazis, East German institutions).

delivery.evidence: Characters argue the worth of a life directly (Tenma, Eva, Johan); TV Tropes lists forgiveness as the moral; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Competing views on the worth of a life are voiced by characters within a thriller plot, and the villain's view gets a full, frightening hearing.

personified.ideology: Death is the only equality; nihilism

30001.dominant: Nihilism (critiqued), Duty ethics (affirmed), Secular humanism, Existentialism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Communitarianism.

59211.heading: Monthly Girls' Nozaki-kun
59211.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai relationships, school clubs (drama, art, choir, basketball), the four-panel gag format and the economics of monthly manga magazines are Japanese settings; Kashima's princely stage persona echoes the all-female Takarazuka Revue's male-role stars (from general knowledge; to verify). The series pokes fun at these conventions rather than criticizing them.

delivery.evidence: Four-panel gags with no lectures; the gender-role commentary is carried by reversals and misunderstandings (The Mary Sue; Anime Feminist).
delivery.note: Its outlook comes through parody of romance-manga clichés and the friend group's comedy, not through speeches.

personified.ideology: Gender roles as a costume one may enjoy

98544.heading: Moriarty the Patriot
98544.label: From summaries
98544.life_message: Cruel privilege deserves to fall, but the man who kills to bring it down still carries real guilt: death is no atonement, and friendship gives him a reason to live and make amends.

content.framing: Mixed: murders of cruel nobles framed as justice; the nobles' own cruelty and the Ripper killings condemned

content.frequency: Builds through the story; peaks at the climax

frames.aligns: Concern for the poor against cruel elites (Rerum Novarum); Holmes's refusal to let William die matches CCC 2280-2283; the vow to atone (ch. 66) echoes repentance and reparation.
frames.concerns: Doing evil so good may come is ruled out (CCC 1753-1756); the hero plans murders as policy and is admired for it; children kill in ch. 1.

frames.aligns: William's longing to repent and Holmes's mercy; the self-giving of Albert, who takes the blame.
frames.concerns: Pride of intellect playing God over who dies; vengeance framed as justice.

frames.aligns: The sins of the powerful exposed; the lowly lifted up; the ending rejects suicide and seeks amends.
frames.concerns: Vengeance taken into human hands (Romans 12:19); "let us do evil that good may come" condemned (Romans 3:8).

frames.aligns: A strong discussion starter on justice, motives and grace: Holmes's rescue reads as unearned mercy.
frames.concerns: A murderer is the sympathetic lead; the lesson that murder is wrong arrives late and gently.

frames.aligns: No occult; clear stakes; deliverance of the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Bloodshed and revenge for a cause; a villain who claims God for his killings.

frames.aligns: Total depravity shown in high places; the ending gives the sword back to lawful authority (the Crown reforms the Lords).
frames.concerns: A private man takes the magistrate's sword (Romans 13:4); murder as a strategy (WLC Q135-136).

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms questions about unjust rulers; grace offered to a guilty man (ch. 55).
frames.concerns: Fifth Commandment broken as policy; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the poor, a working-class student given a chance (ch. 31), reform of an unjust order.
frames.concerns: The means are murder; holiness churches wary of the violence.

frames.aligns: Moral complexity taken seriously; Holmes as a real counterweight; the church-and-crown setting reformed rather than overthrown.
frames.concerns: The glamour of the brilliant killer; violence against children in ch. 10-11.

frames.aligns: The injustice of the powerful is named; the ending refuses death as a solution.
frames.concerns: Killing to reform society is the premise; vengeance and violence throughout; separation from violent media.

frames.aligns: Brotherly loyalty; repentance and restitution as the end of William's story.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on graphic violence; murder and deception as tools.

frames.aligns: Systemic injustice of class directly confronted; a gender-nonconforming ally accepted; reform through law.
frames.concerns: Violence as the answer to injustice; villains drawn as caricatures (WWAC).

frames.aligns: Concern for the poor; mercy at the end.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": constant murder and gore; deception as virtue.

frames.aligns: Exposes the corruption of human governments and of a man who kills in God's name.
frames.concerns: Violence is central; political conspiracy; a gender-identity storyline.

frames.aligns: Intellect and truth (Holmes) outwit evil; life chosen over death.
frames.concerns: Hatred, murder and death dwelt on.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor and the orphan (Deuteronomy 10:18); teshuvah (repentance) and choosing life (Deuteronomy 30:19).
frames.concerns: Murder is among the gravest sins; private vengeance forbidden (Leviticus 19:18); graphic killing.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam concerns; teshuvah; saving a life (pikuach nefesh) when Holmes jumps.
frames.concerns: Revenge and killing as method.

frames.aligns: The prophetic call against oppression (Amos 5:24); social reform; acceptance of a gender-nonconforming character.
frames.concerns: Violence as the solution.

frames.aligns: Standing for justice even against the powerful (Qur'an 4:135); suicide rejected (4:29).
frames.concerns: Extrajudicial killing (5:32 on the sanctity of life); a gender-identity storyline.

frames.aligns: A fight against adharmic rulers echoes the Gita's call to act; karma reaches the brothers (Albert's arrest, William's lost eye).
frames.concerns: Deceit and murder; no Krishna-like guidance, only William's own judgment.

frames.aligns: Shows how hatred breeds more suffering; the ending turns from death to atonement.
frames.concerns: Killing as a method breaks the first precept; the hero's hatred drives the plot.

frames.aligns: Defense of the oppressed against tyranny; seva (Louis serving the nation, anime ep. 24).
frames.concerns: Covert murder, not open and righteous defense; deception.

frames.aligns: Opposes class prejudice; the oneness of humanity; reform through the sovereign.
frames.concerns: Violence and conspiracy against the government; murder.

frames.aligns: Sincere loyalty (makoto) among the brothers; purification and renewal after the fall into the Thames.
frames.concerns: Bloodshed and death (kegare) throughout.

frames.aligns: Opposes exploitation by the powerful; consequences return to the doers (Albert arrested, William maimed).
frames.concerns: Harm done to many; "harm none" broken by the hero.

frames.aligns: Improving society; exposing the corrupt.
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness) broken by the hero.

frames.aligns: Anti-classist critique; a gender-nonconforming character accepted; suicide rejected.
frames.concerns: Glamorized political violence; caricatured opponents (WWAC).

frames.aligns: Reason (Holmes) set against William's methods; human friendship, not faith, saves him; reform by law.
frames.concerns: Utilitarian murder made appealing.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, sacrifice; the Crown and Parliament reformed, not overthrown; crime still requires punishment (Albert arrested).
frames.concerns: Murder of the nobility made heroic; a gender-identity storyline.

frames.aligns: Equity and the dignity of the poor; acceptance of a gender-nonconforming ally.
frames.concerns: Violence as a path to justice.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against arbitrary, cruel authority; responsibility to the responsible.
frames.concerns: The ending's turn to atonement and self-blame sits apart from Satanic self-regard.

frames.aligns: Deliverance of the oppressed (Exodus 3:7-10); the lowly lifted up; second chances when William chooses to live.
frames.concerns: Revenge celebrated as justice (Romans 12:19); murder as a tool; a villain who claims God for his killings.

frames.aligns: No faith-based resolution; reasoned argument between two brilliant men; a man who kills in God's name exposed (ch. 10-11).
frames.concerns: Murder for a cause presented sympathetically.

frames.aligns: Neither hero has final certainty; the story leaves William's guilt open; several sides get reasons.
frames.concerns: Charismatic leader whose followers obey without question (Moran, Fred).

frames.aligns: Loyalty to family and friends; payback for cruel people, then a second chance; karma-like justice.
frames.concerns: Constant killing; a hero who manipulates even his friends.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are answered by personal retribution on behalf of victims (ch. 2-11), not courts; the ending moves toward atonement and law.

Order vs freedom.evidence: William breaks the law to build a new order, and the story ends with order restored under reformed institutions.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Civic goals (the nation's reform) drive the plot; a tight chosen family carries it out.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hereditary hierarchy is the enemy; the band includes a soldier, a disguise artist, a blind inventor and an actress as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Reason and science (deduction, chemistry, Herder's inventions) rule; religion appears only as a villain's pretext and in atonement language.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival of the poor drives the cases; Bonde's self-chosen identity and William's final choice to live for himself lean to self-expression.

folkways.japan: A Japanese shonen reimagining of Victorian Britain: the "gentleman" villain and "rough" detective (Wikipedia, Production), intense bonds between brothers and rivals, and a hero who takes the nation's sins on himself. The title word yūkoku (grieving for one's country) has a long use in Japanese political and literary writing (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: The Beat's Santilli finds Moriarty not sanitized, his methods cruel enough to frighten; WWAC finds the noble targets classist to an implausible degree. Holmes and Watson argue against William at length (ch. 55, 66).
delivery.note: The class critique is built into every case, while the counterargument (no one may decide who dies) is carried by Holmes and lands at the climax.

personified.ideology: Ending the class system by any means
Truth; no one may decide who dies

98544.dominant: Utilitarianism (ends versus means, explored), Duty ethics (Holmes's counterweight), Critical theory and Marxism (class critique), Patriotism (remaking the nation the hero loves).

30740.heading: MPD Psycho

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Heroism means reaching out to save even the villain (Deku and Shigaraki, ch. 423); Stain's purity killings are condemned. Bakugo's pride ends in apology (ch. 322), and forgiveness is honored over vengeance.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Training, teamwork and school discipline win, and reckless solo heroics are punished. The Hero Commission's secret killings are exposed (ch. 314), and the story chooses reform from within.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Help everyone, without being asked. Endeavor's breeding of children for power is condemned (ch. 39, 290-291); found family in Class 1-A carries the warmth (ch. 319-323).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hero rankings and the single "Symbol of Peace" are critiqued; "anyone can be a hero" (Horikoshi, 2024). Mentorship and passing power down (All Might to Deku) are honored.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No real-world faith shapes the plot; vestiges of past users live on inside One For All. Readers find redemption themes, but institutions, science and reform drive the plot.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Helping others and peace are the aims; Toga's self-expression is treated with sympathy and caution (ch. 391-395). War and mass casualties in later volumes keep security in view.

folkways.japan: The school-club and sports-festival culture, respect for teachers and the shōnen ideal of friendship, effort and victory are Japanese school norms the story uses as its setting, while its critique of hero celebrity and a state commission is its own message.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist's Mo Black reads its politics as conservative; Plugged In praises its self-sacrifice message; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Villains such as Shigaraki and Stain state their grievances against hero society directly, and the story answers mainly through Deku; the final chapter states the theme in Deku's own reflections (ch. 430).

personified.ideology: A society that failed a child deserves destruction
Only true heroes deserve the name

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Honor and face matter (clans, rivalries, avenging teachers: Shikamaru buries Hidan, ch. 337), but the story's answer to revenge is forgiveness (ch. 448, 699).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The village's order and the Hokage are honored; Naruto bends rules for friends, and abuses of order (Root) are condemned.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Village before clan: Itachi kills his clan for the village; the alliance of nations goes further. Found family replaces lost kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks, clans and Kage hierarchy are the setting; the story keeps showing that a "failure" or a branch-family member can surpass the elite (Lee, Neji, Naruto).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Inherited will, ancestors, spirits, reincarnation and village founders shape everything.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and survival dominate; Naruto's dream of recognition is the self-expression thread.

folkways.japan: Ninja and samurai lore, kitsune myth, Shinto kami names, Buddhist six realms, the Chinese zodiac in hand signs, senpai-kohai and master-pupil bonds, and Kishimoto's memory of Hiroshima through his grandfather shape the series; its message of loyalty to the group sits comfortably within Japanese norms while its forgiveness of enemies pushes against cycles of revenge.

delivery.evidence: Long dialogues state the message (Naruto and Nagato, ch. 443-449; Naruto and Sasuke, ch. 693-699); villains' motives are given fully (Konieczny via Wikipedia: antagonists shaped by past wars).

folkways.japan: Japanese office culture: senpai-kohai mentorship, company trips after a release, overtime and the black-company debate fans raise (fan wiki); the yonkoma "cute girls" format of the Kirara magazines; the ending imagines a Japan that has legalized same-sex marriage.

delivery.evidence: Four-panel gags carry the message through small workplace moments; no speeches about work or love were reported. No character argues that the work culture is wrong (fan wiki).
delivery.note: A light comedy whose values show in what it rewards: effort, humility and kindness; the same-sex marriage is presented as a happy fact in the final chapter, not argued for.

85697.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (diligence, humility), Communitarianism (team as family), Expressive individualism (pursuing a dream).

31373.heading: Nijigahara Holograph
31373.label: From summaries

61499.heading: Nisekoi: False Love
61499.label: From summaries
61499.life_message: Honesty about your feelings matters more than a promise made long ago or a role arranged by your parents; kindness, loyalty to friends and peacemaking make a good life.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Gang honor and turf drive the premise, but conflicts are defused by the fake couple and comedy rather than avenged (ch. 1-2).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Parents' arrangements are worked around; Marika's forced wedding is stopped (ch. 189-191); the friends act on their own choices.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and gang loyalty come first; Raku succeeds his father (ch. 229); the friend group as chosen kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Gang ranks ("young master"), fathers' authority and teacher roles; peers are equals at school.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular school life; festivals and a childhood promise treated as near-fate; a traditional marriage ending.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Feelings, confession and personal choice in love; careers in design, baking and science; no material struggle.

folkways.japan: The yakuza-family comedy, the "young master" hierarchy, school festivals, class trips, shrine visits and the shonen-magazine harem romance are Japanese conventions that frame the story rather than form its message. A teacher quitting on marriage (ch. 122, per the earlier quick read citing TV Tropes; to verify) reflects a Japanese norm that can surprise Western readers.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it a cliché but cheerful comedy (ANN's Silverman; UK Anime Network's "packed to the rafters with clichés"); none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its view of honesty and chosen love emerges through running gags and the final choice, while the gang setting and harem conventions go unexamined.

personified.ideology: Honest, chosen love and an ordinary, decent life over fate and the family gang

54308.heading: No. 6
54308.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Deliverance from bondage (Exodus) and walls that fall (Joshua 6); the poor and the displaced as the ones God sees; truth spoken to power; a mother's endurance (Karan); confession and repentance (Rou).
frames.concerns: A same-sex romance between the leads (a concern for many families, not all); a forest goddess shown as the power of judgment; violence and a sexual proposition in the setting.

frames.aligns: Characters investigate and expose lies; a manipulative civic religion (the Holy Day) and propaganda are condemned; goodness comes from empathy, not command.
frames.concerns: A goddess's power resolves the climax, though inside a fictional world; graphic deaths.

frames.aligns: Fair treatment of mystery: Elyurias is real in the story but never fully explained as doctrine; humility about what the founders thought they knew.
frames.concerns: Little beyond violence.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends and family, decency, fairness and karma-like justice (the city's crimes come back on it); institutions that control people are the villains; a spiritual force that protects.
frames.concerns: Graphic deaths; the romance for some families.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Nezumi's grudge against the city for his people, tempered by Shion's insistence on mercy (ch. 3, 27).

Order vs freedom.evidence: A controlled utopia is the villain; life outside the wall is harsh but free.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to West Block's people and to each other; Shion's mother's love is a constant.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Elite privilege and class walls condemned (Kronos, Lost Town, West Block).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A technocratic city is condemned and an indigenous forest culture honored, but no religious answer is offered.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in the slum (dogs for heat, bartering) alongside love and art (Nezumi's theater).

folkways.japan: Shion's polite, sheltered upbringing set against Nezumi's outsider bluntness plays on Japanese inside-outside (uchi-soto) distinctions; the forest people and their goddess echo Japanese ideas of nature spirits; the story's anti-war, anti-state tone fits much postwar Japanese youth fiction.

delivery.evidence: ANN's vol. 9 review: much of the final volume explains the city's truth, though the reviewer found it seldom reads as an info-dump. THEM (anime) found the story had to tell the viewer what is wrong. City officials are drawn as cruel; Rou, a founder, is given a fuller account of how idealists built something evil (ch. 22-27).
delivery.note: The critique of the controlled city is carried by the plot and, in the last volumes, by long explanation of the city's secrets.

personified.ideology: control and order over human life
the idealist who built the utopia

54308.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Critical theory (class walls), Environmentalism, Pacifism / nonviolence (explored).

112253.heading: No Longer Allowed In Another World
112253.label: From summaries
112253.life_message: Played as dark comedy: a man who says he wants only to die keeps helping others to live, and listening to each person's story heals them; slowly the story gives him reasons to go on, though it jokes about suicide throughout.

content.framing: Neutral (fantasy action); abuse of power condemned
Played for comedy (fan service); one groping gag
Mixed: suicide played for laughs, but the plot steers toward life

frames.aligns: Mercy and listening heal sinners rather than destroying them; a would-be suicide is stopped (ep. 4); the plot moves toward choosing life.
frames.concerns: Suicide is grave matter (CCC 2280-2283) and here is the running joke; drug misuse played for laughs (CCC 2291); a manipulative Pope and Church in the fantasy world.

frames.aligns: Compassion that sees each person's wound; enemies forgiven.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction treated lightly; the Church's hierarchy shown as scheming; sorcery and summoning.

frames.aligns: Mercy and second chances (Suzuki, Saitō); a reason to live found in others.
frames.concerns: Life belongs to God (Psalm 139); suicide and pill abuse as comedy; fan service; Philippians 4:8 test.

frames.aligns: Every person has a story worth hearing; friends who won't give up on a despairing man.
frames.concerns: Suicide jokes; a religious hierarchy as villains; harem fan service.

frames.aligns: Deliverance of people bound by bitterness and trauma (Yuriko, Suzuki).
frames.concerns: Suicide and drug jokes; magic and summoning; Holiness standards on fan service.

frames.concerns: Pill abuse and suicide gags; fan service.

frames.concerns: Trivializing suicide; Episcopal and ACNA families differ on dark comedy.

frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; suicide, drugs and fan service.

frames.concerns: Drug dependence and death as comedy.

frames.concerns: Taking one's life is forbidden (Genesis 9:5); suicide and drug use as comedy; tzniut and fan service.

frames.concerns: Suicide jokes; pills.

frames.aligns: Mental-health themes taken seriously in places; mercy and justice for the bullied.
frames.concerns: Flippancy about suicide and about a real person's death.

frames.concerns: Suicide is forbidden (4:29); intoxicants and pills; magic; fan service.

frames.aligns: Karma worked out through understanding; duty to help others even when one suffers.
frames.concerns: Suicide treated lightly; drug use.

frames.aligns: Compassionate listening frees others from bitterness; craving for non-existence shown as a trap Sensei slowly leaves.
frames.concerns: Fifth precept (intoxicants); suicide as a gag.

frames.aligns: Seva and compassion for the troubled.
frames.concerns: Intoxicants are forbidden; suicide jokes.

frames.aligns: Service and the healing of hearts.
frames.concerns: Drugs forbidden; suicide is forbidden; fan service.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Disputes are settled by understanding, not revenge; Waldelia's vow of vengeance is the exception (ep. 3).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Sensei rejects the hero role, the Church's orders and later Sacchan's control (fan wiki).

Civic vs kin.evidence: A found family of companions; strangers are helped one by one.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Kings, popes and bishops are mostly foolish or scheming; a demi-human princess and an orphan are equals in the party.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Irreverent toward religion and death; nature spirits treated kindly.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival means nothing to the hero; writing and personal freedom do.

folkways.japan: The series leans on Japanese literary history: Dazai's novels, his 1948 death with his lover, and the shinjū (lovers' suicide) tradition in Japanese drama and fiction (Wikipedia; from general knowledge; to verify). It also parodies the Japanese isekai light-novel boom (summoned by a truck, stats, harems). These are described here as context.

delivery.evidence: Each arc repeats the formula of hearing a villain's past and healing them (Wikipedia ep. 4-11; Real Sound); Sacchan names the change in Sensei outright (ep. 12). Sensei himself scorns people who preach their own righteousness (fan wiki).
delivery.note: The death wish is played as a gag in nearly every chapter, while the counter-message (life is worth living) is shown through his actions and others' reactions rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Romantic despair and the wish to die, slowly turned toward life
Love fused with death; possessive devotion
Religious authority using summoned heroes for its own ends

112253.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Nihilism (critiqued: the death wish loses ground), Postmodernism (isekai parody and metafiction).

43290.heading: No Longer Human
43290.label: From summaries
43290.life_message: None is held up as a lesson: the story shows a man destroyed by fear of others, a false face, drink and the people who use him and whom he uses, and it asks what it means to be fully human, leaving almost no path out.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; no hope offered

frames.aligns: An honest picture of a soul without grace, echoing Augustine's restless heart; sin shown as slavery, not freedom.
frames.concerns: Despair (CCC 2091) and suicide (CCC 2280-2283) left without hope of mercy; sexual scenes and drug use.

frames.aligns: A portrait of the passions enslaving a soul; despair named honestly.
frames.concerns: No repentance or healing; sexual scenes and suicide imagery inflame rather than guard the heart.

frames.aligns: The bondage of addiction and despair shown plainly.

frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content, drugs and suicide; For the Strength of Youth cautions.

frames.aligns: A compassionate look at depression and alienation; harm to women shown as harm.
frames.concerns: Suicide safe-messaging; women used by Yozo.

frames.aligns: Shows how alcohol and drugs destroy body and mind (health message).
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": dark and sexual content; no hope offered.

frames.concerns: Suicide, intoxicants, nudity and promiscuity; despair as conclusion.

frames.aligns: Serious literature on human brokenness.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content; suicide.

frames.aligns: Ethical reflection on harm, alienation and mental illness.
frames.concerns: Suicide portrayal; treatment of women.

frames.aligns: A warning of a life without God-consciousness (taqwa).
frames.concerns: Zina, intoxicants, nudity and suicide; despair of God's mercy, which the Quran forbids (39:53).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Yozo avoids conflict through clowning; family shame matters more than any code.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Yozo drifts outside family and work rules entirely.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Estranged from his wealthy family; lives off strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Family and social rank weigh on him but are not celebrated.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern, godless urban Tokyo in the manga's update (Dacey).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Preoccupied with authenticity and the true self, though he never finds it.

folkways.japan: The gap between tatemae (public face) and honne (true feeling), the shame of failing a powerful father, and the literary tradition of the confessional "I-novel" are Japanese norms the story turns into tragedy (I-novel framing from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: No character argues for another way of living; the narrator records rather than judges (Dacey; novel structure).
delivery.note: The meaning is carried by images (puppet, drowning, flames) and by the arc of decline, not by any stated lesson.

43290.dominant: Existentialism (what makes a person human), Nihilism (explored as ruin), Expressive individualism (the mask versus the true self), Hedonism (shown as empty).

58533.heading: No Matter How I Look at It, It's You Guys' Fault I'm Not Popular!
58533.label: From summaries

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Tomoko stews over slights in her head but seldom retaliates; worth is found in acceptance, not reputation.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Classmate friendships become her main support, while family ties are repaired (ch. 35, 121).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Everyday modern school life; New Year customs kept as habit.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being accepted as oneself is the long arc.

folkways.japan: The fear of standing out, school clique hierarchy, the hikikomori and otaku phenomena, crowded commuter trains (ch. 24) and the Kyoto school trip reflect Japanese school life; the series satirizes the pressure rather than endorsing it.

delivery.evidence: No source describes lectures or stated morals; reviews describe change carried by events (the field trip, study camp, the festival) and by Tomoko's inner monologue (ANN 2023; The Outer Haven).
delivery.note: Its outlook on loneliness and belonging is carried by satire and by friends who keep including Tomoko, not by stated lessons.

personified.ideology: Self-pity, contempt for others, otaku fantasy, slowly giving way

58533.dominant: Communitarianism (belonging through friends), Expressive individualism (accepted as she is), Existentialism (choosing a future).

74347.heading: One-Punch Man
74347.label: From summaries
74347.life_message: A hero is someone who keeps helping people and keeps fighting, without needing praise, rank or even a challenge. Strength, fame and status are empty if they are the goal. Doing the right thing for its own sake is what counts.

frames.concerns: Fan service; a gay hero used for sex gags, including assault jokes; the word "God" for a cosmic manipulator; violence as comedy.

frames.concerns: Saitama's emptiness is left open; fan service.

frames.concerns: Little at the level of message.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Saitama gives up credit and takes the blame after the Deep Sea King (v5); doing good without praise is the ideal. Garou's grudge against heroes is shown as hurt pride turned to hatred.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions are mocked but not abolished: the Hero Association is bureaucratic and image-driven yet organizes defense (Pragmatic lens). Saitama does good on his own terms.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Heroes help whoever is in danger; family barely appears. The outsider Garou's grievance against a system that needs villains is taken seriously (Garou arc).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The ranking system is the main satire: status-seeking heroes are exposed in crises, and the weakest C-class hero, Mumen Rider, is honored for courage (ch. 26-28).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Mostly secular; a being called "God" who grants power for loyalty is a cosmic threat (from ch. 109; fan wiki). Training routines and science (Genos, Metal Knight) solve problems.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Meaning comes from small, ordinary goods: groceries on sale, meals with friends (Philosophy essay). Saitama's boredom after winning is an existential, self-expression question rather than a survival one.

folkways.japan: Saitama is drawn as a failed job-seeker (ch. 2) who never fits the salaryman mold, and the Hero Association mirrors Japanese corporate ranking, exams and public image; the story mocks these norms more than it draws on them.

delivery.evidence: Christ and Pop Culture's Kloosterman draws a lesson on faithful effort; Common Sense Media finds very little positive messaging; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes arrive mostly through parody and anticlimax rather than stated lessons; Garou is the one character who argues a worldview at length.

folkways.japan: The idol system (no-dating rules, handshake events, image control), reality TV, the 2.5D stage-play industry, senpai relations and Takachiho's mythic setting reflect Japanese norms; the story criticizes the idol industry from within rather than rejecting Japanese culture.

folkways.japan: Kanji's death from overwork (karoshi) frames the story (Wikipedia); the isekai conventions of reincarnation and "cheat" powers (AniList; MangaUpdates); and respect for the father's house and the crown reflect Japanese genre norms, set in a pseudo-French empire.

delivery.evidence: Farma states his goal of affordable, effective medicine again and again (Wikipedia; One Peace blurbs). Veron is given a reason (a child who died because a noble doctor refused him, ep. 8), and the Inquisitor's fear is presented as understandable (ANN ep. 7).
delivery.note: The message is spoken outright, but it is carried by case-of-the-week cures rather than lectures.

30128.heading: Pet Shop of Horrors
30128.label: From summaries
30128.life_message: What you desire can destroy you if you will not respect its limits: people who use animals, nature and one another for their own wants pay the price, while honesty, grief faced truthfully and love for the vulnerable can heal.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: D's family is bound by an ancestor's vow of revenge; Leon takes personal vengeance in the final arc (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Contracts must be obeyed; freedom to indulge is punished.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family bonds (Leon and Chris; D's line) matter more than the law, which barely reaches Chinatown (Japanese Wikipedia).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: D treats rich and poor alike as customers; animals ranked above humans by D.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Ancient knowledge and mythic powers defeat modern policing and science.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Desire and self-fulfillment drive the customers, and are punished when unbounded.

folkways.japan: Written for a Japanese women's horror magazine, the series imagines American cities through Chinese myth (kirin, taotie, the nine-tailed fox), the Japanese moral tale of broken taboos, and 1990s Japanese environmental concern; the sequel moves the shop to Tokyo's Kabukichō.

delivery.evidence: Each tale ends with a moral turn; ch. 8 has D give Leon an explicit lesson in ecology (Wikipedia); a MyAnimeList reviewer says the moral is never forced, others call some tales lessons.
delivery.note: The anti-greed and pro-animal message is carried by fable-like plots; D sometimes lectures, and the misanthropic extreme is voiced by D's father and shown as destructive.

folkways.japan: Restless spirits (yūrei) bound by regret, offerings to calm an angry spirit who became a goddess, Kamakura's shrines and shore, hereditary clans of mediums and school clubs are Japanese settings and beliefs; the story honors the folk religion while criticizing the clan's rigid hierarchy.

delivery.evidence: The skeptic Eugene is a lead who is right about many things; Kotaro's objection to forced exorcism changes the club's rule (ch. 4); even the assassin gets his reasons.

folkways.japan: Oni, tengu, the kudan and zashiki-warashi come from Japanese folklore; paper talismans and sealed rooms from folk religious practice; the reluctant hero and the trained heroine are Weekly Shonen Jump conventions, and the early ending reflects Jump's survey-driven cancellations.

31325.life_message: Life is precious because it passes: grasping at immortality and power brings suffering, while compassion and acceptance of the cycle of life and death let people find peace.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Tyrants, computer rule and theocracy are resisted (Future; Sun).

folkways.japan: Buddhist karma and rebirth, Shinto myth from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and postwar Japanese pacifism and skepticism of empire inform Tezuka's epic, described here as context.

delivery.evidence: The Phoenix sometimes speaks the moral directly, and Badman finds Nostalgia forced into a message; Garrity calls the series gleefully strange; tyrants are often caricatures, but Akanemaru and Romi are drawn with sympathy.
delivery.note: Ideas come through adventure, romance and tragedy, with occasional direct statements by the Phoenix or a narrator.

folkways.japan: A seinen workplace drama: a low-status section inside a big corporation, a son measured against a famous father, a mother's promise that he come home alive, and nods to Miyazawa Kenji, whose Guskou Budori gives his life for others (v4). 107098.heading: Record of Ragnarok
107098.label: From summaries
107098.life_message: Human beings have worth the gods cannot take away: ordinary and flawed people prove it by refusing to bow, fighting to the end for those they love, and earning even their enemies' respect.

folkways.japan: A Japanese seinen death-tournament built on world myth; Japanese heroes (Kojiro, Raiden, Okita, Kintoki) get loving backstories, sumo and Shinsengumi lore included. delivery.evidence: Brunhilde and the commentators state the theme (humanity's worth) outright; many gods are arrogant or petty, but Heracles, Zerofuku and Buddha are given full, sympathetic reasons.

Choose your own side, freely and with compassion

98014.heading: Reincarnated as a Sword
98014.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: The isekai (reborn in another world) frame, game-style status screens, the tireless office worker reborn with new purpose, the master-disciple bond (Fran calls the sword Shishō, "master/teacher") and the gentle humor of food reflect Japanese light-novel conventions; a sword with a soul also echoes Japanese folklore of objects that gain spirits (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Slavers and racists (August, Gyuran) are drawn as gloating villains with no inner life; the overtaxed pirates are the rare opponents given a fair hearing (likely ch. 44-45).

folkways.japan: A Japanese shojo retelling of English history and Shakespeare; its gothic beauty, flower symbolism (roses) and focus on a beautiful, gender-ambiguous lead draw on shojo traditions (CBR compares it with Fushigi Yugi's use of threat, via Anime Feminist), rather than on Japanese social norms.

delivery.note: Kanno's gothic melodrama asks whether Richard is fated or chooses his path, and lets the reader decide (VIZ blurb, vol. 1 catalog copy on AniList).

85475.heading: Rikudo
85475.label: From summaries
85475.life_message: A child broken by abuse is not doomed to become what was done to him: through discipline, mentors who do not give up on him and the people who love him, he can turn his fists from a killer's weapon into a craft, and choose who he becomes.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Fighters box for pride, reputation and to answer insults (Gerbera, Kamishiro); the yakuza code shapes Tokorozawa's life; Riku himself seeks self-respect more than revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Strict gym discipline sits beside a lawless underworld; neither order nor freedom is the theme.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is chosen, not given; loyalty runs to the gym and friends more than to society, which mostly rejects Riku.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rankings, belts and old-school trainer authority structure the world; the outcast rises through them.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular; old-style training is questioned but often vindicated.

folkways.japan: Yakuza debt collecting, children's homes (jidō yōgo shisetsu), the professional boxing ranks (East Japan Rookie of the Year, A-class licence, OPBF), and the stigma faced by a youth with a killing on his record reflect Japanese institutions; the hard-luck boxer tradition goes back to Ashita no Joe.

delivery.evidence: Rival boxers each get backstories and reasons to fight (Tsuwabuki's debts, Kaede's abusive father, Fukuro's love of the sport, Mizuki's belief that some wins cannot be bought; Japanese Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message is carried by fights and by what each fighter is fighting for; there are few speeches, and the vol. 23 reviewer says the real subject is Riku and the society that rejects him.

Win at any cost to the body

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Crimes are answered by evidence and courts, not revenge; Ron's trance is the honor-style vengeance the story rejects.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The police and the law are the frame; Ron's freedom to investigate depends on hiding inside it.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Justice for strangers drives each case, while the Holmes and Moriarty families pull at Ron through blood.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A banned genius and a low-ranking cop work as equals; BLUE, the alliance and the police are hierarchies.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Deduction in the Sherlock Holmes mold; folk-god cases likely debunked (to verify).

folkways.japan: A Shōnen Jump+ buddy mystery in the Japanese honkaku (fair-play) tradition, with a manzai-style straight-man and funny-man pairing (Real Sound, via Wikipedia); respect for the Japanese police is mixed with comedy about rank and credit, and the Holmes and Moriarty lineages reflect Japan's long love of Sherlock Holmes.

delivery.evidence: Each case ends with the culprit's motive explained and Ron's trance stopped; the moral (keep them alive, let the law judge) is built into the premise rather than stated in speeches (ANN; Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Values are carried by the case formula and the buddy comedy; the Moriarty family is drawn as cold villains, while culprits' motives are often given a hearing (to verify).

personified.ideology: Brilliant reason with a troubled, dangerous mind

124895.dominant: Duty ethics (culprits must live and face the law), Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism (reason and evidence).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duels, swordsmen's pride and family honor (Kaoru defending her school, v1) run the plot; the story still rejects revenge and killing for honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Kenshin supports lawful Meiji order against a coup, while living as a free wanderer.

Civic vs kin.evidence: A chosen family stands in for kin; Kenshin protects strangers wherever he goes.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Master-student and class ranks remain, but the humble wanderer outranks the powerful in worth.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Samurai tradition, temples and hell imagery against a modernizing state with guns and police.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, protection and duty dominate; personal happiness comes only at the end.

folkways.japan: The Bakumatsu and early Meiji era: the 1876 sword ban, ex-samurai turned police or bandits, the Shinsengumi, the anti-Buddhist movement after 1868 and the Meiji state's suppression of the Sekiho Army. Japanese readers met an optimistic, revisionist picture of samurai (Wikipedia); the story draws on the warrior ideal but sets its hero against the killing at its core.

delivery.evidence: Kenshin states his vow and its reasons often, but Saito's and Shishio's creeds are given strong voices and are never simply mocked; Saito is left standing (Beneath the Tangles, 2015; fan wiki).
delivery.note: The anti-killing, anti-revenge message is carried by plot tests and speeches in the duels; Watsuki said redemption came from the shojo manga he grew up on (Wikipedia).

personified.ideology: Atonement through protecting others, never killing
The strong should rule the weak
Swift death to evil (Aku Soku Zan)

30022.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (the no-kill vow), Classical virtue ethics (atonement), Might makes right critiqued (Shishio), Communitarianism (the dojo family).

125828.heading: Sakamoto Days
125828.label: From summaries
125828.life_message: A good life is a peaceful, ordinary family life. Even a killer can start over, and he makes up for the lives he took by protecting and helping others, never by taking more.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (killing condemned; non-lethal force endorsed)

frames.aligns: Conversion of life through married love; amends by service (Aoi's demand that he help others to make up for past killings); sanctity of life; mercy to a defeated enemy; justice left to a court (ch. 282-283); evil not made attractive in the villain (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Allies who still kill are shown as cool; weight mockery against human dignity; language.

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a turned life; the family as a "little church" of peace; mercy over vengeance.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes constant combat and swearing a concern for stricter families.

frames.aligns: A changed life; a faithful husband and father; protecting children; justice left to lawful authority (Romans 13) at the end (ch. 283).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the gore and profanity; no gospel source for the change. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts violence without endorsing killing; redemption and second chances; marriage as a transforming covenant.
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on violent entertainment; crude language; fat jokes.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; family protection; a changed life.
frames.concerns: Psychic mind-reading (Shin) as a normal power; worldliness of the assassin setting. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a non-Christian work; the sixth commandment (WLC Q135-136) on preserving life shown positively; lawful judgment of Uzuki (ch. 283).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139-style caution on coarse speech; change grounded in human love alone.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Sakamoto leaves final judgment of Uzuki to lawful authority (ch. 282-283); vocation as husband, father and shopkeeper.
frames.concerns: Entertainment as adiaphora, but LCMS and WELS families may weigh the language and violence more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; sanctification as a changed way of life; social concern for orphans exploited as assassins.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about crude language and violence than UMC.

frames.aligns: Framing of good and evil is clear; reform, forgiveness and lawful justice.
frames.concerns: Language and violence for younger readers. Episcopal and ACNA families differ little here.

frames.aligns: Refusal to kill is the hero's defining vow; enemy spared and treated (ch. 282); humble shopkeeping life.
frames.concerns: Force is still the hero's main tool and is shown as heroic and fun (Matthew 5:39); assassins as cool. Closer to the tradition than most action manga, but on the dividing line. Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; a father who puts family first; repentance and restitution; children protected.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: language and constant violence may not "invite the Spirit." Members vary.

frames.aligns: Redemption, mercy, critique of an institution that exploits orphans (Uzuki and Gaku).
frames.concerns: Weight-based mockery (Anime Feminist's fatphobia warning; Common Sense Media); a mentally ill villain; mostly male lead cast.

frames.aligns: Life is sacred; family and quiet ordinary life; temperance (Sakamoto discourages smoking, to verify).
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to constant fighting and swearing; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Valuing life; family loyalty; a peaceful life chosen over a violent one.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question whether entertainment features what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5): violence is the series' main content. Mind-reading may be read as spiritism by some. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love transforms a hardened man; harmony at home outlasts danger.
frames.concerns: Fear, violence and trauma dwelt on as real and powerful; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the value of every life; teshuvah (return) of a former killer; shalom bayit (peace in the home).
frames.concerns: Nivul peh (coarse speech) in the anime; constant violence; many Haredi homes restrict such media. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; shalom bayit; sanctity of life; justice through courts.
frames.concerns: Language and weight mockery (ona'at devarim, hurtful speech). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in rebuilding a life; justice for exploited children; courts over revenge.
frames.concerns: Weight jokes and stereotypes; violence for younger readers. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sanctity of life (Qur'an 5:32); tawbah (repentance) and making amends; protecting family; forgiveness preferred when able to punish.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and smoking shown casually; coarse speech; mocking others' bodies (Qur'an 49:11).

frames.aligns: Ahimsa as a vow; grihastha (householder) duty valued over the warrior's path; karma of past killing worked off through service.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore and swearing.

frames.aligns: The first precept (no killing) is the hero's rule; compassion to a defeated enemy; right livelihood: he leaves killing for a store.
frames.concerns: Fighting remains the plot's engine and is played for fun; what it feeds the mind (right mindfulness).

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier ideal: strength used only to protect; kirat karni (honest work) at the store; vices (anger, ego) shown in villains.
frames.concerns: Language and casual drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Service, family unity, transformation of character.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence: fighting, even non-lethal, is the heroes' path. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude and a harmonious household; purification of a "stained" life.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood as impurity in fights. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.concerns: Little to raise. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "do not murder," care for family, help others.
frames.concerns: The villain's dissociative identity disorder is a psychiatric category; the series treats it as a story device, not medicine. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption; critique of an exploitative institution; courts over revenge; capable women fighters.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist warns of fatphobia, and The Manga Critic finds the body jokes overused; a villain defined by dissociative identity disorder; Aoi has little personality (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Human life valued without religious grounding; people can change; reason and courts over vengeance; powers are clearly fiction.
frames.concerns: Glamorized assassin culture for younger readers.

frames.aligns: A man gives up a dangerous career for marriage, fatherhood and a small business; protective fatherhood; loyalty; the wife's moral authority in the home respected.
frames.concerns: Language; violence for younger readers; distrust of institutions in a book without faith.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of the villain: Uzuki is spared and treated (ch. 282); justice and compassion for exploited orphans.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; weight jokes; portrayal of mental illness. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Self-reliance; distrust of a corrupt authority (the JAA); fierce protection of children; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: The hero binds himself to his wife's rule and a family-first ethic more than self-assertion; the story's ideal is quiet domestic life. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A changed life and a second chance; a father who protects his family; mercy to an enemy and justice left to the courts rather than revenge (Romans 12:19; ch. 282-283); condemnation of a system that turns orphans into killers.
frames.concerns: Frequent profanity and constant violence; psychic powers shown as normal; no faith behind the change. Holiness and COGIC families more cautious. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Goodness comes from love and conscience, not command; no faith is needed for the hero's change; the powers are plainly fiction; reason and law settle the villain's fate.
frames.concerns: Glamorized assassin culture; weight jokes.

frames.aligns: No certainty is pushed either way; the villain's inner life is treated with some sympathy; justice is left open to a trial (ch. 283).
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond violence and body jokes.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to family and friends, everyday decency, second chances and fair payback for villains; a happy ending with a new baby (ch. 283).
frames.concerns: Constant violence and swearing for younger readers; the weight jokes.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Old enemies seek revenge on Sakamoto, but he does not answer insult or attack with killing, and he leaves Uzuki's fate to a court (ch. 282-283). Weight insults are shrugged off.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The household runs by Aoi's rules, obeyed strictly, while the JAA's official order is corrupt and replaced (ch. 283).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and the store's found family come first; arcs are triggered by threats to Hana, Aoi or the staff.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Sakamoto is "boss," and the Order and JAA have rank, but rank-based authority is critiqued and the store staff are friends more than subordinates.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; a secular, practical outlook, with traditional marriage and family life.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security and a peaceful daily life are the highest goods; comedy and personal quirks are tolerated.

folkways.japan: The neighborhood konbini, a wife who manages the household and its rules, school-cohort loyalty (the JCC classmates) and bystanders who keep calm are Japanese everyday norms used as comic setting; the story's own message is the no-kill vow and family over glory.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists the message that it is never too late to change; no review opened calls it preachy; reviewers focus on comedy and action. In ch. 282 Boiled and Seba argue against sparing Uzuki and the story lets them speak.
delivery.note: The no-kill message is carried by a household rule and by action choices more than by speeches; the final fight states it most openly, as Sakamoto rejects his old "prime" self (ch. 281).

personified.ideology: Strength restrained for family; no killing
Sanctity of life; atonement by service
Violent revenge on an abusive system

125828.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (family-first), Pacifism / nonviolence (no-kill form), Secular humanism, Traditionalism.

31461.heading: Sanctuary
31461.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: The plot draws on early-1990s Japanese politics: LDP dominance, seniority, the yakuza's ties to business and politics, debates over Article 9, U.S. trade pressure and the Japan That Can Say No mood (Wikipedia; Thompson). Viz used real party names where the original renamed them.

delivery.evidence: Thompson: the heroes win over enemies with speeches and face consequences only when no one cares about the victim; villains are mostly foreigners or ugly old men. The leads state their goals openly and often.

folkways.japan: The house is drawn from Victorian Europe (ANN), but daily cleaning of soot, group duty rosters, the Debut as a coming-of-age ceremony and the stress on fitting one's role echo Japanese school and company life; the story turns them into a critique of conformity.

folkways.japan: Izumo shamanism, onmyodo (Hao as a Heian-era onmyoji modeled on Abe no Seimei's legend; fan wiki), Aomori's itako mediums and Mount Osore, a samurai ghost, Ainu spirits and an arranged engagement reflect Japanese religious and family custom; Japan's habit of mixing Shinto, Buddhist and folk practice shapes the story's pluralism.

delivery.evidence: Takei states the message outright (Wikipedia); the X-Laws and the Tao father are drawn with real backstories, and Hao is given grief and loneliness rather than pure malice.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The school and partners replace failed families (Medusa and Crona, Spirit and Maka); loyalty extends to a whole academy and finally to former enemies (ch. 113).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Eccentric self-expression is celebrated (Kid's symmetry, Black Star, Excalibur) within a fight for survival against madness.

folkways.japan: The setting is deliberately Western (a Nevada desert city, Gothic and Halloween styling), so fewer values come from Japanese norms than in most shonen. The shinigami (death god) figure, the school as family and deference to teachers reflect Japanese popular culture; they are context, not the story's message.

delivery.evidence: Asura's view that Death's order is arbitrary gets a hearing, and Kid fears his own order could be madness (vol. 25 summary, fan wiki); villains like Medusa are drawn without much depth. No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about courage over fear is stated in key moments (ch. 112-113) but mostly carried by fights and gags.

frames.aligns: Wonder at the big questions (why are we alive? what carries over?) without a doctrine; the ending leaves rebirth open.
frames.concerns: Little to raise.

frames.aligns: Souls, fate and karma-like justice, loyalty, forgiveness and a hopeful ending that the universe can be fair.
frames.concerns: Violence in past lives.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Kouko's revenge is an honor-culture feud across lives; the story moves it toward dignity and forgiveness (v6).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rigid customs (sacrifice, witch hunts) cause harm, but the hero's answer is responsibility, not rebellion.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Adoptive and chosen family carry each life (Vann's daughter, East and Kouko, Carol).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchies of elders, Church and pharaoh do harm; the leads meet as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Superstition condemned, but a spiritual world of souls and rebirth is real.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Fuuta chooses empathy and meaning over safety; Kouko's survival-driven hatred softens.

folkways.japan: Gratitude, endurance (gaman), apologies and the weight of the past reflect Japanese norms; the Houtarou life is set in feudal Japan with temples and a samurai-era feud. The reincarnation and karmic-grudge frame draws on East Asian folk Buddhism, though the series builds its own spirit mechanics.

delivery.evidence: Kouko's grievance is treated as real (her past selves were truly wronged), and the message comes through each life's outcome and Rune's stated hope that something good will happen (Wrong Every Time).
delivery.note: The theme is stated at key moments but carried mostly by the structure: each past life is a case study in how cruelty starts and how it might end.

personified.ideology: Understanding and forgiveness end the cycle
Justice as revenge for past wrongs
Mastery over life, death and the universe
Simple hope: something good will happen

68071.dominant: Buddhist ideas (rebirth and letting go), Pacifism / nonviolence (breaking the cycle of revenge), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics.

108556.heading: SPY x FAMILY
108556.label: From summaries
108556.life_message: A good life is building a family, even an imperfect or "fake" one, and protecting the peace that lets children grow up without war.

content.frequency: Occasional; heavy in a few arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences (Yor's work) / Neutral (spy action, comic)

frames.aligns: Love that grows through sacrifice; the family as a "little church"; grief for war's victims.
frames.concerns: Killing as a profession with little repentance shown (the tradition treats even killing in war as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); lying sits at the heart of the premise. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes comic violence a point to talk through.

frames.aligns: Adoption and orphan care (James 1:27); a father who protects; war framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Lying in the home (Proverbs 12:22) is not yet judged; the mother's violence is played for laughs; drunkenness as comedy, a concern for the many Baptists who abstain. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In (vol. 13) calls the series fun and says it prompts thought about friendship and family; recommends 10 and up. Adoption mirrors spiritual adoption (Romans 8:15).

frames.aligns: Family as refuge; protection of children; love softening a hard heart.
frames.concerns: Anya's telepathy and Bond's foresight may raise spiritual-discernment questions, though the series frames them as a lab experiment (Project Apple; fan wiki), not spirits; drinking and drunkenness (many abstain); lying.

frames.concerns: Heroes' lies and killings rarely judged by the story; drunkenness.

frames.concerns: Lying as a way of life; assassins working "for the nation."

frames.concerns: Drunkenness as comedy (historic abstinence; holiness churches ask members to abstain); killing for pay treated as a job.

frames.aligns: Found family; care for war victims; critique of war propaganda (Henry Henderson; v15, to verify).
frames.concerns: Deception at the heart of the marriage.

frames.aligns: Peace and justice emphasis; critique of militarism and propaganda; egalitarian domestic roles; found family.

frames.concerns: Little at the level of message.
