30642.heading: Vinland Saga
30642.label: From summaries
30642.life_message: A true warrior needs no sword: a good life means turning from violence and revenge, facing one's guilt, and building, by hard and patient work, a place where no one is enslaved and no one is an enemy.

content.frequency: Constant in vols. 1-8; occasional later, rising again in vols. 27-29

content.framing: Condemned (sexual violence and sexual slavery); neutral to warm (marriage)

frames.aligns: Revenge rejected; repentance and atonement central; evil shown so it is understood, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); dignity of slaves and enemies; Willibald's self-giving love (ch. 37).
frames.concerns: Canute's vow to build paradise without God (ch. 39); Willibald is a drunken friar; graphic war violence (CCC 2525 on permissiveness).

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a lifelong turning; the dream of his victims (ch. 70) as the soul's awakening; love of enemies.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses: the early arcs are long and bloody; Canute's defiance of God is never repented on the page (to verify).

frames.aligns: A clear arc from sin to repentance; the father's sacrificial love (ch. 16); evil shown with consequences.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: much of vols. 1-8 is violent and grim; implied sexual violence; Thorfinn's change comes by his own effort, with no word of grace.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads the slave arc as freedom from sin through facing guilt, and Canute as a man who rejects love; CLARITAS links the no-enemies line to Matthew 5:44.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence in the first arc; Christianity shown through a drunken friar and a king who defies God.

frames.aligns: No occult practice shown as power; repentance and a changed life; the cost of following peace.
frames.concerns: Norse religion, Valhalla and a Mi'kmaq shaman's visions appear as belief; a berserker's drug-like mushroom; graphic violence.

frames.aligns: Total depravity shown honestly; common grace in a non-Christian author's moral seriousness.
frames.concerns: Redemption appears earned by works; Canute's rejection of God's rule; WLC Q139 concern about violent images and implied sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel themes: guilt crushes Thorfinn before he can live again; vocation as farmer, husband and father.
frames.concerns: Little sign of grace from outside; the violence is a conscience matter; confessional families stricter.

frames.aligns: Sanctification as a long road of changed life; concern for slaves and the poor; social holiness in the Vinland plan.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may weigh the violence against Wesley's General Rules; the UMC is more open.

frames.aligns: A literary epic that frames good and evil clearly, in the line of Lewis and Sayers; set when Cnut ruled England.
frames.concerns: Violence and grim tone in the first arc.

frames.aligns: Nonresistance is the core message: Thorfinn declares he has no enemies (ch. 96), the hero takes blows without striking back, and the settlement bans weapons. Many Mennonite readers could see Matthew 5:39 in story form.
frames.concerns: Violence shown in detail for eight volumes before the turn; Old Order families avoid the medium itself; nonresistance rests on a father's ethic, not on Christ. Some readers would grade S on message.

frames.aligns: Repentance, restitution and family; a promised land settled in peace (a theme many members know from the Book of Mormon).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that invites the Spirit; the graphic first arc and implied sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Anti-war, anti-slavery, enemy-love; attention to the enslaved and the vulnerable; Mi'kmaq portrayed with Mi'kmaw advisers (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Women's stories are thin in early arcs; the Vinland arc raises questions about settler colonialism.

frames.aligns: Peace, repentance, temperance set against drunken warriors; Adventist noncombatancy.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": long war scenes and dark tone (Fundamental Belief 22).

frames.aligns: Refusal to take part in war; condemnation of royal power struggles; violence shown as what God hates (Psalm 11:5), without glory in the end.
frames.concerns: Violent entertainment is discouraged; Norse gods and Christendom's clergy shown; graphic battles.

frames.aligns: Spiritual change transforms outward life; hatred dissolves when Thorfinn sees no enemies.
frames.concerns: Long dwelling on fear, killing and suffering; "stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Revenge is forbidden (Leviticus 19:18) and the story agrees; teshuvah-like repentance; justice for the enslaved (Exodus 21).
frames.concerns: Christian theology framing much of the moral world; immodest scenes and implied sexual violence (tzniut); time spent on secular media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah, the dignity of the enslaved, rejection of vengeance; the injured party (Hild) must forgive.
frames.concerns: Violence and implied sexual violence; Christian frame.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the dream of a land without war or slavery; ethics over ritual.
frames.concerns: Colonial setting in the last arc; violence level.

frames.aligns: Mercy over revenge; freeing slaves praised (Qur'an 90:13); repentance (tawbah).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and drunkenness; nudity in bathing scenes; Christian theological framing; strict nonviolence differs from Islam's permitted just defense.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences: violence returns; renunciation of violence (ahimsa); duty to family.
frames.concerns: The Gita teaches that a warrior's duty can require fighting, and Thorfinn rejects this; tamasic violence in the first arc.

frames.aligns: Non-harm as the story's goal; the cycle of hatred and revenge produces suffering; insight through suffering; Anime Feminist reads Thorfinn as a bodhisattva.
frames.concerns: Long violent sections; the hero's peace is relational and ethical rather than meditative.

frames.aligns: Rejects vengeance; anger and ego shown as destructive; equality of all people.
frames.concerns: Sikh teaching honors defending the oppressed by arms when needed (Guru Gobind Singh); Thorfinn's absolute nonviolence differs.

frames.aligns: Non-violence, the oneness of humanity and a peaceful mixed community in Vinland; end of slavery.
frames.concerns: Violence and immodest scenes against a "chaste and holy life"; alcohol.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; purification from past wrong; harmony with community and land.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere in the first arc; no kami or Japanese setting.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" fits the turn from violence; respect for land and the Mi'kmaq, whose folktale of coexisting with nature shaped the last arc (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Norse religion appears mainly as a warrior-death cult; contemporary Heathens may object to the stereotype.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: "Do not murder," "Honor and help your parents"; recovery from trauma through action.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence in the first arc; drunkenness.

frames.aligns: Anti-war, anti-slavery, critique of warrior masculinity; Anime Feminist treats its nonviolence as a full political ethic (2026).
frames.concerns: Few major female characters in early arcs (Wikipedia); settler colonialism in the final arc; implied sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Moral change through empathy and responsibility; a human-made good society; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: Graphic cruelty in the first arc.

frames.aligns: Fatherhood, marriage and family, hard work on the land, keeping one's word.
frames.concerns: The story critiques warrior honor and royal authority; strict nonviolence may read as naive; Sigurd's break with his father is honored.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, including slaves and enemies; justice, peace and a free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence for younger readers; colonial themes.

frames.aligns: Questioning arbitrary authority (Canute's challenge to God); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2); critique of religion used for power.
frames.concerns: The Church of Satan accepts proportionate retaliation, and Thorfinn's turn-the-other-cheek ethic runs against it; harm to children (child soldiers).

frames.aligns: Slavery is indicted from the side of the enslaved (ch. 87-93), Vinland is a promised land without slavery, and a former killer turns to repentance and nonviolent love of enemies (ch. 96), close to Exodus, Matthew 5:44 and the nonviolence of the Civil Rights movement.
frames.concerns: The first eight volumes are violent war stories with implied sexual violence, and Thorfinn's peace is won by his own effort with no word of grace.

frames.aligns: Moral change comes through empathy and responsibility, no god intervenes, and Norse belief in glorious death is answered rather than honored.
frames.concerns: Graded on harm: graphic cruelty in the first arc; Christian themes are treated with respect, which some families may not expect.

frames.aligns: Religious and secular readers can both read Thorfinn's change in their own way; Willibald's questions about love and Canute's quarrel with God are left as real questions (ch. 37-39).
frames.concerns: The violent prologue (vols. 1-8) is a hurdle for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Family, hard work, second chances and choosing to have no enemies are the heart of the story, and the hero comes home to his family at the end (ch. 220).
frames.concerns: The first arc's battles and implied sexual violence call for an age check.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Blood revenge is the early Thorfinn the story rejects; his declaration that he has no enemies (ch. 96) is the thesis. Hild's forgiveness (vol. 26) is honored.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Kingship is power that must stay violent to stay in place (Canute, vols. 11-14), and slavery is condemned; the settlement is a patient, ordered community, not a free-for-all.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the moral anchor (Thors, Helga and Ylva, Gudrid, Karli and the newborn), but the goal is a place where no one is enslaved and no one is an enemy, extended to strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Slavery is indicted (Arnheid and Gardar, ch. 79-93); Ketil's wealth built on slaves is critiqued; Thorfinn wins Cordelia's freedom (vol. 24).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christianity is treated with respect and questions (ch. 37-39), and Thorfinn's arc reads as repentance and atonement; Norse Valhalla belief is answered, not honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard, patient work and farming are the path to peace (vols. 8-14, 24-29); peace and care for others, not personal expression, are the goals.

folkways.japan: Set in Viking-age Europe and North America, so few norms are directly Japanese; Yukimura contrasts free, expressive Vikings with samurai bound by obedience and honor (Wikipedia). Repentance through patient labor, Japanese postwar pacifism and the double meaning of ch. 96's title (無敵) carry a Japanese reading of nonviolence.

delivery.evidence: Yukimura states his aim openly (violence does not lead to good outcomes; hope is the main message), and Thors' and Thorfinn's lines state the theme; but Askeladd, Canute and Thorkell argue their views well, and the Vinland arc shows nonviolence failing to hold the settlement.
delivery.note: The message is stated directly at key moments (ch. 16, 96) and then tested at length rather than lectured.

personified.ideology: Cunning survival in a rotten world
Weapons as security; pacifism as cowardice

30642.dominant: Pacifism / nonviolence (affirmed), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

folkways.japan: Japanese high school life: ethics (rinri) is a real social studies subject in Japanese high schools (from general knowledge; to verify); uniform rules, class group chats, club coaches' corporal punishment, young carers, compensated dating (enjo kōsai) and a teachers' smoking room reflect Japanese school norms, which the series often questions.

delivery.evidence: Every chapter turns on a philosopher's idea stated by Takayanagi, and year-end classes debate a set theme (Japanese Wikipedia). Reviewers split: most say he invites reflection rather than preaching; some find chapters heavy-handed or name-dropping (MyAnimeList).

folkways.japan: Draws on the ninkyō ideal of the chivalrous yakuza (the "ninkyō eiga" film tradition, from general knowledge; to verify): giri-ninjō, sworn brothers, a protected turf in Kabukicho, irezumi tattoos. The fantasy world is a standard Japanese role-playing-game setting (TV Tropes).

folkways.japan: A Shinto shrine family, kagura dance, kumihimo braiding, kuchikamizake, the autumn festival, Suga Shrine in Shinjuku, rural depopulation and the shadow of the 2011 earthquake and tsunami are distinctly Japanese; the red thread of fate is East Asian folklore (ANN interview).

delivery.evidence: The meaning of musubi is stated once by Hitoha (Wikipedia); otherwise the theme of connection is carried by images (threads, the braid, the comet) and action. The mayor's resistance is shown as human, not cartoonish.
delivery.note: The story shows rather than argues; its spirituality is presented as quietly true.

97337.dominant: Pantheist/New Age (musubi, the binding of people and time), Communitarianism (saving the town), Traditionalism (the shrine's ways prove true).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Challenges must be fought and Brago's honorable duel is respected (ch. 321), but the kind king ideal rejects feuds and revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The tournament has fixed rules set by the mamodo world; partners choose freely how to fight.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to partner and allies; Zatch's royal family and his twin are central (ch. 259-275).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A contest for a throne, yet the kind king ideal raises the weakest; Zatch goes back to ordinary school as king (fan wiki, ch. 322-323).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Monarchy and magic beside a modern Japanese school and a scientist father.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival battles, but character, trust and friendship matter most.

folkways.japan: Kiyo's isolation as a gifted student who stands out reflects Japanese school pressure against standing out; the story prizes group harmony, loyal friendship and a gentle ruler, and the shōnen tournament format of rivals who become allies.

delivery.evidence: Thompson (ANN) says the early chapters hammer the self-esteem and friendship messages through shouting and repetition, easing later; the villains are rotten enough to cheer against, but Zeno and Koko are redeemed.
delivery.note: The kind-king message is spoken aloud in battle and repeated, especially early, but carried by big emotional scenes rather than lectures.

2-5-dimensional-seduction.weigh: a romance and harem comedy among high school students built on sexualized cosplay, with undressing and nudity of first-year students (ch. 1 and likely ch. 2-3, v1; ch. 48.5) presented as comedy; a hero who refuses to take advantage of a girl who offers herself (late volumes) and ends in a committed couple (ch. 200); healing of abandonment and bullying through friendship; a warm subplot of two adult women who become a couple (Mayuri and Eli); fandom and consumer culture as identity; almost no violence, drinking or profanity. Sexualized content involving minors exists in this manga (high school characters; see ch. 1, likely ch. 2-3, ch. 48.5); it is reported here only by chapter and volume.

No scene sexualizing a minor was found in sources opened; all main characters are adults.

The series is unfinished. The writer's 2020 conviction for indecent acts against two middle-school girls ended it; this is real-world context, not part of the story's message, and is not graded.

The heroine is a high school student; **no sexual content involving her was found**, but a first-world arc in which she seeks to make an adult man love and depend on her is listed in the checklist (ch. 78-85).

No sexual activity involving anyone was found in sources opened.

No scene sexualizing a minor was reported by any source opened (see checklist on ch. 7 and 16).

bakemonogatari.weigh: a story whose stated rule is that people must save themselves by facing what they tried to discard; a cult that ruins a family and an attempted sexual assault, both condemned (ch. 1-4); constant fan service of high school girls, including a scene where a high school girl undresses in front of the hero (ch. 5, v1), praised by no reviewer and criticized by most; folk gods and spirits treated as real and handled with rituals (ch. 3-4, c. v6-8); a hero who becomes a vampire's thrall and drinks or gives blood (v8-15); violent supernatural battles; a teen hitting a child ghost as a joke (ch. 11). Sexualized content involving minors exists in this manga (high school characters; see ch. 5 and the Kizumonogatari and Tsubasa Cat arcs, v8-21); it is reported here only by chapter and volume.

basara.weigh: a girl who leads a revolt against a slave-holding, child-killing monarchy and learns to mourn enemy dead (vols. 1-3); war violence throughout, including beheading, crucifixion and burial alive; a tyrant (Shuri) who changes and is forgiven; an unmarried teenage couple who consummate their love before the final battle and later raise children without marrying (late volumes; MJ; TV Tropes); sexual violence in backstory (a father's rape of his daughter) and in a prison (Ageha, vols. 11-12), condemned; suicide of a loyal general; real gods and prophecy as setting; a revolution that sets up no ruler. A sexual relationship involving Sarasa while she is about 16 or 17 is reported (TV Tropes); no source opened says it is shown explicitly (see checklist).

biomega.weigh: a synthetic agent's mission to protect a 17-year-old girl whose blood can cure a plague (vols. 1-3); a cult-like foundation that wants to infect everyone in a forced "baptism" and remake humanity, shown as evil (vols. 2-6); constant gun, blade and monster violence with gore and body horror; the destruction and remaking of the Earth (vol. 4); an AI's self-sacrifice (vol. 6); and an ending in which the hero accepts a new world rather than restoring the old one (vol. 6). No sexual content involving a minor was reported in sources opened; the only sexual note is one reader's mention of a woman undressing (see checklist).

black-jack.weigh: a doctor who fights for every life and treats the poor for free while humbling the arrogant (English Wikipedia); a long argument against euthanasia through Black Jack's rivalry with Dr. Kiriko, who is given his reasons (v3, v5); the limits of medicine and the deaths of good people; greed, war, nuclear testing and prejudice condemned; graphic surgery in nearly every story; horror and supernatural cases; a suicide attempt (v17); a drug addict (v4); a lover who lives as a man after surgery (v1); a child-sized ward who calls herself his wife as a joke, with nothing sexual reported; a 1977 protest over a story's portrayal of psychosurgery and dialogue changed for discriminatory terms (Japanese Wikipedia). No sexual content involving a minor was found in sources opened.

black-lagoon.weigh: a crime story that neither punishes nor praises its smugglers and lets several worldviews argue; constant stylized gun violence that the art clearly enjoys; heavy profanity, drinking and smoking; a religious order that is a criminal front and abused characters who say God abandoned them; Nazis, terrorists and child traffickers shown as evil; Rock's empathy and his growing skill at manipulation; the twins arc, in which two abused children are killers and a child exposes herself in ch. 15 (sexual content involving a minor, reported here only by chapter); a teenage heir's suicide in an honor-bound yakuza tragedy (likely ch. 36-37); Roberta's revenge broken by love and mercy (ch. 76).

bleach.weigh: an afterlife run by "death gods," with souls, Hollows and Hell shown as real; a hero who defies an unjust death sentence (v9-21) and protects family and friends; a proud schemer who seeks heaven's throne (ch. 178) and a tyrant named after God (YHWH, ch. 565) both defeated; a "Soul King" who is a limbless sealed being, killed and absorbed (ch. 614-625); constant bloody sword violence; light fan service (adult nudity gags, ch. 115-116; a classmate's groping gag with 15-year-olds; Nemu, ch. 306); a villain disclosed as a man in disguise and mocked for it (ch. 588); Nazi-styled villains and a "selection" that kills the weak (ch. 603); marriage and children in the epilogue (ch. 686). No sexual content involving minors beyond the groping gag was reported in sources opened.

btooom.weigh: a death game in which killing for gain is condemned and trust is rewarded; a shut-in who repents of how he treated his family and learns to protect others; constant, gory bomb violence; sexual violence against minors that the story condemns: an attempted rape of a 15-year-old girl who kills her attacker (vol. 1-2), a flashback of her teenage friends being drugged and raped (vol. 3), and a 14-year-old boy's sexual abuse by his father (chapter not confirmed); underwear fan service of the same girl; a near-sexual scene between a 22-year-old and a 15-year-old that he stops; two suicides (Ryōta's mother, Taira); a daughter who kills her villainous father to end his plan (v26). Sexual content involving minors exists in this series (vol. 1-3 and later chapters not yet located); it is reported here only by volume. Yen Press rates it 18+.

cardcaptor-sakura.weigh: a kind, brave ten-year-old heroine and a loving widowed father (throughout); magic, sorcery and spirit-cards used for good, and cards some readers liken to tarot; love in many forms shown without judgment, including a same-sex couple (v9-10) and a girl who loves her best friend; romances between adults and children presented approvingly: a teacher engaged to his ten-year-old pupil (ch. 9), a student teacher who dated a junior high student (v4), a teacher who married his sixteen-year-old student (backstory); a gentle story with almost no violence. No sexual content involving minors was reported in sources opened; the adult-child romances are romantic, not sexual, in every source (see checklist).

No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened; the bathing scene noted by TV Tropes is on the checklist.

claymore.weigh: an exploitative institution that turns orphaned girls into weapons, exposed and destroyed (v15-23); constant graphic violence and body horror; loyalty and self-sacrifice among comrades; revenge as Clare's starting motive, tempered by mercy; the black card, a practice of being killed by a comrade before losing one's humanity; uncensored adult nudity, a childlike awakened being (Priscilla) often nude, and a pre-teen warrior breastfed by a comrade (v13); threats of rape against Teresa and of sexual slavery against the child Clare, stated and stopped (v3-4); a fictional church that first excludes, then shelters, the warriors (v2, v14); Teresa's spirit rising within Clare at the end (sc. 150-155). Sexual content involving minors: no sexual act involving a child is shown; a bandit states his intent to sell the child Clare into sexual slavery and is killed (v4); Miata (drawn as a pre-teen) is breastfed by Clarice (v13); the regressed, childlike Priscilla is often nude (from v10). See the checklist.

This is sexual content involving minors as described here; see the checklist (ch. 1, 18-27 and the hot spring scene) for the adult-flag decision.

detective-conan.weigh: a hero who finds the truth by reason and hands every culprit to the law; a firm stance that murder, even for revenge, is never justified and that a culprit's suicide must be prevented (ch. 62-67); a murder in nearly every case, usually not gory but sometimes grim; ghosts and curses always explained away; Conan's lies to Ran and his drugging of Kogoro as running devices; a charming gentleman thief (Kaito Kid); Kogoro's comic drinking, smoking, gambling and leering; a chaste slow-burn romance (ch. 1000-1005); a hot-spring bath gag in which Ran bathes with Conan without knowing who he is. No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened.

devilman.weigh: a hero who saves the world by merging with a demon; Satan as a sympathetic fallen angel who loves Akira, and God described by the author as the true villain (Wikipedia), with angels descending on a dead world (ch. 53); a powerful condemnation of mob hatred, scapegoating and war (v5); the love of Akira for Miki and her family; extreme gore, including the murder of children and the display of Miki's family's remains (v5); frequent nudity and a naked, drug-fueled "Black Sabbath" party (early chapters); an ending with no survivors and no redemption. Content involving minors: a gang tries to undress Miki, a high-school student (ch. 1), and she is attacked while bathing (v1); both are reported here only as facts to check. In the Seven Seas vol. 1 time-travel chapters (from Shin Devilman), a Jewish banker is revealed as a demon in a story about the young Hitler (fan wiki; Gaffney called the chapter a low point).

drifters.weigh: warriors who free enslaved and persecuted peoples (elves, dwarves) and fight a genocide; a code of honor kept under pressure (Yoichi, Toyohisa sparing Jeanne); constant, gory war violence shown as heroic, including beheadings, executions and urging victims to kill their oppressor; sexual slavery of elf women condemned and punished (likely ch. 15-18); sexual harassment of Olminu played for comedy; a villain heavily implied to be Jesus Christ, and Joan of Arc and Rasputin as servants of a genocidal crusade; Hitler as the founder of a racist empire, condemned; magic and onmyōdō as tools on both sides. No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened; the ages of the captive elf women are not stated (see checklist).

fool-night.weigh: a system that turns poor volunteers, including children, into oxygen plants and lumber, shown as unjust (Ivy and Paupertown arcs, ch. 11-69); a hero who sold his own life out of despair and then finds purpose in helping others; a child-killing serial murderer shown with both condemnation and pity (Ivy); a violent, mentally ill mother cared for rather than abandoned (v1-2); a Buddhist temple arc and a Pure Land vision presented as real within the story (ch. 63-88); self-mutilation by a monk (likely ch. 82-88); body horror; political violence on all sides. No sexual content was found in sources opened.

gin-tama.weigh: a lazy hero who risks his life for anyone close to him; found family and loyalty across species (Kagura) and old enemies (Shinsengumi); a teacher's execution forced on his student, and the guilt that follows (v56-58); revenge and nihilism (Takasugi, Utsuro) defeated and partly redeemed; crude sexual and toilet humor, penis jokes and a masochist gag character played for laughs; a red-light district arc that condemns the district's owner and frees its women (v25-26); comic drinking, smoking and gambling; mockery of police and government, and terrorism by former samurai shown sympathetically at times; religion as comic background. No scene sexualizing a minor was found in sources opened.

Sexual content involving minors exists (nudity of high school girls; the ch. 1 undressing; Sayaka's stated past relationship with a teacher) and is reported only by chapter here.

goodnight-punpun.weigh: abuse, neglect, coercion and killing shown as harm with lasting consequences, never glamorized; survival chosen over death at the end (ch. 143-147); a mother's deathbed apology (ch. 67); Asano's statement that no single set of values is right; no grace or transcendent hope beyond ordinary survival; an abortion weighed without moral comment, though Sachi keeps her child (ch. 105, 121); the protagonist's sexual coercion, only partly answered (ch. 64, 104); an abuser never held to account (ch. 50, 144); a comic "God" whom Punpun finally renounces (ch. 141); cults shown as deadly (ch. 134-136). On the page: Mental health 9 and Sexuality 8, including the sexual abuse of a 15-year-old boy (ch. 50) and a 16-year-old's sexual advances to an adult (ch. 35); suicide by hanging (ch. 139); VIZ rates it Mature, so nearly every tradition treats it as adult reading whatever the grade. The series has no occult or demonic content.

hima-ten.weigh: a hard-working boy who supports his family and is valued for his care (throughout); a famous girl learning to show her real self (ch. 15, 57-58); honest confession and choosing one person (ch. 92-95); Himari and Kanna losing gracefully and staying friends (ch. 93, 96); recurring fan service of high-school characters, centered on a first-year gravure model, including swimsuits, a bath scene and a blouse removed to a swimsuit (ch. 33-34, 56-57, 59-60); and an epilogue in which the couple lives together after college, unmarried (ch. 96). No sexual activity is reported; the fan service involves teen characters and is described as partial nudity at most (MangaUpdates).

hinamatsuri.weigh: an unrelated man taking responsibility for a girl and becoming her father (ch. 1-16); a stranded girl learning honest work and gratitude among homeless men, then adopted (ch. 6-7, anime ep. 6); a yakuza lifestyle (debt collection, gang rivalry) treated as a comic workplace and never condemned; a 13-year-old bartending and later working adult jobs as a running joke (ch. 4, 11); adult drinking, a hostess-club night and gambling as comedy with hangovers and losses; shoplifting corrected (ch. 7); two minors arriving unclothed from their pods in non-sexual scenes (ch. 1, 6). No sexual scene involving a minor was found in sources opened (see checklist on ch. 1, ch. 6 and the post-skip coffee-shop job).

No religion in the story.

All main characters are high school students; the fan service involves teens but nothing explicit was reported in sources opened.

land-of-the-lustrous.weigh: a richly Buddhist cosmology (a monk-like master, souls seeking release, 108 chapters) in which salvation is release into nothingness; a fragile hero who, seeking love and purpose, betrays friends and massacres nearly all of them (ch. 86-92), shown as tragedy rather than triumph; constant bloodless shattering and some decapitations; despair, a suicide attempt and repeated wishes to cease existing; genderless characters; mild fan service (a nude backside scene; short uniforms); and a quiet ending with new life and remorse. No sexual content involving minors was reported by any source opened.

love-of-kill.weigh: two professional killers as heroes, with killing for money shown as normal work (vols. 1-13); a romance that begins with stalking, information-brokering and pressure, which the story presents as love and critics call coercion (vol. 1; Anime Feminist); physical control framed as care (choking Chateau unconscious to stop her suicide attempt, vol. 4; a threat to break her wrist, vol. 6); child trafficking and orphans raised as killers condemned (vols. 5-7); a child's accidental killing of her rescuer and her long guilt (vol. 7); the honored adoptive family and a rejected aristocratic bloodline (vols. 7-10); and a quiet shared life at the end (vol. 14). No sexual content involving a minor was found; the leads are adults, and the children in flashbacks face violence, not sexual content.

No sexual content involving minors was reported in sources opened; ages in the Serendine scene are not confirmed.

make-the-exorcist-fall-in-love.weigh: a story that condemns child abuse, sexual assault and coerced faith; a named Catholic Church shown as an abusive, controlling institution that tortures a child to death (ch. 75-76) and covers things up, while Scripture and miracles are real and many believers are good; a hero who leaves the Church and chooses his own path (ch. 97-99); a teen's romance with a succubus sent by Satan, ending in a consensual night together when he is 17 (ch. 100); sexual content involving minors, stated plainly: an attempted sexual assault on a 12-year-old (ch. 1), a demon undressing a 16-year-old against his will (ch. 51) and his masturbation and shame (ch. 55); sympathetic demons and gay and lesbian characters; heavy gore, self-harm and suicide themes. A MyAnimeList reviewer warns the series shows rape, child sexual abuse and child abuse graphically; how much is shown on the page has not been checked (see checklist).

me-and-the-devil-blues-the-unreal-life-o.weigh: a Faustian bargain that grants real power and destroys what RJ loves (Virginia and their child die, ch. 4); hoodoo and the crossroads devil taken literally; a young man who neglects his work and pregnant partner for music; white supremacist violence and an attempted lynching shown as evil (likely ch. 10-14, 15 onward); an outlaw road trip with Clyde Barrow played for thrills; strong language, sex and graphic violence noted by About.com; and a critics' split on the drawing of Black characters, which ANN's Brienza saw as caricature close to minstrel imagery and Comic Book Bin and Goboiano saw as frank and researched. No content involving minors was reported, apart from a villain described as a child-murderer.

message-to-adolf.weigh: a strong condemnation of racial hatred, the Holocaust and wartime militarism in both Germany and Japan; a sympathetic child indoctrinated into Nazism and forced to kill (Part 1); torture by the Gestapo and the Kenpeitai; the hero's rape of the woman who betrayed his brother, followed by her suicide and never repented (Part 1); a villain's rape of a young woman, condemned (Part 2); a father killing his son for treason and then himself (Part 2); a cycle of revenge carried into the Arab-Israeli conflict, with the Jewish friend becoming a killer too (final chapters); the plot device that Hitler had Jewish ancestry, a theory TV Tropes calls largely discredited; one Jewish character drawn as a greedy stereotype (TV Tropes); and an ending of witness rather than forgiveness. No sexual content involving a minor was reported by any source opened (Eliza's age at the 1945 rape is on the checklist).

mushishi.weigh: a gentle, episodic story of a wandering healer who treats every living thing with respect and seeks understanding rather than blame; a spirit-like natural world (mushi, a life force beneath the land, a mountain's guardian, rebirth in ch. 21) presented as nature rather than gods; tragedies accepted rather than undone (ch. 3, 13); a village's hidden bargain of one life per harvest (ch. 13); eerie body horror without gore; the hero's constant smoking; no sexual content, profanity or violence of note reported. No scene sexualizing a minor was found in sources opened.

No sexual content involving minors; Kaya (17) is a villain, not a romantic subject.

No sexual content involving minors and no nudity were reported in sources opened.

naruto.weigh: an outcast orphan who wins his village's respect through effort and loyalty (ch. 1-450); forgiveness of enemies and the breaking of a cycle of hatred (ch. 445-449, 693-699); constant ninja combat and many deaths, with sacrifice honored and revenge shown as a trap; a state-ordered massacre exposed (ch. 399-402); a demon fox sealed in a child, summoned spirits, a death-god cult (ch. 311-337) and reanimation of the dead as weapons; Pain and Kaguya as would-be gods; Buddhist and Hindu names (Six Paths, Indra, Ashura) and Shinto god-names as techniques; comic nudity by transformation (the "Sexy Technique," ch. 1 onward) and a mentor who peeps and writes erotic novels; drinking for laughs. Anime Corner and Uoto himself note that the persecution of heliocentrism is largely fiction.

ouran-high-school-host-club.weigh: a heroine who values honesty, study and frugality over wealth and status; a parody of flirtation and boys'-love tropes in which the hosts' romance is a performance; a crossdressing father shown as a loving parent, and other gender-nonconforming characters accepted; the twins' staged incest-themed flirting for customers, which the story outgrows as the twins seek independence; a family reconciliation won by honesty and Tamaki's patience with a cold grandmother (ch. 72-81); a chaste romance that ends in a couple (ch. 80-83); dated terms for Ranka in some translations and a stereotyped all-female club. No sexual content beyond kissing was found; the main characters are 15 to 17.

pet-shop-of-horrors.weigh: moral horror tales in which greed, vanity, obsession and cruelty to animals are punished, often by death; a supernatural shopkeeper who deals in desires and is hostile to humanity but grows attached to two brothers; Chinese mythic creatures, incense and magical contracts treated as real; frequent violent deaths, a serial killer, mafia and terrorists, and a 15-year-old hitman (ch. 25); buyers who see pets as ideal lovers and a womanizing detective; a strong pro-animal, pro-nature message whose extreme form (D's father's revenge on humanity) is shown as destructive; a child healed by family reconciliation. Content involving minors: a 15-year-old hitman (ch. 25), a child whose pets are killed (ch. 31) and the mute child Chris living at the shop; no sexual content involving minors was reported in sources opened.

No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened.

rave-master.weigh: a quest of light against an organization that uses evil stones to conquer (throughout); friendship and self-sacrifice (Gale, v9; Reina, v16; Shiba, v29); mercy toward enemies and many enemies redeemed (Shuda, Let, Sieg Hart, Iulius, Branch; Haru will not kill Lucia, v21); constant sword and magic combat with on-page deaths; magic stones, spirits of the dead, demon lords and a demon sword (v20-21) treated as fantasy powers; Elie's gambling played as a comic habit (v10 and throughout); a villain's suicide (King, v9); a romance that ends in marriage (v35). reborn.weigh: a timid, bullied boy who grows brave out of love for his friends; a crime family played as heroes, with an infant hitman, children carrying guns and dynamite, and a Russian roulette gag (ch. 6); a classmate's suicide attempt stopped by Tsuna (ch. 5); slapstick violence that becomes battle violence from ch. 61, with some deaths and Tsuna killing the villain Byakuran (ch. 279-288); Tsuna refusing to inherit the Vongola's past sins (ch. 154-164) and, at the end, the title of Mafia boss (ch. 402-409); reconciliation of feuding families (ch. 331-351); comic sexual harassment by an adult doctor, including an attempted kiss of 14-year-old Kyoko (ch. 15); a 14-year-old smoking; occult-flavored powers (illusions, possession, Buddhist-named "Six Paths"). One comic scene shows Kyoko and Haru, both about 14, stripped to underwear by the Dying Will Bullet (ch. 25, manga only); nothing more is reported in sources opened (see checklist).

requiem-of-the-rose-king.weigh: a tragedy in which revenge, ambition and murder destroy nearly everyone (Richard stabs Henry, v7; the purge of rivals, v9-13; the princes' murder, v15; Bosworth, v17); an intersex hero condemned as a demon by a pious mother, shown with sympathy (v1 onward); a gentle, devout king who refuses war and is broken by it; same-sex love (Richard with Henry and with Buckingham) shown sympathetically (v3-8, v13-16); sex outside marriage, adultery, an orgy scene (v8, ANN) and abuse of Henry by his wife (fan wiki; TV Tropes); witches, curses and Joan of Arc's ghost; repeated threats to expose and force the teenage Richard in early volumes (v1-3; Anime Feminist). Sexualized threat against Richard while he is a teenager is reported in early volumes (exposure of his body, a knife threat, a stolen-kiss attempt, v1-3); no on-page sex scene involving a minor is confirmed in sources opened (see checklist).

sengoku-youko.weigh: a peace-between-peoples message (humans and spirits as equals with the same kind of soul); a world of kami, fox spirits and spirit arts shown as real and mostly good; Buddhist warrior monks who experiment on people as the main human villains, later reformed; frequent sword and spirit battles with deaths; a girl sold by her father and fused with a spirit; a hero who chooses mercy and nonlethal liberation (Senya) and another who takes revenge (Shinsuke on Yazen); a comic undressing gag in front of a young boy and a lecherous master's backstory; heavy drinking by an adult hero shown as a flaw; three marriages at the end. No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened (see the checklist on the tanuki scene and on Mudo and Tsukiko).

seven-days.weigh: a gentle same-sex high school romance between a first-year and a third-year, carried by kisses, dates and feelings with no sex or nudity (Comic Book Bin; Teen rating); the critique of disposable dating, as Seryou's one-week rule hurts people and is given up for a committed relationship; honesty and vulnerability rewarded. For traditions that hold sexual relationships belong only in marriage between a man and a woman, the concern is the relationship the story celebrates, not explicit content.

shadows-house.weigh: a system that enslaves and brainwashes children, condemned; a mistress and servant who treat each other as persons and work to free others; truth uncovered by courage and planning; mind-altering drink and memory erasure as tools of control; a Doll's death from soot sickness and other deaths in the house; a suicide (Christopher) and a leap from a bridge (Maryrose and Rosemary) shown as tragedy; growing violence among adult Shadows in the final arc (ch. 231-241); no sexual content found. The series is ongoing, so the ending, and the means the rebels finally use, are not yet known.

shaman-king.weigh: heroes who are spirit mediums and channel the dead as their power (throughout); a Great Spirit that holds all souls and an afterlife pictured as Hell, the Great Spirit and reincarnation; a necromancer hero descended from Doctor Faustus (v5); Christian angel names used by violent zealots whose angels prove to be car spirits, while Buddhist spirits are shown as genuinely divine (v12-25); Takei's stated message that fighting is no good, and a climax won by forgiveness (kanzenban ch. 297-299); a child who tortures herself for justice (v14-25); an African American character whose original design resembled blackface caricature, and who is redeemed after killing as a gang leader (v13-24); constant non-gory battle violence and many deaths reversed by resurrection. No sexual content involving minors was reported in sources opened (see checklist on Jeanne's depiction).

The teen fan service is described plainly in Content scores; no sexual act involving minors was reported in sources opened, but see the checklist on the prologue bondage scene and ch. 75.

tamon-s-b-side.weigh: a fan who learns to care for the real, struggling person behind a star's image; depression, anxiety and a moment of hopelessness on a rooftop (likely vol. 3) met with care but often played for laughs; comic 'worship' of an idol (a home shrine, 'Tamon is god') that the story slowly turns into friendship; a chaste teen romance with mild innuendo (frosting licked from a cheek, staying the night at her family home, vol. 12); a young man following a girl home and a possessive streak played as romantic comedy (vol. 7); an adult bandmate's drinking, smoking and gambling played as comedy (vol. 6); family duty honored (Keito, Utage); forgiveness and reconciliation. No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened.

No sexual content beyond the kiss and no fan service were found in sources opened; the kiss involves a 16-year-old and is noted here plainly.

toriko.weigh: thanksgiving for food and for the lives taken (Food Honor; grace before and after meals); loyalty between hunter and chef and among adopted brothers; protecting people and ecosystems from greedy hunters; constant violent hunting and combat, with some gore; appetite and feasting celebrated, while a devouring appetite (Neo, Acacia) is the final evil; an invented religion whose worshipped founder proves to be a deceiver (ch. 369-396); a temple that teaches giving up desire (ch. 181-193); demons that live inside the heroes as a source of power; social drinking. The creator's 2002 criminal conviction is real-world context, not part of the story's message, and is not graded. No sexual content involving minors was found in sources opened.

uzumaki.weigh: an impersonal curse that destroys a town and cannot be resisted; obsession and fear shown as equally ruinous (ch. 1-2); a father's suicide and a mother's self-mutilation and death (ch. 1-2); graphic body horror, including monstrous pregnant women (ch. 10-11) and survivors eating transformed neighbors (ch. 15-16); a classmate's sexual pursuit of the hero, framed as horror (ch. 3, details unconfirmed); nothing evil made attractive; a loyal, chaste teenage romance that lasts to the end; and a bleak, cyclical ending (ch. 19). No sexual content involving a minor beyond the ch. 3 scene (see checklist) was reported by any source opened.
